design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study in Campinas, Brazil (two sessions, 14-day washout, order randomized, 12 people LSD first): 24 healthy adults with at least one previous LSD experience received LSD or placebo in the morning and did a neuropsychological battery the next morning: Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure, 2D object-location memory, Rey auditory-verbal learning, verbal fluency (letter, category, switching), design fluency, Wisconsin Card Sorting, Trail Making, Stroop and Block Design. Memory material for the object-location and word-list tasks was learned before dosing. Part of a larger study whose other measures are published elsewhere. Repeated-measures GLM (treatment within, order between), then with body mass index and time since last psychedelic use as covariates; exploratory, no correction for multiple tests.
can_establish: Whether one low laboratory dose of LSD, compared with placebo in the same people, shifts performance on standard thinking tests the next morning.
cannot_establish: Effects of higher, repeated or recreational doses; effects on mood, sleep or everyday functioning (not measured in this paper); effects after the next morning; or whether the scattered significant results are more than chance, given about 66 test variables without correction and results that depended on covariates.

sample.recruitment: Convenience sample of healthy volunteers screened by clinical and psychiatric interview, physical and mental state examination and a recent electrocardiogram (pp. 9-10).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 22 or older, at least one LSD experience, no psychedelics from two weeks before until the end of the study, no alcohol or other drugs for three days before each session, no tobacco or caffeine on study days. Excluded: psychiatric symptoms, personal or first-degree family history of psychotic disorder, psychiatric medication, severe complications after psychedelic use, alcohol or drug use disorder, heart disease or other relevant illness, pregnancy, not a native Brazilian Portuguese speaker (p. 9).
sample.demographics: Mean age 35 (SD 11, range 25-61); 8 women; on average 3 cups of coffee a day (SD 2, 0-6); one third smoked tobacco between every third day and several times a day (p. 9).
sample.attrition: One participant stopped after the first session for personal reasons; data from one or two people were lost on the object-location, word-list, verbal fluency and Stroop tasks through application errors (pp. 9-10).
sample.selection_effects: People with LSD experience and no psychiatric history volunteered; prior psychedelic use beyond the inclusion threshold is not described. The authors note that caffeine and tobacco habits, withheld on study days, mean a stimulating effect of LSD cannot be ruled out (p. 9).

exposure.measurement: Given orally by the investigators under double-blind conditions.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: a single 50 microgram dose of LSD dissolved in alcohol solution, or an inactive alcohol-solution placebo, diluted in 30 ml of water, given at 9:30 a.m.; participants left at 5:30 p.m. in the care of a relative or friend and returned at 8:00 a.m. the next day for testing, released around 10:00 a.m. (about 22.5 to 24.5 hours after dosing). Two sessions 14 days apart (pp. 9-10).
exposure.polysubstance: Abstinence rules by self-report: psychedelics from two weeks before, alcohol and other drugs three days before each session, no tobacco or caffeine on study days; no drug testing reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Same rules; not verified in this paper.

comparison.matching: Within-person comparison; parallel test versions balanced across participants and counterbalanced across treatments.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for the within-person comparison; frequency of earlier psychedelic use and sleep on the night after dosing are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same people under the same abstinence rules.

outcomes.instruments: ROCF copy, immediate and delayed recall; 2D Object-Location Memory Task consolidation; RAVLT consolidation and recognition; Verbal Fluency (phonological F-A-S, semantic animals, switching); Design Fluency (basic, filter, switch); Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (categories, errors, perseveration indices, conceptual level responses and their percentages); Trail Making A and B; Stroop (Victoria version); WASI Block Design (pp. 9-10).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard tests; Brazilian versions or norms cited for some (RAVLT, WASI, WCST manual). No baseline testing on the morning after each session, only the drug-placebo contrast.
outcomes.operationalization: Improvement or impairment = the next-morning difference between the LSD and placebo sessions in the adjusted GLM.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, stated as exploratory (p. 10). Editors' count of the variables listed in Methods: ROCF 6, object-location 2, word list 4, verbal fluency 9, design fluency 9, card sorting 20, Trail Making 5, Stroop 9, Block Design 2; each tested for treatment, order and period effects, with and without covariates.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The study is described as double-blind; blinding integrity is not reported in this paper, and whether the people scoring the tests knew the condition is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Partial eta squared for significant effects only, from the GLMs adjusted for body mass index and abstinence period (Table 1, p. 11). LSD against placebo: ROCF immediate recall points F(1,20) = 4.63, p = 0.044, 0.19, and percentage 6.62, p = 0.018, 0.25; object-location consolidation percentage F(1,19) = 6.23, p = 0.022, 0.25; letter fluency total 5.08, p = 0.036, 0.20, and correct 5.69, p = 0.027, 0.22; card sorting categories achieved 8.11, p = 0.010, 0.29 (fewer), total errors 7.86, p = 0.011, 0.28, perseverative responses 7.53, p = 0.013, 0.27, perseverative errors type 3 9.55, p = 0.006, 0.32, and ten further card-sorting indices at p 0.004 to 0.031. Means appear only in Fig. 1 (estimated marginal means with SEM) and supplementary Table S3; values were not extracted.
analysis.covariates: Body mass index and time since last psychedelic use, added after the unadjusted models (p. 10), justified as proxies for dose and washout.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration or protocol is mentioned in the paper.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 lists only significant and two marginal effects from the adjusted models; the unadjusted results are in supplementary Table S2 (not read), and the Limitations state that the unadjusted analyses yielded few treatment effects and many period effects (p. 15).
analysis.power: Not addressed; the authors call for replication with larger samples (p. 15).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In adjusted models, the morning after one low dose of LSD people did somewhat better than after placebo on two visual memory measures and on letter fluency, and worse on the card-sorting test of flexibility (fewer categories, more errors and perseveration); about a dozen other tests did not differ; practice effects were large and the unadjusted models showed few treatment effects.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the low dose moderately induced both afterglow and hangover and that the memory and fluency improvements suggest LSD-assisted therapy should be explored for brain injury, stroke or dementia (p. 8); the discussion adds that impaired flexibility may call for a rest day after therapeutic or recreational use (p. 15). Both rest on uncorrected, covariate-dependent differences in 24 healthy volunteers, from a study that measured no clinical population and no everyday functioning; the authors acknowledge the multiplicity, practice effects and covariate dependence in the Limitations (p. 15).

timeline.event: This study: by the authors' account the first placebo-controlled study of next-day cognition after a psychedelic.
Evens et al.: systematic review of the days after classic psychedelics (afterglow), mostly mood and wellbeing measures.

replication.where_it_stands: Single exploratory study, not replicated; companion papers from the same sessions (creativity, stream of thought, psychosis-like experiences) report other measures and share the sample, so they are not independent evidence.

funding.funder: Beckley Foundation, which supported the implementation of the study and whose director is a co-author; CAPES (Finance Code 001); CNPq (grants 308775/2015-5 and 408145/2016-1); Sao Paulo Research Foundation (grants 2013/07699-0 and 2014/10068-4). The funders are stated to have had no further role in design, analysis, writing or submission (p. 16).
funding.declared_conflicts: One author declares a pending patent application (applicants the Beckley Foundation and the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte; application number 1 911 024.6) (p. 16).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Campinas (ICARO), Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte, Beckley Foundation. The director of the funding foundation reviewed the manuscript as a co-author.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered placebo-controlled crossover study with more participants, a small set of prespecified next-day outcomes (memory, flexibility, mood, sleep) with correction for multiple tests, a pre-dose baseline on each session, a blinding check, and doses closer to those people use.

domains.note: Order was randomized (12 LSD first), but sequence generation and concealment are not described; within-person comparison limits the impact.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Described as double-blind, but a noticeable dose was chosen deliberately and blinding was not checked, so expectations may have differed between sessions.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A randomized placebo-controlled crossover with objective tests, which is the right design for the question, but the reported effects come from an unregistered analysis choice (adding between-person covariates to a within-person comparison) among many uncorrected tests. The study can be cited for what was found the morning after one low dose in 24 experienced volunteers, as exploratory and unreplicated; not for lasting or clinical benefit, and not for the absence of effects on the tests that did not differ.

reporting_issues.consequence: The impairment summary in the abstract overstates the consistency of the card-sorting results.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 is titled as listing the significant effects but includes two results with p = 0.058 and p = 0.056.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says testing took place 24 h after dosing; the procedure gives dosing at 9:30 a.m. and next-day testing from 8:00 to about 10:00 a.m.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: about 22.5 to 24.5 hours.

design_detail: Pooled analysis of the raw data of nine double-blind crossover laboratory studies of LSD at the University Hospital Basel (2014-2023), eight of them with a placebo session: 213 healthy volunteers, 297 LSD-alone sessions and 189 placebo sessions (sessions combining LSD with another substance excluded). Two studies gave several doses to the same people. The paper asks which characteristics measured before dosing predict the acute response. The predictors vary between people and were not randomized, so the analysis is observational; the paper does not say whether session order was randomized in the source studies. Each of 19 predictors was related to each of 29 response variables (differences between the LSD and the placebo session) in linear mixed models with a random intercept for participant, adjusted for the dose given, with standardized coefficients, semi-partial R2 and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across 551 tests; LASSO models ranked predictors; a sensitivity analysis kept one dose per study (the dose closest to 100 µg; 213 sessions). All coefficients are in Figure 1 (an image) and Supplementary Table S4; the main text gives directions and significance only.
can_establish: Which characteristics measured before dosing were associated, at a given dose, with the size of LSD's acute subjective and autonomic effects relative to placebo in healthy volunteers mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room with one investigator present (some sessions with MRI scanning), and which predictors penalized regression ranked as most important.
cannot_establish: How large any association other than dose is (the main text gives no coefficients, intervals or variance shares, and the figure holding them could not be viewed); whether mood or personality cause the differences; anything about people with psychiatric disorders or about settings other than a hospital room (setting barely varied: an MRI scan was the only setting variable); or whether sex matters (significant for several outcomes in the main analysis; women's less positive experience not significant in the sensitivity analysis, and the temperature difference not reported there).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers recruited from the University of Basel campus into nine studies, each registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01878942, NCT02308969, NCT03019822, NCT03321136, NCT03604744, NCT04227756, NCT04516902, NCT04558294, NCT04865653), eight previously published (Methods and materials › Study design, 1st paragraph; Subjects, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy participants; the exclusion criteria are given only in the supplement, which was not read.
sample.demographics: Age 25-64 (mean 32, SD 9); 108 women; body weight 70 (SD 12) kg, range 50-104. Previous hallucinogen experience is a predictor; its distribution is in a supplementary figure (not read).
sample.attrition: Not reported. Missing predictor and response data were imputed in ways described in the supplement (Table S2, not read).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy, screened campus volunteers, with exclusion criteria not stated in the main text; the authors note that psychedelic studies may attract people high in openness. People with mental disorders, for whom the predictors matter most in therapy, are outside the sample.

exposure.measurement: Characteristics measured before dosing (19 predictors): sex, age, body weight, the dose given (also the covariate), CYP2D6 genetic activity score, number of previous hallucinogen experiences, whether the session included an MRI scan, mood before intake on the Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AMRS: performance-related activity, general inactivation, extraversion, introversion, general well-being, emotional excitability, anxiety) and personality on the NEO Five-Factor Inventory (neuroticism, extraversion, openness to experience, agreeableness, conscientiousness). Details are in the supplement (Methods and materials › Predictor variables, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one oral dose of LSD base per session, 25, 50, 100 or 200 µg nominal, as gelatin capsules or as a drinking solution in ethanol; analytically confirmed amounts 26-197 µg, except in the first two studies, where each person's dose was estimated from the area under their plasma LSD curve. Session conditions: participants mostly in a bed in a quiet hospital room with a single investigator present; music was mostly present but neither restricted nor recorded; some sessions included MRI scanning (Methods and materials › Study drug, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 8th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Sessions combining LSD with another substance were excluded from the analysis; drug-use screening and abstinence rules are in the supplement (not read).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not described in the main text.

comparison.controls: The placebo session of the same person in eight of nine studies; responses are LSD-minus-placebo differences (peak change from placebo for vital signs; area under the effect-time curve, 0-11.5 h, for ratings). Study #8 had no placebo session, and the main text does not say how its differences were formed. For the predictors, the comparison is between people.
comparison.matching: Each predictor adjusted for dose only; predictors were not adjusted for one another except in the LASSO models and in supplementary full models (not read). Random intercept for participant; no term for study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Expectations, motivation and the music played were not measured. Differences between studies (years 2014-2023, capsule or solution, co-administration designs, MRI) are not modelled except through the MRI predictor.

outcomes.instruments: Visual analogue scales (including any, good and bad drug effect); the 5D-ASC total, dimensions and subscales (among them oceanic boundlessness, anxious ego dissolution, visionary restructuralization, auditory alteration, vigilance reduction, experience of unity, spiritual experience, blissful state, insightfulness, disembodiment, impaired control and cognition, changed meaning of percepts, elementary imagery, audio-visual synesthesia, anxiety); the MEQ30 total and subscales (mystical, positive mood, transcendence of time and space); peak change in mean arterial pressure, heart rate and body temperature; and plasma LSD area under the curve (0 to infinity). Ratings by the participant (Methods and materials › Response variables, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Validated instruments routinely used in this laboratory; norms are not needed for within-person differences.
outcomes.operationalization: All responses are continuous LSD-minus-placebo differences. 'Bad drug effect' is a visual analogue rating that, the authors note, covers any negative state including nausea; challenging experiences are represented by 5D-ASC anxious ego dissolution, anxiety and impaired control and cognition. No thresholds are used.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction across all 551 tests (19 predictors by 29 responses; Figure 1 legend); the text describes associations that were significant after correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind; the authors acknowledge that blinding is a recognized problem with psychoactive substances and that expectations may influence subjective effects (Discussion, 7th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Not given in the main text: standardized coefficients, corrected p values and semi-partial R2 are in Figure 1 (an image; the figure image was not viewable in this reading) and Supplementary Table S4 (not read). The text reports direction and significance after correction, and for LASSO the number of predictors selected per response (12 on average, range 8-14) and the number of responses for which dose had the largest coefficient (21 of 29). No sizes can be quoted for any non-dose predictor from the main text.
analysis.covariates: The dose given (in every model except those of dose); random intercept per participant.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The nine source studies are registered (numbers above); the pooled analysis is not described as preregistered.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 551 adjusted tests are said to be shown in Figure 1 and listed in Table S4; supplementary full models and restricted cubic-spline dose models are described as giving largely the same results (not read). The summary statements on sex and body weight rest on the sensitivity analysis for sex, while the other conclusions rest on the main analysis.
analysis.power: No power calculation; 297 sessions from 213 people.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At a given LSD dose, in healthy volunteers in a hospital room, higher general well-being rated just before dosing went with stronger subjective effects (the Discussion's summary; significant for nearly every scale, the anxiety-type scales included, with directions per scale only in Figure 1); anxiety rated just before dosing went with higher 5D-ASC anxiety and, with emotional excitability and general inactivation, with heart rate; openness went with more oceanic boundlessness, spiritual experience, insightfulness and MEQ30 mystical and positive-mood scores; extraversion with more visual and auditory alteration; previous hallucinogen experience with a smaller overall altered state and less anxious ego dissolution; lower CYP2D6 activity with higher plasma LSD and more anxious ego dissolution; older age with more bad drug effect and higher body weight with less; women with smaller increases in good drug effect, experience of unity, insightfulness, MEQ30 positive mood and body temperature. Neuroticism, agreeableness and conscientiousness showed no significant association with any effect. Dose was the strongest predictor of everything except body temperature. Sizes are not reported in the text.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract ends that sex and body weight “were not significant factors in influencing the drug experience”, which contradicts the main analysis (sex: four subjective outcomes and body temperature; body weight: bad drug effect) and rests, for sex, on the sensitivity analysis. The Discussion infers that acute effects are profoundly influenced by pre-drug disposition, and that LSD's autonomic effects stem mainly from psychological arousal rather than a direct cardiostimulant action, causal readings of between-person associations whose sizes the text does not give; it then speculates about pharmacological preparation and about the order and size of doses across sessions before psychedelic therapy, none of which this analysis tested (not reproduced here). The Results say MRI sessions went with more impaired control and cognition, while the Discussion says MRI went with more elementary imagery and no more anxiety.

timeline.event: Studerus et al. pooled psilocybin laboratory studies to find predictors of response; this paper compares its findings (extraversion-like traits and visual effects, emotional excitability; but not well-being or anxiety before dosing, which did not predict psilocybin response there).
Haijen et al., prospective online study: feeling prepared and ready before use predicted fewer challenging experiences, which this paper calls consistent with its pre-dose anxiety finding.
Aday et al. systematic review of pre-drug predictors, cited here.
Studerus et al., the same approach for MDMA in 194 volunteers from the same laboratory, sharing one source study (NCT03019822); this paper says 'set' was far less influential for MDMA.
This analysis.

replication.where_it_stands: The largest pooled laboratory analysis of predictors of the LSD response found for this page. It comes from the laboratory that ran all the source studies and shares authors and one study with the MDMA analysis. The direction of its findings on pre-dose mood and openness agrees with the psilocybin analysis it cites and, for pre-dose anxiety, with Haijen (2018), but no independent laboratory has repeated it, and the sizes must be taken from Supplementary Table S4 before any claim states one.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered multi-site study with placebo-controlled sessions in several settings (laboratory, clinic, supervised naturalistic) that measures mood, expectations and personality before dosing, reports effect sizes with intervals in the main text, and tests whether mood and personality improve prediction beyond dose in data not used to build the model; and randomized trials that change pre-dose preparation to test whether the mood association is causal.

domains.note: Each predictor was adjusted only for dose; correlated predictors (mood scales, personality traits, age and experience) were not adjusted for one another in the inferential models; study-level differences were not modelled, and the MRI predictor is entangled with the studies that used MRI. Adequate for prediction, not for the causal wording of the Discussion.

Standardized sessions; sessions with co-administered substances excluded. Music was not controlled but was present in most sessions.
Provisional: imputation methods and amounts are in the supplement (not read), and one study had no placebo session although every response is defined as a difference from placebo.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As for the MDMA analysis by the same group (sc_studerus_2021) and the editors' card for Schmid et al. (2016), the question is answered by between-person comparisons that were not randomized, so ROBINS-E is used even though the source studies were double-blind and placebo-controlled. Measurement before dosing is good and correction for multiple tests is applied; the concerns are adjustment for dose only, no study-level term, a partly circular dose estimate in two studies, an unexplained placebo difference for one study, and the absence of effect sizes from the text. The source can be cited for the direction of associations in healthy volunteers in a hospital room: higher pre-dose well-being with stronger subjective effects, pre-dose anxiety with more acute anxiety, openness with more mystical-type and oceanic effects, previous hallucinogen experience with less anxious ego dissolution, and lower CYP2D6 activity with higher blood levels; sizes need Supplementary Table S4. It should not be cited for causal effects of mood or personality, for patients, for settings outside a laboratory, or as showing that sex and body weight do not matter.

key_findings.finding: Design facts: nine crossover studies (2014-2023), 213 healthy volunteers (108 women; age 25-64, mean 32), 297 LSD-alone and 189 placebo sessions; one oral LSD dose per session of 25 to 200 µg nominal (26-197 µg confirmed), as study conditions; participants mostly in a bed in a quiet hospital room with one investigator present, music mostly playing but not recorded.

key_findings.finding: Analysis: 19 predictors by 29 responses (551 tests), each response the difference between the LSD and placebo sessions; mixed models with a random intercept per participant, adjusted for dose; Benjamini-Hochberg correction; N = 297 sessions in Figure 1.
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials › Response variables, 1st paragraph; Statistical analyses, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Fig. 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Dose was the strongest predictor of every LSD effect except body temperature, most strongly of plasma LSD, VAS any drug effect and the 5D-ASC total; LASSO selected dose for all 29 responses (12 predictors per response on average, range 8-14) and dose had the largest coefficient for 21. Body temperature was predicted only by sex (women had smaller changes) and by emotional excitability before dosing.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: General well-being rated on the AMRS before dosing was the second strongest predictor of subjective effects, significant for all of them except VAS bad drug effect, 5D-ASC changed meaning of percepts and MEQ30 positive mood; strongest for the 5D-ASC total, VAS good drug effect and oceanic boundlessness; in LASSO it ranked first for good drug effect, vigilance reduction, spiritual experience and blissful state.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th and 7th paragraphs
key_findings.note: By the text, the scales significantly associated with pre-dose well-being include the 5D-ASC anxious ego dissolution and anxiety scales (every subjective scale except three), and the Discussion (1st paragraph) says subjective effects were more pronounced with higher pre-dose well-being, and also with higher pre-dose anxiety; the direction scale by scale is only in Figure 1 (not viewable). The text therefore does not show that a better mood before dosing went with a less challenging session.

design_detail: Secondary analysis of the Global Drug Survey (GDS) 2017, an anonymous, self-nominating online survey open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages (119,108 respondents). People who reported LSD use in the last 12 months (13,769) were asked whether they had sought emergency medical treatment (EMT) after LSD in that year; 10,293 answered, and the 102 who said yes completed a specialist section on the incident (symptoms ticked from a list of 20, number of doses, other substances, time to feel back to normal, hospital admission, perceived reasons, change in use). EMT seekers and the others were compared with univariate Mann–Whitney and chi-square tests. Companion paper on magic mushrooms from the same survey and authors: kopra_2022.
can_establish: How often respondents to a large self-selected online drug survey who had used LSD in the past year reported seeking emergency medical treatment afterwards (102 of 10,293), how those 102 described the incident, its course and its perceived causes, and which respondent characteristics went with reporting it.
cannot_establish: The risk among all people who use LSD or per real-world occasion (no sampling frame; incidents per person not recorded); whether the drug taken was LSD (nothing was tested, and about 13 of the 102 named 'not LSD' among the reasons); whether the reported symptoms, hospital admissions and lasting problems happened as described or were caused by LSD (no records; two-thirds had taken another substance); deaths; or any causal effect of age, mental health or frequency of use.

sample.recruitment: Self-nominating online sample: the GDS is advertised on social networking sites in collaboration with media partners and harm-reduction organizations; anonymous, encrypted, in 10 languages, no payment (p. 957, Methods › Design, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). The 13,769 people who reported past-year use lived mainly in Germany (19.7%), the USA (19.6%), the UK (8.2%), Denmark (7.5%), Canada (5.8%) and Australia (5.0%), with 34.1% elsewhere (Table 1, p. 958).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All GDS 2017 respondents who reported LSD use in the last 12 months; no exclusions for other drug use or mental health. Each analysis used complete cases for its variables (p. 958, Data analysis, 4th paragraph).
sample.demographics: People who reported past-year use (n=13,769): 63.9% under 25, 28.1% aged 25–34, 7.9% 35 or older; 79.6% men and 20.4% women (no other category shown); of 8208 answering, 84.8% White, 6.5% Hispanic/Latino, 4.7% mixed; of 8335 answering, 26.2% reported a lifetime mental health diagnosis (depression 19.0%, anxiety 13.4%, ADHD 6.3%, bipolar 2.6%, psychosis 1.2%); 33.3% had used in the last month; median 2 days of use in the past year (IQR 1–5) (Table 1, p. 958; answering totals are editors' sums of the table rows). The 102 EMT seekers are described by age (median 21, IQR 18–25) and by the predictor percentages only (p. 959).
sample.attrition: Not a follow-up study, but item non-response is large: 10,293 of 13,769 past-year respondents (74.8%, editors' calculation) answered the EMT question (Figure 1, p. 959). Unlike the mushroom companion paper, no analysis of survey completers is reported. The drop-out finding the authors cite as reassurance comes from a different survey: Hübner et al. (2020), an attrition analysis of the prospective psychedelic survey of Haijen et al. (2018), in which neither baseline attitudes towards psychedelics nor the intensity of challenging experiences predicted drop-out; the authors say this could theoretically apply to GDS respondents who do not finish the psychedelic sections (p. 962, Discussion, 10th paragraph; reference list, p. 963). The mental health test used N=8299. Time to recovery was answered by 98 of 102 (editors' reading of Figure 2 and of the 59.2% and 11.2% in the text); the hospital-admission share of 54.5% implies 101 or 99 answers.
sample.selection_effects: Self-nominated respondents reached through GDS media partners, social networks and harm-reduction organizations: mostly young, male and White, which the authors say limits generalization and may partly reflect the survey's reach (p. 961, Discussion, 9th paragraph). There is no sampling frame and no response rate. People who died or were too unwell to take part are outside the design. The authors note that psychedelic surveys may attract people with positive attitudes, but argue a general drug survey is less affected (p. 962). The incident details come only from the 102 who said yes.

exposure.measurement: Self-report only: time since last use; days of use in the last 12 months; first use in the last 12 months; number of doses normally taken on a day of use; and, for EMT seekers, the number of doses in the incident session and any other substances (pp. 957–958, Methods › Measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Nothing was tested; the authors note that NBOMes and other LSD analogues, linked to deaths and serious poisonings, may have been taken as LSD in some incidents (p. 962, Discussion, 11th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Recorded here only as study conditions. Past-year frequency: median 2 days (IQR 1–5) in the whole past-year group (Table 1); mean 5.21 days (SD 11.60) among the 10,293 who answered the EMT item, the basis of the per-event estimate (p. 958). Doses on a usual day of use: median 1.0 (IQR 1.0–2.0) in both EMT seekers and others (p. 959). EMT seekers reported a median of 2.0 doses (IQR 1.0–3.0) in the incident session (p. 959). The authors call 'number of doses' vague, with high variability within each answer (p. 962). Route is not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Asked only of EMT seekers, about the incident session (Table 3, p. 960): 33 of 102 (32.4%) had taken nothing else; the others reported cannabis 51 (50.0%), alcohol 24 (23.5%), MDMA 12 (11.8%), benzodiazepines 6, cocaine 5, amphetamine 4, other 4, new psychoactive substances 3, ketamine 2, and 2C-B, mephedrone and opioids 1 each. No figure is reported for sessions without EMT. The authors note that the causal role of these substances is unclear, since some people may have taken them to relieve anxiety (p. 961, Discussion, 7th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (retrospective survey covering the previous 12 months).

comparison.controls: Within the sample: the 10,191 EMT-item respondents who did not report EMT seeking, compared with the 102 who did, on age, sex, lifetime mental health diagnosis, first use in the past year, doses per day of use and past-year frequency. No group without LSD use; the comparison with magic mushrooms comes from the companion paper (kopra_2022).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Personality, earlier difficult experiences, setting and company on the day, and current medication are not reported; the authors raise drug–drug interactions with psychiatric medication as a possible contributor (p. 961, Discussion, 6th paragraph), but no data on medication are reported. Mental health entered the analysis only as a lifetime diagnosis, and specific diagnoses could not be compared (p. 961).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported for people who did not seek EMT.

outcomes.instruments: One self-report item on seeking EMT after LSD in the past 12 months; EMT is not defined in the paper and the number of incidents per person was not recorded (pp. 957–958, Methods › Measures, 1st paragraph). EMT seekers then ticked symptoms from a list of 20 compiled from the literature, gave the number of doses in that session, other substances, duration of symptoms and whether they were hospitalized, chose up to 3 of 6 reasons, and reported any change in their use (p. 958, Methods › Measures, 2nd paragraph). Recovery categories ran from 6 h to more than 4 weeks, plus not recovered (Figure 2, p. 960).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation of any item is reported. The authors state that the survey did not define hospital admission (p. 960). Two multiple correspondence analyses of symptoms and reasons are shown as factor maps only in supplementary figures, which were not among the files; the Results describe the groupings in words (p. 959).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm was operationalized as self-reported seeking of emergency medical treatment; severity only through self-reported hospital admission (undefined) and time to feel back to normal.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six predictor tests; age (p=0.003) and mental health diagnosis (p<0.001) would stay below a Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/6 = 0.008, past-year frequency (p=0.029) would not (editors' calculation).

analysis.effect_sizes: 102 of 10,293 (1.0%) reported seeking EMT in the past year; editors' Wilson 95% CI 0.82% to 1.20% (about 1 in 100 respondents, editors' calculation). Per-event estimate: 102 divided by 53,627 estimated days of use (mean 5.21 × 10,293) = 0.001902, given as 0.2% of past-year uses (about 1 in 526 days of use, editors' calculation) (p. 958). Predictors (p. 959): age median 21 (IQR 18–25) vs 22 (IQR 19–27), Mann–Whitney z=2.96, p=0.003; lifetime mental health diagnosis 1.8% vs 0.7%, χ2(1, N=8299)=19.33, p<0.001 (ratio about 2.6, phi about 0.05, editors' calculation); men 1.0% vs women 0.9%, χ2(1, N=10,293)=0.12, p=0.725; first use in the past year 1.0% vs 1.0%, χ2(1, N=10,235)=0.04, p=0.845; doses per day of use median 1.0 vs 1.0, z=0.914, p=0.361; past-year frequency median 3.0 (IQR 2.0–8.5) vs 2.0 (IQR 1.0–5.0), z=2.18, p=0.029. No intervals or effect sizes are printed for any comparison.
analysis.covariates: None: univariate tests only; age, mental health and frequency were not examined together, so their associations may overlap.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is reported; the authors describe the study as an exploratory analysis (p. 957, Introduction, 5th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Recovery times and two of the six reasons are given only in figures without values (read by the editors; see key findings). Hospital admission is given only as 54.5%, with no count. The change-in-use categories leave about a fifth of EMT seekers undescribed. The two multiple correspondence analyses are described in words in the Results (psychological versus physiological symptom groupings; wrong setting and wrong mindset commonly reported together, p. 959), but their methods and factor maps are only in the supplement, which was not among the files.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The authors state that the sample gave enough cases and power to establish predictors (p. 961, Discussion, 8th paragraph) but did not allow comparison between mental health conditions (p. 961, Discussion, 5th paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a self-selected online sample, 102 of 10,293 people (1.0%) who had used LSD in the past year and answered the question reported seeking emergency medical treatment afterwards (0.19% per day of use by the authors' calculation, counting each person once). Reporting it was more common with a lifetime mental health diagnosis (1.8% vs 0.7%), at younger age (median 21 vs 22) and with more days of use (median 3 vs 2 a year). Among the 102, anxiety/panic (70%), confusion (65%) and paranoia (49%) were commonest, but 21 reported thoughts or acts of self-harm, 17 an accident or trauma, 13 seizures and 12 passing out, none verified; 54.5% reported hospital admission (undefined). Of 98 who answered, 58 felt back to normal within 24 hours, 17 took longer than a week, and 11 still had problems after 4 weeks, 6 of whom reported not having recovered. Two-thirds had taken another substance, half of all seekers cannabis.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the final paragraph conclude that LSD is “a relatively safe drug in recreational settings” and that adverse reactions are “typically short-lived, self-limiting and psychological in nature” (pp. 956, 962). Gaps: (1) the paper's own figures sit uneasily with 'short-lived, self-limiting': 40 of 98 took longer than 24 hours, 17 longer than a week, 11 still had problems after 4 weeks, and over half reported hospital admission, which the authors themselves call surprising and undefined (p. 960); (2) 'psychological in nature' leaves out that about a fifth reported self-harm thoughts or acts and about one in eight seizures or passing out, though none was verified; (3) 'relatively safe' has no comparison drug within this paper, and deaths and people unable to answer are outside the design; (4) the abstract's statement that screening, preparatory sessions and supervision in clinical settings “should reduce these acute risks considerably” was not studied; (5) the Discussion's suggestion that incidents may be preventable with policy focused more on harm reduction and less on criminalization (p. 960) rests on respondents' choices among six fixed reasons; (6) the abstract gives the per-event 0.2% without the authors' own caveat that it is an underestimate (p. 962). A headline saying that only 1% of people who take LSD end up in the emergency room, and that it is all short-lived panic, would overstate the data. The limitations section is candid about sampling, recall, unknown substance content, possible false alarms and unrecorded repeat incidents (pp. 961–962).

timeline.event: Leonard et al., exposures to LSD and psilocybin mushrooms reported to US poison centres 2000–2016, cited as including some EMT visits with no symptoms raised by concerned relatives; read here only as cited (p. 962).
GDS 2019 key findings report (Winstock et al., 2019): 0.9% of respondents who used LSD in the past year reported EMT seeking, as cited (p. 959); same survey programme and team, report not read.

GDS key findings reports for 2020 and 2021 (Winstock et al., 2021): 1.0% (GDS 2020, data from 2019) and 0.8% (GDS 2021), with falls across most substances that the authors link to the pandemic, as cited (pp. 959, 962); report not read.
Companion paper from the same GDS 2017 data on magic mushrooms: 19 of 9233 (0.2%) reported EMT seeking, and a lifetime mental health diagnosis was not associated with it there.

replication.where_it_stands: The headline rate of about 1% recurred in later waves of the same survey according to the authors (same team and method, grey-literature reports not read here); the incident details, recovery times and predictors come from this single wave. No validation of the self-reported EMT item against hospital or ambulance records is reported.

what_would_settle_it: Linkage of emergency-department, ambulance and poison-centre records to a population survey that counts use occasions in the same area and period, recording every incident per person, with laboratory confirmation of what was taken (LSD or an analogue such as an NBOMe) and follow-up for weeks to months; this would give a per-occasion risk with a known denominator, verified outcomes and a defined measure of lasting harm.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame: self-nominated GDS respondents reached through social media, media partners and harm-reduction organizations, while the target is people who use LSD in general.
Self-nominating convenience sample (p. 957).

10,293 respondents give a precise headline proportion (Wilson 0.82% to 1.20%, editors' calculation) and 102 events allow a rough description of incidents, though shares among the 102 carry intervals of up to about plus or minus 10 points.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The past-year group is described by age, sex, country, ethnicity, diagnoses and use (Table 1); the EMT seekers only by age and the predictor percentages, and where and what kind of emergency care they sought is not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 10,293 of 13,769 (75%) answered the EMT item and no completer analysis is reported in this paper; the mental health test used 8299; recovery time has about 98 of 102 answers and hospital admission an unstated number; complete-case analyses throughout.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: One face-valid but undefined and unvalidated self-report item over a 12-month recall period, with the respondent attributing the incident to LSD although nothing was tested; symptoms ticked from an unvalidated list and not verified; hospital admission undefined (p. 960).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same online items for everyone, but in 10 languages without any described translation check; reliability not assessed.

No interval for the headline proportion or any comparison; a per-event estimate that assumes one incident per person and equal risk on every day of use (the authors call it an underestimate); univariate tests only, so age, mental health and frequency are not separated.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed
domains.note: Open online survey with no denominator of people invited; item non-response on the EMT question is judged under item 5.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist (editors' summary: high risk of bias) because what the encyclopedia uses are the proportion reporting EMT seeking and the shares describing the incidents. As an estimate for people who use LSD in general, the 1.0% could be biased in either direction: the sample has no frame, the outcome is an undefined self-report, the substance was not confirmed, and people who died, were badly harmed or did not answer are not represented. As a description of this sample the counts are consistent and the limitations are stated. The source may be cited for the proportion of GDS 2017 respondents who reported seeking EMT after LSD (102 of 10,293), how those 102 described their incidents and recovery, and the univariate associations with mental health diagnosis, younger age and frequency of use. It may not be cited for a population risk per occasion, for causes of the reported symptoms, or for safety beyond self-reported help-seeking.

key_findings.finding: 119,108 respondents took part in GDS 2017; 26,601 (22.3%) reported lifetime LSD use and 13,769 (51.8% of them) use in the last 12 months; 10,293 of these answered the EMT question.
key_findings.locator: Results › Frequency and risk of EMT incidents, 1st paragraph (p. 958); Figure 1 (p. 959)

key_findings.finding: 102 of the 10,293 who answered (1.0%) reported having sought emergency medical treatment after LSD use in the past year.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 956); Results › Frequency and risk of EMT incidents, 1st paragraph (p. 958)
key_findings.note: Editors' Wilson 95% CI 0.82% to 1.20%, about 1 in 100 respondents. The abstract presents the 10,293 as the past-year group; 13,769 reported past-year use and 10,293 answered this item.

key_findings.finding: Per-event estimate: among the 10,293, mean days of LSD use in the past year was 5.21 (SD 11.60), giving an estimated 53,627 days of use; 102 divided by this is 0.001902, which the authors give as 0.2% of past-year uses.
key_findings.locator: Results › Frequency and risk of EMT incidents, 2nd paragraph; Data analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: About 1 in 526 days of use (editors' calculation). The authors state that this is an underestimate because the calculation assumes one incident per person, the number of incidents not having been recorded (p. 962, Discussion, 11th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: EMT seekers were younger (median 21, IQR 18–25, vs 22, IQR 19–27; Mann–Whitney z=2.96, p=0.003). EMT seeking was more common among people with a lifetime mental health diagnosis (1.8% vs 0.7%; χ2(1, N=8299)=19.33, p<0.001) and did not differ by sex (men 1.0%, women 0.9%; χ2(1, N=10,293)=0.12, p=0.725).
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors of EMT seeking, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: No effect sizes or intervals are printed; the ratio of the mental health percentages is about 2.6 and phi about 0.05 (editors' calculation). The authors call the age differences in this and earlier studies small (p. 961, Discussion, 4th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: EMT seeking did not differ by first use in the past year (1.0% vs 1.0%; χ2(1, N=10,235)=0.04, p=0.845) or by doses per day of use (median 1.0, IQR 1.0–2.0, in both groups; z=0.914, p=0.361); EMT seekers reported more days of use in the past year (median 3.0, IQR 2.0–8.5, vs 2.0, IQR 1.0–5.0; z=2.18, p=0.029).
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors of EMT seeking, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The frequency association would not survive a Bonferroni correction for the six tests (0.05/6 = 0.008; editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Symptoms ticked by the 102 EMT seekers (median 5.0, IQR 2.0–7.0): anxiety/panic 71 (69.6%), confusion 66 (64.7%), paranoia/suspiciousness 50 (49.0%), seeing/hearing things 46 (45.1%), extreme agitation 40 (39.2%), memory loss 29 (28.4%), extreme sweating 27 (26.5%), palpitations 26 (25.5%), very low mood in the days afterwards 23 (22.5%), thoughts or acts of self-harm 21 (20.6%), difficulty breathing 21 (20.6%), aggression/violence 18 (17.6%), nausea/vomiting 18 (17.6%), accident/trauma 17 (16.7%), other 16 (15.7%), chest pain 13 (12.7%), fits/seizures 13 (12.7%), passed out/unconscious 12 (11.8%), headache 7 (6.9%), bladder/kidney problems 4 (3.9%).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Self-reported and unverified; the authors note it is unknown which symptoms were induced by LSD rather than other drugs taken (p. 962, Discussion, 13th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: 54.5% of EMT seekers reported being admitted to hospital; the authors call this surprising and note that the survey did not define hospital admission.
key_findings.locator: Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 2nd paragraph (p. 959); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 960)
key_findings.note: No count is printed; 54.5% is not a whole number of 102 (it fits 55 of 101 or 54 of 99; editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Of those who answered, 59.2% felt back to normal within 24 h, while 11.2% had ongoing consequences more than 4 weeks after taking LSD; the abstract gives this as 11 participants with persistent issues after 4 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 2nd paragraph (p. 959); Abstract, Results (p. 956)
key_findings.note: The percentages fit 58 and 11 of 98 respondents (editors' calculation); the denominator is not printed.

key_findings.finding: Cumulative number back to normal (editors' reading of Figure 2, which prints no values; 98 respondents): 27 by 6 h, 42 by 12 h, 50 by 18 h, 58 by 24 h, 66 by 48 h, 72 by 72 h, 77 by 96 h, 81 by 5–7 days, 85 by 1–2 weeks, 87 by 2–4 weeks, 92 after more than 4 weeks, and 6 marked not recovered.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2
key_findings.note: Point heights measured on a 300-dpi rendering against the gridlines; every point falls on a whole number of 98 and matches the text's 59.2% and 11.2%. The 11 with consequences beyond 4 weeks are 5 who recovered after more than 4 weeks and 6 who had not recovered when they answered; how long before the survey their incident happened is not known.

key_findings.finding: EMT seekers reported a median of 2.0 doses (IQR 1.0–3.0) in the session that led to EMT, against a median of 1.0 (IQR 1.0–2.0) on a usual day of use; the authors call the number of doses vague, with high variability within each answer.
key_findings.locator: Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 3rd paragraph; Results › Predictors of EMT seeking, 2nd paragraph (p. 959); Discussion, 11th paragraph (p. 962)
key_findings.note: Study conditions as reported, not a dose–risk relation. The Discussion says doses in sessions leading to EMT were higher than usual (p. 961), but no test of this within-person difference is reported, and the incident-session dose has no counterpart for people who did not seek EMT.

key_findings.finding: In the session that led to EMT, 33 of 102 (32.4%) had taken nothing else; the others reported cannabis 51 (50.0%), alcohol 24 (23.5%), MDMA 12 (11.8%), benzodiazepines 6 (5.9%), cocaine 5 (4.9%), amphetamine 4 (3.9%), other 4 (3.9%), new psychoactive substances 3 (2.9%), ketamine 2 (2.0%), and 2C-B, mephedrone and opioids 1 each (1.0%); so by the editors' subtraction 69 of 102 had taken at least one other substance.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (p. 960); Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 3rd paragraph (p. 959)
key_findings.note: Co-use in sessions without EMT is not reported, so the share cannot be compared with ordinary sessions.

key_findings.finding: Perceived reasons (up to 3 of 6 options): wrong setting 53.9%, wrong mindset 50.0%, taking too much 40.2%, mixing with other drugs 34.3%; the remaining two options shown in Figure 3 are not LSD and don't know.
key_findings.locator: Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 4th paragraph (p. 959); Figure 3 (p. 960)
key_findings.note: Figure 3 prints no values; the editors' reading of the bar heights (300-dpi rendering) gives about 12.7% for 'not LSD' and 9.8% for 'don't know', that is about 13 and 10 of 102. The mushroom companion paper gives 'don't know' for LSD as 10% (kopra_2022, p. 970).

key_findings.finding: After the incident, 62.7% of EMT seekers said they cut down their LSD use and 16.7% reported no change; 35.3% reduced and 4.9% increased their use of other illicit drugs or alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: These correspond to 64, 17, 36 and 5 of 102 (editors' calculation); 62.7% and 16.7% leave 20.6% (about 21 people) undescribed.

key_findings.finding: The authors report that the share of GDS respondents who used LSD and reported EMT seeking was similar in later survey waves: 0.9% in GDS 2019, 1.0% in GDS 2020 and 0.8% in GDS 2021, with the last fall seen across most substances and possibly linked to the pandemic.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 959); Discussion, 12th paragraph (p. 962)
key_findings.note: Cited from GDS key findings reports (Winstock et al., 2019, 2021), grey literature from the same survey programme, not read for this card.

key_findings.finding: Background stated in the introduction from cited sources, not from this survey: only two cases are known in which a massive LSD overdose appears directly responsible for death, and the lethal amount has been estimated at roughly a thousand times or more the usual recreational amount; other deaths first attributed to LSD toxicity were later attributed to prone maximal restraint by police or to other substances; and since 1997 the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths, which compiles coroners' reports from England, Wales and Northern Ireland on a voluntary basis, has recorded LSD as directly implicated in causing death in only two cases, a suicide after combined LSD and cannabis use and a jump or fall from a 10th-floor window.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand: cited to Nichols and Grob (2018) and to Copeland (2021), the latter from the programme of an author of this paper; neither read for this card.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the incidents captured likely represent only a proportion of LSD-related adverse events, most likely the more severe ones; some serious reactions may not lead to EMT, for example from fear of legal consequences, and some EMT visits may be false alarms raised by others; substances mistaken for LSD, such as NBOMes, may account for some incidents; the number of doses is vague; repeat incidents were not recorded; and recall and response biases apply.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th to 10th paragraphs (p. 961); Discussion, 11th and 13th paragraphs (p. 962)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports 102 EMT seekers out of 10,293 people presented as the past-year group; the Results and Figure 1 show 13,769 reported past-year use and 10,293 answered the EMT question.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator is item responders (75% of the past-year group); the Discussion repeats the 1.0% as a share of people reporting past-year use (p. 959).

reporting_issues.issue: Hospital admission is given only as 54.5% of EMT seekers, with no count.
reporting_issues.consequence: 54.5% cannot be a whole number of 102; by the editors' arithmetic it fits 55 of 101 or 54 of 99, so at least one seeker did not answer, which the paper does not state.

reporting_issues.issue: The recovery percentages in the text (59.2% within 24 h, 11.2% beyond 4 weeks) give no denominator, and Figure 2 prints no values.
reporting_issues.consequence: They fit 98 respondents, which is consistent with the plotted points (editors' reading); four seekers did not answer, which is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The change in LSD use after the incident is given as 62.7% cut down and 16.7% no change, with no figure for the rest.
reporting_issues.consequence: By the editors' arithmetic 20.6% (about 21 of 102) are undescribed: they may have stopped, increased use or not answered.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives first use in the past year as 4271 (41.6%) in a table of 13,769 people; by the editors' arithmetic 4271 is 31.0% of 13,769, so the valid percentage rests on an unstated denominator of about 10,270. Ethnicity and mental health rows likewise use unstated denominators (8208 and 8335, editors' sums of the rows).
reporting_issues.consequence: Valid percentages in Table 1 rest on different, unprinted denominators. Mental health, asked towards the end of the survey (p. 958, Methods › Measures, 3rd paragraph), was answered by about 61% of the 13,769 (8335) and ethnicity by about 60% (8208), while the age, gender and country rows each sum to all 13,769 (editors' sums). The paper says a wide range of demographic information was collected at the start of the survey (p. 957, Methods › Measures, 1st paragraph) and does not explain the missing ethnicity answers.

reporting_issues.issue: This paper describes a list of 20 symptoms, and Table 2 has no 'overheating' row; the mushroom companion paper describes a list of 21 for the same survey section and shows 'overheating' among its symptoms.
reporting_issues.consequence: Symptom profiles from the two papers are not fully comparable; whether overheating was offered after LSD is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that doses taken in sessions leading to EMT were higher than usual (p. 961), but no test of the within-person difference is reported; the only data are the medians of 2.0 (incident session) and 1.0 (usual day of use) among seekers (p. 959).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement is descriptive only, based on a measure the authors call vague; it is not evidence of a dose–risk relation.

reporting_issues.issue: The aims describe the outcome as 12-month incidence, while the measure is the proportion of respondents reporting EMT seeking in the past 12 months, which the mushroom companion paper calls prevalence.
reporting_issues.consequence: Terminology only; the figure is a self-reported 12-month period prevalence among respondents, not an incidence rate.
