design_detail: Secondary cross-sectional analysis of the public-use US National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), survey years 2001 to 2004 pooled (half of the 2004 respondents excluded because questions changed), adults aged 18 or older: 130,152 respondents, of whom 21,967 (13.4% weighted) reported lifetime use of LSD, psilocybin, mescaline or peyote. Weighted multivariable logistic regression of twenty past-year mental health indicators (serious psychological distress on the K6; four kinds of mental health treatment; CIDI-SF symptom screens for eight disorders; seven psychotic symptoms) on lifetime use of any psychedelic, of LSD, psilocybin, mescaline/peyote and peyote, and on past-year LSD use, adjusted for demographics, risk-taking, lifetime extremely stressful events and lifetime use of ten other drug classes; analyses stratified by sex, age, past-year illicit drug use and stressful events. Written by two researchers at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology.
can_establish: Whether, in the US household adult population of 2001–2004, people who reported ever using a classic psychedelic had higher or lower rates of past-year mental health indicators than people who had not, after adjustment for the measured confounders, and how large a population-level increase the estimates can exclude.
cannot_establish: Whether psychedelic use causes, prevents or has no effect on mental health problems (one time point, no measurement before first use), whether harm or benefit occurs in particular people or subgroups, the effects of recent, frequent or heavy use (exposure is lifetime ever-use, with past-year use only for LSD), or outcomes in people living in prisons or hospitals, who were not sampled.

sample.recruitment: Household survey: NSDUH draws a randomly selected sample intended to represent the US civilian non-institutionalized population; trained interviewers visited homes and respondents answered recorded questions privately on a computer (audio computer-assisted self-interview). Response rate 78%; about 10% of participants were excluded from the public-use file, for excessive missing drug-use data or at random to protect anonymity (p. 2, Materials and Methods › Source, Population and Data).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults aged 18 or older in survey years 2001–2004, with half of the 2004 participants excluded because of changes in the questions; participants missing the relevant outcome or past-year illicit drug use were excluded from each analysis (under 2%) (pp. 2, 5).
sample.demographics: Weighted, people who had used psychedelics vs people who had not (Table 1, p. 4): aged 18–25 20.6% vs 13.9%; male 61.0% vs 45.9%; white 85.7% vs 69.5%; married 45.4% vs 58.7%; like to test themselves with risky things sometimes or always 30.4% vs 12.2% (editors' sum of two rows); lifetime extremely stressful event 52.3% vs 33.9%; lifetime cannabis 98.2% vs 33.0%, cocaine 70.1% vs 6.7%, MDMA 24.7% vs 1.2%. All differences p < 0.001 (p. 3).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). Non-response 22%, removal of about 10% from the public-use file, and under 2% missing per analysis; setting missing values to no or zero changed adjusted odds ratios by under 4% on average and did not change significance (pp. 2, 5).
sample.selection_effects: People in prisons, hospitals or military service (under 2% of US adults) were not sampled (p. 5), and people with severe mental illness may be over-represented among those living in institutions; non-response and the public-use exclusions add uncertainty. As in any cross-sectional survey, only living, reachable people are counted. Native Americans had a high rate of lifetime use (25%) but made up under 1% of people who had used psychedelics; excluding them changed odds ratios by under 2% on average (p. 3).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported lifetime use of LSD, psilocybin, mescaline or peyote (any use = any of these; mescaline and peyote combined as mescaline/peyote and peyote also analysed alone), and past-year LSD use, in a confidential computer interview. No information on number of uses, amounts, recency (except past-year LSD), setting or what the substances contained (p. 2, Use of Psychedelics).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: exposure is ever-use. Past-year use was available only for LSD (1,220 respondents; Table 2, p. 5).
exposure.polysubstance: Very common and handled by adjustment: lifetime non-medical use of ten drug classes (cannabis, opiates, cocaine, tranquilizers/sedatives, stimulants, MDMA, inhaled anaesthetics, alkyl nitrites, other inhalants, PCP) entered as covariates, and for past-year LSD also past-year use of other drugs (p. 2, Control Variables; footnotes to Tables 3–4). 98.2% of people who had used psychedelics had used cannabis (Table 1). Alcohol and tobacco are not among the listed covariates. The authors note that substances sold as mescaline often contain LSD or other substances (p. 5).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; lifetime ever-use with time since last use unknown, except that past-year LSD use was recorded.

comparison.controls: Respondents who reported never using any of the four psychedelics (108,034; Table 1, p. 4).
comparison.matching: None; weighted logistic regression adjusted for age (11 categories), gender, race/ethnicity (7 categories), education (4), household income (4), marital status, liking to test oneself with risky behaviour (4 categories), lifetime extremely stressful event, and lifetime use of ten other drug classes (p. 2, Control Variables).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mental health before first psychedelic use, family history of mental illness (the authors name this, p. 5), childhood adversity beyond the single stressful-event item, and personality beyond the risk-taking item were not available. Some covariates (other drug use, stressful events, risk-taking) may have followed psychedelic use rather than preceded it, so adjusting for them could remove part of any real effect or introduce bias; the direction is not predictable.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison group included people who had used other drugs (lifetime cannabis 33.0%, cocaine 6.7%; Table 1), handled by adjustment.

outcomes.instruments: K6 scale, score of 13 or more = serious psychological distress in the worst month of the past year; past-year inpatient and outpatient mental health treatment, psychiatric medication, and felt need without receiving treatment (described as including treatment for alcohol or drug problems); short form of the WHO Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI-SF) screening items for eight DSM-IV disorders and seven psychotic symptoms, two or more symptoms = non-affective psychosis; psychosis data available for 2001–2002 only, which by the table counts probably covers the seven single items as well as the composite (p. 2, Mental Health Indicators; Table 3 footnote b, p. 6; Table 4 footnote c, p. 7).
outcomes.validity_norms: The K6 cut-point is described as validated and recommended; the CIDI-SF is said to overestimate diagnoses and was used to compare groups, not to estimate prevalence (p. 2).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm = higher weighted adjusted odds of a past-year indicator in people with lifetime use (adjusted OR above 1 at p < 0.05); lower odds were reported as a lower rate (p. 3, Data Analysis, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (stated by the authors, p. 5). Editors' count: 20 indicators for each of 6 exposure variables give 120 adjusted odds ratios in Tables 3–4, plus stratified models in 8 strata, reported only where p < 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: self-completed computer interview; the authors analysed a public data set.

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted ORs (95% CI), lifetime use of any psychedelic vs none (Table 3, p. 6): serious psychological distress 1.0 (0.9–1.1); inpatient treatment 0.9 (0.7–1.2); outpatient 0.9 (0.8–1.0); psychiatric medication 0.9 (0.8–1.0); needed but did not receive treatment 0.9 (0.8–1.1); panic disorder 1.0 (0.9–1.1); major depressive episode 1.0 (0.8–1.2); mania 1.1 (0.8–1.6); social phobia 0.9 (0.7–1.3); generalized anxiety disorder 0.9 (0.7–1.1); agoraphobia 1.0 (0.6–1.6); PTSD 1.0 (0.8–1.3); non-affective psychosis 0.8 (0.6–1.1); single psychotic symptoms 0.7 to 1.0, only feeling a force taking over the mind below 1 at p < 0.05 (0.7, 0.5–1.0; p = 0.03). Unadjusted weighted rates were higher in people who had used psychedelics for every indicator (for example serious distress 15.5% vs 7.5%); editors' calculation: 1.8 to 3.2 times higher. Unadjusted odds ratios are not reported. Specific drugs and past-year LSD in Table 4 (p. 7); see key findings.
analysis.covariates: Age, gender, race/ethnicity, income, education, marital status, risky behaviour, lifetime extremely stressful event and lifetime use of ten drug classes; for past-year LSD also past-year use of other drugs. Survey weights and complex-design variables used (SPSS Complex Samples); variance inflation factors under 2.5 (pp. 2–3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; secondary analysis of a public data set.
analysis.selective_reporting: Stratified estimates are reported only for the twelve associations with lower odds at p < 0.05; unadjusted odds ratios and estimates without the drug-use covariates are not shown. The abstract highlights the lower-rate findings without mentioning that no correction for multiple comparisons was made (pp. 1, 3, 5).
analysis.power: No power calculation is reported. Precision can be judged instead: 21,967 exposed respondents, and for any psychedelic use the upper 95% limits are at most 1.6 (mania, agoraphobia; Table 3), so large population-level increases in these indicators are unlikely in this population; past-year LSD estimates are imprecise. The events per predictor variable the authors report (at least 10 in all unstratified analyses, 21 to 379 for indicators other than single psychotic symptoms, as few as 5 in some stratified analyses of three rare psychotic symptoms; p. 3) concern model adequacy, not power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After adjustment, people who had ever used a classic psychedelic did not have higher rates of any of twenty past-year mental health indicators than people who had not (adjusted ORs 0.7 to 1.1; upper 95% limits up to 1.6). Fifteen of the 120 adjusted estimates in Tables 3–4 showed lower odds at p < 0.05, 8 of them with p < 0.01 (editors' count), with no correction for multiple testing; the twelve lower-odds results of the stratified models were mostly of marginal significance. Before adjustment, rates were about twice as high in people who had used psychedelics, who also had far more use of other drugs, more stressful events and more risk-taking.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that psychedelic use was not found to be an independent risk factor for mental health problems and adds that in several cases use was associated with lower rates (abstract, p. 1). The Discussion offers benefit, better initial mental health or chance as explanations for the lower rates (p. 5) and says the findings do not support flashbacks or hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (p. 7). That last inference rests on four of the study's own screening indicators, of which only one is perceptual (seeing a vision others could not, in the past year; adjusted OR 1.0, 0.7–1.3) and none measures persisting perceptual disturbance or recurrent episodes; a null association across a population cannot rule out a rare syndrome. The null result also depends on adjusting for other drug use, stressful events and risk-taking, which may partly follow psychedelic use. The authors themselves state that causal inference is impossible and that harm in some people could be offset by benefit in others (p. 5). A headline version (psychedelics do not cause mental illness, or psychedelics protect mental health) overstates a cross-sectional association with lifetime ever-use.

timeline.event: Halpern et al.: Native Americans who regularly used peyote in religious services showed no cognitive or mental health deficits compared with those who did not (as described by Krebs and Johansen, Discussion, p. 6).

Bonn-Miller et al.: retrospective population study, no association of lifetime psychedelic use with panic attacks or depression but an association of psychedelic dependence with panic attacks; PCP was counted as a psychedelic (as described, p. 6).

Kuzenko et al.: in a community sample, lifetime use of cocaine and/or psychedelics was associated with two or more psychotic symptoms, without adjustment for cocaine and amphetamine use in the psychedelic analyses (as described, p. 6).
Bouso et al.: people taking part in ayahuasca rituals scored lower on psychopathology than members of non-psychedelic religious groups at baseline and one year (as described, p. 6).
This study: no higher adjusted odds of twenty past-year mental health indicators with lifetime psychedelic use, NSDUH 2001–2004.

Johansen and Krebs, J Psychopharmacol: a further population study by the same authors whose title reports psychedelics not linked to mental health problems or suicidal behaviour (listed in search-logs/LSD_DOI-LIST.md, item 16; not read for this card).

Hendricks et al., J Psychopharmacol: US adult population study whose title reports classic psychedelic use associated with lower psychological distress and suicidality (listed in search-logs/LSD_DOI-LIST.md, item 17; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: This analysis is one of several cross-sectional population studies that report no higher rates of mental health problems among people who have used classic psychedelics after adjustment; the 2015 studies above are listed by title only and remain to be appraised. All of these share the limits of lifetime self-report and no measurement before first use; none can show that psychedelics prevent or cause mental illness.

funding.funder: Both authors were supported by the Research Council of Norway (grant 185924); the funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript (p. 1).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist (p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Neuroscience, Faculty of Medicine, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Trondheim (p. 1). The abstract's background figure of over 30 million people in the US having used these drugs cites the authors' own paper, then in press (reference 4, p. 8). NSDUH data files were provided by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Data Archive (p. 8). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective population cohort that measures mental health before and after first psychedelic use, records frequency, amount and setting, compares people who start using with similar people who do not, and assesses rare outcomes such as persisting perceptual disturbance and psychosis with diagnostic interviews; for harm in particular, long-term follow-up of participants in randomized trials.

domains.note: Many measured confounders adjusted for, but mental health before first use, family history and childhood adversity beyond one item were not available; other drug use, stressful events and risk-taking may partly follow psychedelic use, so adjustment may over-correct. Residual confounding and over-adjustment can move estimates in either direction.

Self-reported lifetime ever-use in a confidential computer interview; no frequency, amount, recency (except LSD) or content; substances sold as mescaline often contain other drugs (p. 5); under-reporting possible.
Representative household sample, but 78% response, about 10% removed from the public-use file, and people in prisons or hospitals not sampled; only living, reachable people are counted.
Not a material issue for this cross-sectional comparison; mental health treatment is analysed as an outcome.
Under 2% missing per analysis; a sensitivity analysis changed adjusted odds ratios by under 4% on average (p. 5).

Self-completed screening items (K6, CIDI-SF) that overestimate diagnoses; psychosis indicator from 2001–2002 only; treatment items include treatment for alcohol or drug problems. Errors are probably similar in both groups, which tends to pull estimates towards no difference.
No protocol; 120 adjusted estimates plus stratified models without correction; stratified results shown only where p < 0.05; unadjusted odds ratios not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large, weighted, nationally representative survey with many covariates: it can show that a large population-level increase in these indicators among people who had ever used classic psychedelics is unlikely in the US household population of 2001–2004. But exposure is lifetime ever-use with no measurement before first use, important confounders are unmeasured, and some covariates may follow psychedelic use, so the estimates cannot be read causally in either direction. Cite it for the adjusted null associations with their intervals and for the unadjusted doubling of rates; not for the claim that psychedelics protect mental health, and not for conclusions about flashbacks or HPPD.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 130,152 adult respondents to the US National Survey on Drug Use and Health, 2001–2004 (a household sample of the civilian non-institutionalized population); 21,967 (13.4% weighted) reported lifetime use of LSD, psilocybin, mescaline or peyote, of whom 80.1% had used LSD, 61.5% psilocybin and 37.8% mescaline/peyote; 1,220 reported past-year LSD use.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Source, Population and Data (p. 2); Results › Characteristics of Psychedelic Users (p. 3); Table 1 (p. 4); Table 2 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: The Results text gives 21,979 (p. 3); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Before adjustment, people who had used psychedelics had higher rates of every mental health indicator, for example serious psychological distress 15.5% vs 7.5%, inpatient treatment 2.9% vs 0.9%, symptoms of a major depressive episode 6.8% vs 2.7% and of non-affective psychosis 4.4% vs 1.8% (weighted), and they differed from people who had not used psychedelics on every control variable (all p < 0.001). Editors' calculation from Table 3: unadjusted rates 1.8 to 3.2 times higher across the 20 indicators.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Psychedelic Users (single paragraph, p. 3); Table 3 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: People who had used psychedelics differed sharply in other risk factors (weighted, used vs not used): lifetime cannabis 98.2% vs 33.0%, cocaine 70.1% vs 6.7%, MDMA 24.7% vs 1.2%; an extremely stressful event 52.3% vs 33.9%; never liking to test themselves with risky things 24.5% vs 53.7%; aged 18 to 25 20.6% vs 13.9%; male 61.0% vs 45.9%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: After adjustment, lifetime use of any psychedelic was not associated with higher odds of any of the twenty past-year indicators (adjusted ORs 0.7 to 1.1): serious psychological distress 1.0 (95% CI 0.9–1.1); inpatient treatment 0.9 (0.7–1.2); psychiatric medication 0.9 (0.8–1.0); major depressive episode 1.0 (0.8–1.2); mania 1.1 (0.8–1.6); generalized anxiety disorder 0.9 (0.7–1.1); posttraumatic stress disorder 1.0 (0.8–1.3); non-affective psychosis 0.8 (0.6–1.1). One psychotic symptom, feeling a force taking over the mind, was less common (0.7, 0.5–1.0; p = 0.03).
key_findings.locator: Table 3

key_findings.finding: Specific psychedelics: lifetime use of LSD, psilocybin, mescaline/peyote or peyote, and past-year LSD use, were not associated with higher odds of any indicator at p < 0.05; several odds were lower, for example psilocybin and serious psychological distress 0.8 (0.7–1.0; p = 0.009), psilocybin and psychiatric medication 0.8 (0.7–0.9; p < 0.0001), mescaline/peyote and agoraphobia symptoms 0.6 (0.4–0.9; p = 0.005), and past-year LSD and serious psychological distress 0.7 (0.6–0.9; p = 0.01).
key_findings.locator: Table 4; also Results › Logistic Regression Results, 2nd to 4th paragraphs (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Past-year LSD estimates (1,220 respondents) were imprecise, and several point estimates were above 1 though none reached p < 0.05: feeling a force inserting thoughts 1.7 (0.8–3.5), feeling a force stealing thoughts 1.3 (0.7–2.5), force used special signals 1.4 (1.0–1.9; p = 0.06), saw a vision others could not 1.3 (0.8–2.1), social phobia 1.2 (0.6–2.4).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 5); Table 4, past-year LSD column (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Stratified by sex, age, past-year illicit drug use and lifetime stressful events, no stratum showed significantly higher odds of any indicator (stratified estimates are reported only for lower odds); twelve associations with lower odds were reported, most of marginal significance, for example among women, feeling a force taking over the mind 0.5 (0.3–0.7; p = 0.0005), and among people without a stressful event, feeling a force stealing thoughts 0.3 (0.1–0.7; p = 0.008).
key_findings.locator: Results › Logistic Regression Results, 5th paragraph (Stratified samples)

key_findings.finding: Robustness checks: under 2% of participants were missing data in each analysis, and setting missing values to no or zero changed adjusted ORs by under 4% on average without changing significance; Native Americans had a high rate of lifetime use (25%, weighted) but were under 1% of people who had used psychedelics, and excluding them changed adjusted ORs by under 2% on average, though the lower odds of feeling a force taking over the mind with mescaline/peyote use was then no longer significant (0.7, p = 0.06).
key_findings.locator: Results › Logistic Regression Results, 6th paragraph (Native americans, p. 3) and 7th paragraph (Missing data, p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Model adequacy and precision: the authors report at least 10 events per predictor variable in all unstratified analyses (21 to 379 for indicators other than single psychotic symptoms) and as few as 5 in some stratified analyses of three rare psychotic symptoms; for any psychedelic use the upper 95% limits in Table 3 reach at most 1.6 (mania, agoraphobia). No power calculation is reported; events per variable describe model adequacy, not power.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Data Analysis, 3rd paragraph (p. 3); Table 3 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Perceptual phenomena: having seen a vision others could not in the past year, one of the seven psychotic-symptom screening items, was not associated with lifetime psychedelic use (1.0, 0.7–1.3) or past-year LSD use (1.3, 0.8–2.1); from this and the absence of associations with panic attacks, psychosis and serious psychological distress, the authors conclude that their findings do not support flashbacks or hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD); the rest of the paragraph cites other studies.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (p. 6); Table 4 (p. 7); Discussion › "Flashbacks" and Perceptual Phenomena, 1st paragraph (p. 7)
key_findings.note: The vision item probably comes from the 2001–2002 data only, about two thirds of the respondent base of the other indicators (see key_findings[10]).

key_findings.finding: What the treatment outcomes counted: inpatient and outpatient mental health treatment are described as including treatment for alcohol or drug problems, and the felt need for treatment as including need for alcohol or drug treatment. The footnotes to Tables 3 and 4 give the data on symptoms of non-affective psychosis as available only for 2001–2002; the marker sits on the composite indicator, but all seven single psychotic-symptom rows, including seeing a vision others could not, have about two thirds of the respondent base of the other rows (editors' reading of counts against weighted percentages in Table 3), so the restriction probably covers them too.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Mental Health Indicators, Mental health treatment (p. 2); Table 3, N and wt % columns, and footnote b (p. 6); Table 4 footnote c (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: a retrospective cross-sectional design that makes causal inference impossible; no family history or data on mental health before use; harm in some people could be balanced at population level by benefit in others; no correction for multiple comparisons; screening questions rather than diagnostic interviews; self-report open to memory errors and under-reporting; unknown dose and purity; people in prison, hospital or military service (under 2% of adults) not sampled; no data on acute or short-term effects.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations (single paragraph)

reporting_issues.issue: The number reporting lifetime psychedelic use is 21,967 in the abstract and Tables 1–2 but 21,979 in the Results text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the tables are internally consistent with 21,967.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 21,967 respondents who had used psychedelics and 108,034 who had not; editors' calculation: together 130,001, which is 151 fewer than the 130,152 respondents stated in the abstract and the Results, and the difference is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; perhaps respondents with missing psychedelic-use data, but this is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The stratified results describe most of the twelve lower-rate associations as of marginal significance, printed as (0.05<p<0.01), an impossible range, presumably meaning between 0.01 and 0.05; two are reported as significant at p = 0.05 with 95% CIs reaching 1.0 (generalized anxiety disorder 0.7, 0.5 to 1.0; agoraphobia 0.6, 0.4 to 1.0) under an alpha of 0.05.
reporting_issues.consequence: Several lower-rate findings sit at the significance threshold, among many uncorrected tests, and should not be cited as protective associations.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that adjusted ORs for psychedelic use were all at most 1.2 (p. 5); this holds for any-psychedelic use in Table 3 (highest 1.1) but not for all of Table 4, where past-year LSD estimates reach 1.7 (feeling a force inserting thoughts, 0.8–3.5), 1.4 (force used special signals, 1.0–1.9; p = 0.06) and 1.3 (feeling a force stealing thoughts; saw a vision), and lifetime peyote and feeling a force inserting thoughts is 1.3 (0.8–2.3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The reassurance applies to ever-use of any psychedelic; estimates for recent LSD use are imprecise and compatible with sizeable increases in some psychotic symptoms.

reporting_issues.issue: Footnote b of Table 4 says nine types of past-year drug use were adjusted for but lists eight; the Methods describe the ten lifetime drug classes with the three inhalant classes merged into one for past-year use, which also gives eight.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors read odds ratios as relative risks because the outcomes are all relatively uncommon (p. 3), but several are not rare among people who had used psychedelics: serious psychological distress 15.5%, psychiatric medication 16.3%, panic disorder symptoms 16.5% (Table 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: For these outcomes an odds ratio somewhat exaggerates the relative risk; immaterial for estimates close to 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Unadjusted odds ratios are not reported (only weighted percentages), no model without the drug-use covariates is shown, and stratified estimates are given only for the twelve associations with lower odds.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot see how much each group of covariates, notably other drug use, moved the estimates, nor any stratified estimates above 1.

design_detail: Laboratory cell-culture study with one patient added. Whole-blood microcultures of peripheral leukocytes (white blood cells) from two healthy adults, one man and one woman, were grown for 72 hours; LSD-25 was added to the medium at final concentrations of 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01 or 0.001 µg/ml for the last 48, 24 or 4 hours before harvest (100 and 50 µg/ml were also tried but degenerated the cells and suppressed division). Each concentration and time was run twice and the two donors' results were pooled. Controls were untreated cultures from the same two donors and from four further adults (two men, two women). Coded slides were scored for chromatid and isochromatid breaks, counted as break-equivalents, with gaps excluded (p. 1417). Separately, leukocytes of one 51-year-old man with paranoid schizophrenia, who had taken LSD-25 by mouth 15 times with psychotherapy between 1960 and 1966, were cultured (without added LSD) 8 months after his last session and compared with the laboratory's control rate (p. 1418).
can_establish: That, in this laboratory, adding LSD-25 directly to cultured white blood cells from two donors at 0.001 to 10 µg/ml was followed by more chromatid breaks per cell than in untreated cultures, and that the breaks were not spread across the chromosome groups in proportion to their length.
cannot_establish: Whether LSD taken by people damages their chromosomes: dividing cells in a dish were bathed in the drug for hours at concentrations the paper does not relate to blood levels in people, only two donors were exposed, no statistical test of treated against untreated break rates is reported, and the one patient had no sample from before LSD, had also taken other psychiatric drugs and was compared with cultures from other people.

sample.recruitment: Not described for the donors: two healthy adults (one man, one woman) gave blood for the treated cultures, and four further adults (two men, two women) for control cultures only (p. 1417). The patient was referred by a physician thanked in the acknowledgments (ref. 15, p. 1419).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Donors: described only as healthy (p. 1417). Patient: physically healthy apart from schizophrenia, with no history of malignancy, viral infection or radiation treatment beyond routine diagnostic procedures (p. 1418).
sample.demographics: Donors: sex only (treated cultures 1 man and 1 woman; added controls 2 men and 2 women); ages not reported (p. 1417). Patient: man aged 51 with paranoid schizophrenia (p. 1418).
sample.attrition: At 100 and 50 µg/ml cell degeneration and suppressed division left too few analysable cells, so those concentrations are not reported (p. 1417). The target of 200 cells per condition (25 per slide) was not reached in several treated cultures: 125 to 200 cells were scored per condition (p. 1417; Table 1).
sample.selection_effects: Two donors cannot show how far people differ in their cells' response; the control rate pools these two donors with four other people, so treated against control is partly a comparison between different people. Cells were chosen as well-spread metaphases at low power and then all scored (p. 1417); cells killed or arrested by the drug are missing from the counts, which the authors offer as the reason for lower rates at the highest concentrations and longest times (p. 1417).

exposure.measurement: In vitro: LSD-25 dissolved in sterile distilled water and added to the culture medium at fixed final concentrations (p. 1417); the acknowledgments thank Sandoz Pharmaceuticals for the LSD supplied to one of the authors, N. Back (ref. 15, p. 1419); purity is not stated. Patient: a treatment history of 15 sessions with stated amounts (p. 1418); the source of the record and of his LSD is not stated.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: In vitro conditions: 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 µg/ml for the last 48, 24 or 4 hours of a 72-hour culture at 37°C; colcemide 0.05 µg/ml for the last 2 hours (p. 1417). Patient (exposure history as reported): 15 sessions by mouth from 30 September 1960 to 9 March 1966, of 80, 100 (three times), 150 and 175 µg for the first six and 200 µg for the last nine, about 2,505 µg in all (editors' arithmetic); blood cultured 8 months after the last session (p. 1418).
exposure.polysubstance: In vitro: not applicable. Patient: treated for short periods with chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide before and during the LSD treatment; no other known drug intake in the 8 months between the last LSD session and the blood sample (p. 1418). The authors set the other drugs aside by citing unpublished data (Sandberg, ref. 11) on 35 people with schizophrenia, some given these drugs, without increased breakage (p. 1418).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Patient: 8 months after the last LSD session; how drug intake in that interval was established is not stated (p. 1418).

comparison.controls: Untreated cultures from the two donors and from four other adults: 34 breaks in 925 cells, 0.037 per cell (Table 1, p. 1417). The patient was compared with this in vitro control rate, called the normal 3.7 percent (p. 1418); there was no matched control and no sample from before his LSD treatment.
comparison.matching: None. Treated and control cultures were processed by the same method; donor ages are not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Patient: no chromosome study before LSD treatment; schizophrenia and its other treatments are not separated from LSD. Donors: no information on age, smoking, infections, medicines or radiation.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported for the six control donors.

outcomes.instruments: Chromosome preparations from whole-blood microcultures (modified Moorhead method, ref. 4), scored under oil-immersion phase-contrast microscopy at about ×1560 (p. 1417). A break was scored only for a clear discontinuity of the chromatid; chromatid and isochromatid breaks both counted as single breaks, single fragments with chromatid breaks, double fragments as isochromatid breaks, dicentrics and translocation figures as two breaks; pale attenuated regions scored separately as gaps and excluded from rates; breaks assigned to chromosome groups by the Denver classification (p. 1417).
outcomes.validity_norms: The outcome is a break-equivalent count per metaphase (exchange figures count twice), not the share of cells with an aberration that some later studies used (Tjio et al., 1969, p. 850). The control rate of 3.7 percent was higher than control rates from other laboratories, as later papers point out: Loughman et al. (1967, p. 509) cite published controls with 0.76 percent aberrations other than gaps in 1569 cells, and Sparkes et al. (1968, p. 1344) note that laboratories reporting damage also had higher control rates.
outcomes.operationalization: Chromosomal damage = breaks per metaphase in break-equivalents, gaps excluded (p. 1417). For the patient, a chromosome breakage rate of 12 percent in 200 metaphases (p. 1418).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: one significance test (chi-square on the distribution of breaks across chromosome groups); break rates were compared with the control rate descriptively, without a test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Cultures: slides were coded by people who did not take part in the microscopic scoring (p. 1417). Patient: coding of his slides is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Breaks per cell in treated cultures ranged from 0.050 (0.001 µg/ml, 4 h; 10/200) to 0.368 (1 µg/ml, 24 h; 46/125), against 0.037 in controls (34/925) (Table 1, p. 1417). Pooled over all 15 conditions, 384 breaks in 2678 treated cells, 0.143 per cell, about 3.9 times the control rate (editors' calculation from Table 1; no interval is given because the treated cells come from two donors' cultures and no culture-level data are reported). No consistent concentration–response: the highest rate was at 10 µg/ml after 4 h, at 1 µg/ml after 24 h and at 0.1 µg/ml after 48 h (Table 1). Distribution across chromosome groups: chromosome 1 (A1) carried 74 breaks against 30.8 expected for random breakage per unit length, about 2.4 times (editors' calculation); chi-square 104.2, df 8, P<0.001 (Table 2, p. 1418). Patient: 12 percent breakage in 200 metaphases against the 3.7 percent control rate, with one quadriradial between two No. 1 chromosomes (p. 1418).
analysis.selective_reporting: Per-donor and per-replicate counts are not shown although each condition was run twice in two donors; the 100 and 50 µg/ml cultures are described only as cytotoxic. The patient's count of breaks and the types of aberration are not tabulated; only a rate and Figure 1e are given.
analysis.power: Not reported. Two donors; 125 to 200 cells per condition.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this laboratory, cultured white blood cells from two donors exposed to LSD-25 for 4 to 48 hours showed more chromatid breaks per cell than untreated cultures (0.050 to 0.368 against 0.037), without a consistent concentration–response, and breaks were concentrated on chromosome 1. One man who had taken LSD in therapy, and had also had chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide, showed 12 percent breakage 8 months after his last session, against the laboratory's control cultures from other people.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the increase marked and says the patient showed a similar increase (abstract, p. 1417). The discussion says LSD-25 is apparently able to produce chromosomal damage quickly in vitro and that the patient's result "suggests an additional long-term effect of the drug", proposing damage to stem cells or long-lived lymphocytes (pp. 1418–1419). It links the single quadriradial to Bloom's syndrome, Fanconi's anemia, tumour cells and the raised risk of neoplasia in those syndromes (p. 1418). It concedes that the significance cannot yet be fully assessed and that the patient's other drugs call for caution (p. 1418). No statistical test supports the treated-versus-control difference, the dose–response relationship stated in the text is not visible in Table 1, and the steps from cells in a dish, and from one patient without a baseline, to effects in people who take LSD are not supported by these data.

timeline.event: This report: LSD-25 added to cultured leukocytes increased breaks per cell; one patient treated with LSD showed 12 percent breakage.

Cohen, Hirschhorn and Frosch (N Engl J Med 277:1043) extended the work to people: 13.2 percent aberrations in 18 people who had used LSD against 3.8 percent in 12 controls, after two controls with 22.5 percent were excluded for viral infections said to have developed after sampling (as summarized by Tjio et al., 1969, p. 854; not read).

Irwin and Egozcue (Science 157:313) reported more aberrations in leukocytes of people who had used LSD: 23.6 percent in 8 against 9.5 percent in 7 controls (as summarized by Tjio et al., 1969, p. 854; not read).

No chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use; the authors argue the control rate in this report was unusually high and estimate, from mouse data, that 100 µg in a person gives at most about the lowest concentration used here (pp. 509–510).

Sparkes et al. state that two studies agree on the effects of LSD in vitro, citing Cohen, Hirschhorn and Frosch and Bender and Sankar (Science 159:749) (p. 1343), and find no significant difference in break rates between 8 people exposed to LSD and 4 controls.

Before-and-after study of 32 patients given one oral dose of pharmaceutical LSD: no significant change in aberrant metaphases. Its summary of this report (6.7 to 36.8 percent against 3.7 percent) reads breaks per cell as percentages and leaves out the lowest treated value, 0.050 (p. 849).
Review in Science of whether LSD damages chromosomes or is carcinogenic, mutagenic or teratogenic (not read for this card; to be appraised from its full text).

replication.where_it_stands: Among the papers read in this round, the in vitro observation was not retested; the studies of people's cells after LSD found no consistent increase (Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969, which sampled the same patients before and after pharmaceutical LSD and found no lasting increase, with large transient increases in 3 of 32). Sparkes et al. state that two studies agree on the in vitro effects, the same group's later paper and one other laboratory (Bender & Sankar, 1968); neither was read. The patient observation, one person without a baseline, has no direct replication. A later review (Dishotsky et al., 1971) is in the library but has not been appraised for this card.

what_would_settle_it: For cells: blinded culture experiments with many donors, concentrations matched to blood levels measured in people, per-donor and per-culture counts and a pre-specified statistical comparison. For people: chromosome studies of the same people before and after LSD of known content, with comparison people who take no LSD sampled at the same times and slides scored blind (Tjio et al., 1969, did the before-and-after part without such a concurrent group).

domains.note: Treated cultures from two donors only, pooled; each condition run twice but per-donor and per-replicate results not shown; control rate pools these two donors with four other people.

Defined concentrations and times with pharmaceutical LSD, but purity not stated and no link between culture concentrations and levels in people; cytotoxicity at high concentrations and long times removes cells from the counts.

Slides coded by people who did not score them; explicit criteria for breaks; all cells chosen at low power were scored. A second reader may judge this some concerns because the target of 200 cells was not met in several conditions.
No test of treated against control rates; irregular concentration–time pattern explained after the fact; chi-square on pooled breaks ignores clustering and has no control distribution.
One misprinted rate (22/175 printed as 0.216) and two text statements that Table 1 contradicts (twofold increase; lowest rate at 4 hours).

One person, no pre-treatment sample, compared with other people's cultures; also given chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide; coding of his slides not stated; the reassurance about other drugs rests on unpublished data.
A long-term effect in people is suggested from one patient, and the single quadriradial is linked to cancer-prone syndromes and tumour cells.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for a cell-culture experiment (METHODS 5.3 lists none, and scripts/rob_vocab.py assigns none to in-vitro), so the editors' checklist is used with domains adapted to this design, as on the other in-vitro cards; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. Coded scoring is a strength. The concerns are two donors pooled without per-donor or per-culture data, no statistical comparison of treated with control rates, an irregular concentration–time pattern explained after the fact, a misprinted rate and two text statements contradicted by Table 1, and a single patient compared with other people's cultures while also exposed to chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide. Citable for: the break rates in Table 1 as observations in cultured cells from two donors under these conditions; the excess of breaks on chromosome 1 in pooled treated cultures; the patient's reported 12 percent as one observation without a baseline. Not citable for: chromosome damage in people who take LSD, a dose–response relationship, a long-term effect, or any link to cancer or birth defects.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Human peripheral blood leukocytes in 72-hour whole-blood microcultures. LSD-treated cultures from two healthy adults (one man, one woman); untreated control cultures from these two and four other adults (two men, two women); ages not reported (p. 1417). Also the cultured leukocytes of one patient, without LSD added in culture (p. 1418).
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: LSD-25 in sterile distilled water added to the culture medium at final concentrations of 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 µg/ml (100 and 50 µg/ml cytotoxic) for the last 48, 24 or 4 hours of a 72-hour culture at 37°C; colcemide 0.05 µg/ml for the last 2 hours; each condition run twice (p. 1417).
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None given: the paper does not relate the culture concentrations to blood or tissue levels in people. Loughman et al. (1967, p. 509) later estimated from mouse distribution data that 100 µg in a 70-kg person would give about 0.0004 µg/g in blood after 30 minutes and on average about 0.0012 µg/g in the liver, where concentrations are highest, about the lowest concentration used here (0.001 µg/ml); that is their estimate, not a measurement.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: No. Dividing cells in culture were bathed in a constant concentration for 4 to 48 hours; in the body, circulating lymphocytes are mostly not dividing at the time of exposure (Loughman et al., 1967, p. 510) and drug levels change over hours. The one patient had taken LSD in a clinical setting and had also had other psychiatric drugs.

key_findings.finding: LSD-25 added to cultured leukocytes of two donors (results pooled) was followed by 0.050 to 0.368 breaks per cell across the 15 concentration–time conditions, against 0.037 in untreated cultures (34 breaks in 925 cells from six people).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; text, 5th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.note: 22/175 is 0.126, not 0.216 (see reporting issues). Pooled over all conditions, 384 breaks in 2678 treated cells (0.143 per cell), about 3.9 times the control rate (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: At 100 and 50 µg/ml the cells degenerated and division was suppressed, leaving too few analysable cells; several treated cultures did not reach the target of 200 cells per condition (125 to 200 scored).
key_findings.locator: Text, 2nd paragraph (left column, continuing in the middle column) and 3rd paragraph (middle column); Table 1

key_findings.finding: Finding: The authors report at least a twofold increase over the control rate for every treatment except 0.001 µg/ml for 4 hours, and a dose–response relationship that appeared time dependent; at 10 µg/ml damage was greater after shorter exposures, and the same was seen at 1 µg/ml for 48 hours, which they take as an indication that longer exposure may have destroyed cells. (Note unchanged.) Reason: the source hedges this ('an indication', 'may have caused'); 'attribute' states it firmly.
key_findings.locator: Text, 5th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: No statistical test is reported. The 1 µg/ml, 48-hour rate (0.067) is 1.8 times the control rate (editors' calculation), so two conditions fall short of twofold.

key_findings.finding: Breaks assigned to chromosome groups (354 identifiable, plus 30 unidentifiable fragments and breaks) were not spread in proportion to chromatin length: chromosome 1 (A1) carried 74 against 30.8 expected, group C 161 against 131.9, group D 15 against 35.6 and group G 2 against 13.1; chi-square 104.2, df 8, P<0.001.

key_findings.note: 354 + 30 = 384, the sum of the treated counts in Table 1, so Table 2 covers treated cultures only; no distribution is given for control cultures.

key_findings.finding: Scoring: slides were coded by people who did not score them; well-spread metaphases were chosen at ×250 and every chosen cell was scored at about ×1560; chromatid and isochromatid breaks counted as single breaks, dicentrics and translocation figures as two; gaps recorded but excluded from the rates.
key_findings.locator: Text, 3rd paragraph (middle column) and 4th paragraph (middle column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: One 51-year-old man with paranoid schizophrenia, given LSD-25 by mouth 15 times between 30 September 1960 and 9 March 1966 (80, 100 three times, 150 and 175 µg, then 200 µg nine times) with psychotherapy, had a chromosome breakage rate of 12 percent in 200 metaphases 8 months after his last session, against the 3.7 percent of the laboratory's control cultures; one quadriradial between two No. 1 chromosomes was seen.

key_findings.finding: The patient had also been treated for short periods with chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide before and during the LSD treatment; the authors advise caution and cite unpublished data on 35 people with schizophrenia, some given these drugs, without increased breakage.

key_findings.finding: The authors link the single quadriradial to the cytogenetic picture of Bloom's syndrome and Fanconi's anemia, to tumour cells and to cells transformed by SV40, noting the raised risk of neoplasia in those syndromes.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints 22 breaks in 175 cells (0.001 µg/ml, 24 hours) as 0.216 breaks per cell; 22/175 is 0.126. The count is the one that fits: the treated counts in Table 1 sum to 384, which equals the 354 identifiable plus 30 unidentifiable breaks of Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The rate is misprinted. With 0.126, breaks at 0.001 µg/ml rise with exposure time (0.050, 0.126, 0.138) instead of peaking at 24 hours.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says breaks at least doubled over the control rate for all treatments except 0.001 µg/ml for 4 hours, but 1 µg/ml for 48 hours gave 0.067 breaks per cell, 1.8 times the control rate of 0.037.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two of 15 conditions, not one, were below twofold; minor, but the text summarizes the table generously.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the lowest break frequency followed the 4-hour exposure in most cases (except at 10 µg/ml) and infers that LSD may cause breaks during the G1 or S phase; in Table 1 the 4-hour rate is lowest at only 2 of 5 concentrations (0.1 and 0.001 µg/ml), and at 1 and 0.01 µg/ml the 48-hour rate is lowest. (Consequence unchanged.) Reason: the source says 'may cause' (p. 1418).
reporting_issues.consequence: The cell-cycle inference rests on a pattern that Table 1 does not show consistently.

reporting_issues.issue: No statistical comparison of treated with control break rates and no per-donor or per-replicate counts, although cells came from two donors and each concentration and exposure time was repeated twice (whether twice per donor is not stated); the dose–response relationship is asserted without a test, while the highest rate falls at a different concentration for each exposure time. (Consequence unchanged.)
reporting_issues.consequence: The size and reliability of the increase cannot be judged; the variation between cultures that an interval would need is not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The chi-square test of the distribution of breaks pools all treated cultures and treats each break as independent, although breaks cluster within cells and cultures; no distribution is given for the 34 breaks in control cultures (Table 1, p. 1417).
reporting_issues.consequence: P<0.001 overstates the certainty, and the excess on chromosome 1 cannot be attributed to LSD rather than to breakage in culture generally, which the authors note also concentrates on chromosome 1 with other agents (p. 1417).

reporting_issues.issue: The patient's result is a single rate without a count of breaks, a pre-treatment sample or a matched control; it is compared with untreated cultures from six other people, and the reassurance about his other drugs rests on unpublished data (ref. 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: The observation cannot separate LSD from schizophrenia, its other treatments, or differences between people and between cultures.

design_detail: Narrative review in Science (30 April 1971) by four California authors (two from the Department of Research, Mendocino State Hospital; one from the Donner Laboratory of Medical Physics and Biophysics, University of California, Berkeley; one professor of psychology at San Francisco State College) of 68 studies and case reports from roughly 1967 to 1970 on whether LSD breaks chromosomes, causes cancer, causes mutations or causes birth defects. No search method or inclusion criteria are stated. The authors tabulate in-vitro chromosome studies (Table 1), chromosome studies of people who used illicit LSD (Table 2), of people given pharmaceutical LSD compared with controls (Table 3) or with their own pre-treatment samples (Table 4), and rodent teratology studies (Table 5); they count people with raised breakage across studies and argue that positive findings reflect illicit multiple-drug use and laboratory artefacts. The tables include unpublished data and the authors' own unpublished study (ref. 35).
can_establish: What the 1967–1970 chromosome, mutation and birth-defect studies of LSD reported, how the authors counted them, and their argument for discounting the early positive reports, as an account of that literature and a pointer to its primary studies.
cannot_establish: That LSD causes no genetic harm, cancer or birth defects in humans: the human evidence is microscope counts of chromosome breaks in cultured blood cells from small, heterogeneous groups scored by different laboratories, a few case reports and one small pregnancy series, and the cross-study tallies are not a systematic review or meta-analysis.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). People in the reviewed chromosome studies were either given pharmaceutical LSD in medical or research settings (several groups were patients: for example a single patient with paranoid schizophrenia in Cohen et al. and 37 patients in Tjio et al.) or were people using illicit drugs sold as LSD, recruited by the original investigators (pp. 432–435).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; studies chosen by the authors, including personal communications (refs 8, 22, 56), unpublished studies (refs 36, 49) and the authors' own study in preparation (ref. 35) (pp. 439–440, reference list).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own and mixes published, unpublished and personally communicated data. The reviewed human groups were small (1 to 46 people each; Tables 2–4) and drug histories in the illicit-LSD studies rested on self-report (p. 434). The authors' own unpublished data contribute 14 people who used illicit LSD and 5 given pure LSD to Tables 2 and 3 (ref. 35).

exposure.measurement: As in the primary studies: pharmaceutical LSD given under supervision (amount and timing known), or self-reported use of illicit drugs sold as LSD, of unknown composition and strength (pp. 432, 434).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in the reviewed work: in the before-and-after studies, single or up to three treatments, oral except in one intravenous study (Table 4 caption, p. 434); time from last LSD to blood sampling from about an hour to years (Tables 2–4). Human lymphocyte cultures were exposed in vitro to 0.0001 to 10 μg/ml for 4 to 72 hours (Table 1, p. 432).
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the argument: nearly all people in the illicit-LSD studies used many other drugs, including amphetamine, opiates, barbiturates, cannabis and cocaine (p. 434). Several pure-LSD and control groups included patients treated with psychotropic medication (Table 3 footnotes, p. 433). How other drug use was handled varied by study and was mostly not controlled.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Varied across studies: for example 0.033 to 12 months since last LSD in the largest illicit-LSD group, and 0.5 to 240 hours after treatment in the before-and-after study of Tjio et al. (Tables 2 and 4, pp. 433–434).

comparison.controls: Unexposed control groups in after-only studies, whose breakage rates varied widely between laboratories (from 0.0% to 11.9% in Tables 2–3; general-population series listed in Table 3 from 0.0% to 7.4%), or each person's own pre-LSD sample in the before-and-after studies (Tables 2–4, pp. 433–434).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; the authors note that in the illicit-LSD studies the exposed and control groups were not comparable in other drug use or health (pp. 433–434).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Breakage before any drug use was measured only in the before-and-after studies of pharmaceutical LSD (56 people). Viral infection, malnutrition and other drug exposures, which the authors propose as explanations for positive findings, were not independently assessed in the positive studies (p. 434).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Varied: one comparison group used other drugs but not LSD (Cohen et al., 6 people); some control groups included patients on psychotropic medication (Table 3 footnotes, p. 433).

outcomes.instruments: Chromosome breakage rates, printed as percentages, from microscope examination of dividing white blood cells (lymphocytes) cultured with phytohaemagglutinin; some studies also built karyotypes or used autoradiography. Mutation tests in Drosophila and a fungus; teratology in mice, rats, hamsters, rabbits and rhesus monkeys; human case reports of leukaemia and of malformed infants; one series of pregnancies (pp. 431–439).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors argue that chromatid-type aberrations in cultured cells mostly arise from culture procedures, that many common substances (including aspirin and caffeine) break chromosomes in vitro, and that control rates differ widely between laboratories, so results from different laboratories are hard to compare (pp. 431–433).
outcomes.operationalization: Damage = a breakage rate above the control group's mean, or significantly above the control rate, as each study defined it; some studies reported only that rates were within normal limits (Table 2). The authors count people meeting these criteria across studies (pp. 432–435).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis; the cross-study tallies are counts, not tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not discussed for the reviewed cytogenetic studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimate. Counts by the authors: pure LSD, at most 18 of 126 people (14.29%) with breakage above control means; illicit LSD, at most 90 of 184 (48.9%), or 80 of 174 (45.98%) leaving out a study with incomplete data; of 108 people reported with damage, 18 (16.67%) had received pure LSD (pp. 432, 434, 439). Before-and-after group means (Table 4, p. 434): 5.7% to 4.9% (10 people), 0.0% to 0.0% (6), 2.81% to 3.57% (5) and 4.28% to 5.91% (32), none significant; 1.0% to 4.78% after intravenous LSD (3 people, significant).
analysis.selective_reporting: The authors remove one person with a 9% breakage rate from a negative pure-LSD group as widely deviant (Table 3 footnote, p. 433), and they present the largest before-and-after data set (Tjio et al., 37 patients) as showing no significant difference, mentioning its increases only as evidence against a dose–response (greater increases in the low-dose group, p. 435), without weighing that the group means rose in both of its groups (2.81% to 3.57% and 4.28% to 5.91%, not significant; Table 4, p. 434).
analysis.power: Not discussed. The reviewed studies were small and some scored few cells (Nielsen et al.: on average 71.6 cells per LSD subject and 34.4 per control, criticized as insufficient by Tjio et al.; p. 435), so modest increases in breakage could have been missed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the reviewed 1967–1970 literature, raised chromosome breakage in cultured white blood cells was reported mainly by three early teams studying people who used several illicit drugs, nine other teams found none in similar people, and few people given pharmaceutical LSD showed raised rates; in 56 people sampled before and after pharmaceutical LSD, 6 had raised breakage afterwards (3 of them after intravenous LSD, 1 with a viral infection), the only significant group change was after intravenous LSD, and 5 of the 6 were back at baseline on retesting. In fruit flies, mutations appeared only at 2,000 μg/ml or more, against an estimated 0.0001 μg/ml of unchanged LSD in the body after a clinical dose (authors' figures); rodent teratology findings were inconsistent; human data on cancer and birth defects were case reports and one small pregnancy series.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The closing paragraph gives as the authors' belief, from their own work and the literature, that pure LSD in moderate doses does not damage chromosomes in the body, causes no detectable genetic damage and "is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man" (p. 439), and within these bounds suggests no present contraindication, other than in pregnancy, to continued controlled experimental use; the framing as belief softens these statements only slightly. For chromosomes, the authors' own qualifier in the summary, no damage detectable by the methods then available (p. 439), is the accurate version: the methods counted gross breaks in cultured cells in small groups, and group means rose, not significantly, in both groups of the largest oral before-and-after study (Tjio et al.; Table 4, p. 434). For cancer and birth defects, the review itself says no significant work on carcinogenic potential had been reported and that there was no evidence of teratogenicity in humans (p. 439), and it calls its own preliminary primate data suggestive of a teratogenic effect that deserves further investigation (p. 439); an absence of evidence from a few case reports and one series with 3 pregnancies exposed to pharmaceutical LSD during gestation becomes a negative conclusion. The attribution of positive findings to heavy illicit drug use, infection and malnutrition is plausible but rests on one small comparison (6 vs 18 people) and on the authors' clinical impressions. A headline version (science showed in 1971 that LSD does not damage chromosomes) overstates: this is a narrative review showing that the early alarm was not supported by the better-controlled studies available then.

timeline.event: Cohen et al.: increased chromosome breakage in cultured human white blood cells exposed to LSD, and damage in one patient treated with LSD (Science; as described by Dishotsky et al., pp. 431, 435).
Irwin and Egozcue: first report of raised chromosome breakage in people who used illicit LSD (as described, p. 432).
Hungerford et al.: increase in chromosome aberrations after each of three intravenous LSD injections in 3 people, apparently back to baseline 1 to 6 months later (as described, p. 435).
Tjio et al.: before-and-after study of 37 patients given LSD, no significant change in breakage (JAMA; as described, p. 435).
Houston: brief review of 15 studies reaching conclusions similar to this review (note added in proof, p. 439).
By this date nine teams had failed to find raised breakage in people who used illicit LSD (as tabulated in Table 2, p. 433).

replication.where_it_stands: As of 1971 the authors judged the early positive chromosome reports unconfirmed for pharmaceutical LSD in moderate doses. No later studies were read for this card; the question of cancer and birth-defect risk in humans was, by the review's own account, unstudied at the time.
