what_would_settle_it: For chromosomes: people given pharmaceutical LSD in a controlled study, with blood samples before and after, scored blind to timing with a pre-specified number of cells per sample and with current genotoxicity methods. For cancer and birth defects: cohort or registry studies that record exposure before the outcome and are large enough to detect plausible increases.

domains.note: No search, sources or criteria; 68 items chosen by the authors, including personal communications and unpublished studies.

Methods are critiqued in detail (culture artefacts, control rates, cells scored, illicit drug composition, regrouping of data), but scrutiny falls mainly on positive studies; negative studies are rarely appraised, and one deviant value was removed from a negative study.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The authors' own unpublished study (ref. 35) and a co-author's earlier negative study (ref. 2) contribute to the tallies, and the closing conclusion draws on the authors' own work; most of the evidence is from other groups.

Explanations for positive findings (malnutrition, infection, the debility of people using amphetamine described from the authors' experience) are offered without data, and the closing statement that LSD is not a teratogen or carcinogen in man goes beyond the stated absence of research.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against genetic harm
domains.note: Positive and negative studies are both tabulated, but positive reports are explained away more readily than negative ones are examined; the non-significant rises in the largest before-and-after data set are mentioned only as evidence against a dose–response, and animal and primate signals are set aside for humans.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review tabulates its sources openly, which lets readers check its counts, but its selection is unsystematic, it relies partly on unpublished data, and its strongest conclusions (no carcinogenicity or teratogenicity in man) exceed what it shows. Cite it for the history of the LSD chromosome scare, for what was actually measured (breaks in cultured blood cells in small groups), and for the observation that raised breakage was reported mainly in people using several illicit drugs; cite primary studies for numbers where possible; do not cite it as evidence that LSD causes no birth defects or cancer.

key_findings.finding: What was measured: in the human studies, breaks and other structural aberrations seen under the microscope in chromosomes of white blood cells (lymphocytes) taken from people and stimulated to divide in culture with phytohaemagglutinin; in most in-vitro studies, human lymphocytes exposed to LSD in the dish (Table 1, p. 432, also lists barley root, broad bean (Vicia faba) and hamster fibroblasts and embryos). The authors note that these cells do not normally divide in the body, that most reported lesions were of the chromatid type, which in cultured cells mostly arise from the culture procedures, and that some laboratories (Cohen et al.; Irwin and Egozcue) combined chromatid- and chromosome-type changes into equivalent numbers of breaks.
key_findings.locator: Chromosome Studies in vitro, 4th paragraph and 5th paragraph, consideration 1 (p. 431, right column); Table 1 (p. 432); Illicit LSD and Chromosome Damage, 6th paragraph (p. 433, middle column)

key_findings.finding: Scope: the authors counted 68 studies and case reports published in roughly the previous four years on whether LSD breaks chromosomes or causes cancer, mutations or birth defects in humans, and reviewed them without a stated search method or inclusion criteria.
key_findings.locator: Opening paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: In vitro, six of nine studies (eight teams) found some increase in chromosome breakage in cultured cells exposed to LSD and three did not; damage was mostly of the chromatid type, showed no consistent dose–response and, with one exception, occurred at concentrations or exposure times the authors judge unattainable in people given reasonable doses. In one study LSD, aspirin and ergonovine each roughly doubled breakage in control cells (10.2%, 9.6% and 10.0%).
key_findings.locator: Chromosome Studies in vitro, 4th paragraph (p. 431), consideration 2 and summary paragraph (p. 432); Table 1 (p. 432); Summary and Conclusion, 1st paragraph (p. 439)

key_findings.finding: The authors' worked example: after a 100 μg oral dose in a 70-kg man, unchanged LSD in the body would be about 0.0001 μg/ml, a concentration tested in vitro only by Kato and Jarvik, who found no increase in breakage (p. 431; Table 1, p. 432); the lowest concentration in the first study by Cohen et al., 0.001 μg/ml for 4 hours, showed no difference from control cells (a later repeat by the same group found one, not confirmed by Tjio). Editors' calculation: Cohen et al.'s lowest concentration is about ten times the estimated body concentration.
key_findings.locator: Chromosome Studies in vitro, 2nd to 4th paragraphs (p. 431); Table 1 (p. 432)

key_findings.finding: In vivo, 21 reports from 17 laboratories covered 310 people: 126 given pharmaceutical (pure) LSD and 184 exposed to illicit drugs sold as LSD. By the authors' count, at most 18 of 126 (14.29%) in the pure-LSD group and at most 90 of 184 (48.9%) in the illicit group had breakage above the control means; of the 108 people reported with chromosome damage, 18 (16.67%) had received pure LSD.
key_findings.locator: Chromosomal Studies in vivo, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 432); Summary and Conclusion, 2nd paragraph (p. 439)
key_findings.note: The 'at most' figures count all 19 subjects of Nielsen et al. (9 given pure LSD, 10 using illicit LSD) as raised, because their individual data were not given; without them the authors give 80 of 174 (45.98%) for the illicit group (p. 434) and 3 of 61 (4.9%) for the comparisons of pure LSD with unexposed controls (p. 435). Editors' calculation: 18 = 12 + 6 and 90 = 80 + 10; without Nielsen et al., 9 of 117 (7.7%) for the whole pure-LSD group.

key_findings.finding: The positive in-vivo reports came from three teams studying people who used illicit drugs: Irwin and Egozcue found mean breakage of 23.4% in 8 people vs 11.0% in controls, then 18.76% (range 8 to 45) in 46 people vs 9.03%, with only 3 of the 46 not above the control mean; Cohen et al. found breakage in 18 people three times the control mean of 3.8% (13.2% in Table 2); Nielsen et al. found 2.5% in 10 people vs 0.2%. Together, 80 of 86 people studied by Cohen et al. and by Irwin and Egozcue had raised rates.
key_findings.locator: Illicit LSD and Chromosome Damage, 1st to 4th and 6th paragraphs; Table 2 (p. 433)
key_findings.note: The control rate for Irwin and Egozcue's first study is 11.0% in the text (p. 432) but 11.9% in Table 2 and in the text on p. 433; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Nine teams found no raised breakage in people who used illicit LSD (groups of 3 to 20 people; Table 2); three of them built karyotypes and found no translocations, deletions or other structural changes, and another found no difference in autoradiographic labelling in cells from 20 people. The authors count only one instance in these studies (an infant exposed in utero) of damage beyond that in the general population.
key_findings.locator: Illicit LSD and Chromosome Damage, 5th paragraph (p. 433, left column); Table 2 (p. 433); last paragraph (p. 434, right column)

key_findings.finding: Other drugs and street samples: nearly all people in the illicit-LSD studies also used other drugs; among those with raised breakage and detailed drug histories, 43 of 77 (56%) used amphetamine. In the data of Cohen et al., 6 people who used other drugs but not LSD had breakage of 12.6%, not significantly different from 13.2% in 18 people who used illicit LSD with other drugs. Laboratory analyses cited by the authors found that only 54% of 57 samples sold as LSD contained it in relatively pure form; some contained no LSD, or DOM or PCP instead of or besides LSD.
key_findings.locator: Illicit LSD and Chromosome Damage, 8th to 12th paragraphs (p. 434); Table 2 footnote (p. 433)

key_findings.finding: In studies comparing people after pharmaceutical LSD with unexposed controls, at most 12 of 70 (17.1%) had raised breakage, all but one reported by a single team (Nielsen et al.) whose methods the authors criticize (the same data regrouped into new comparison groups; on average 71.6 cells scored per LSD subject and 34.4 per control, as noted by Tjio et al.); leaving out that team's incomplete data, the figure could be as low as 3 of 61 (4.9%).
key_findings.locator: Chromosome Studies after LSD Treatment, 2nd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In before-and-after studies of 56 people given pharmaceutical LSD, 6 (10.7%) had raised breakage after treatment, 3 of them given LSD intravenously and 1 with a viral infection; 5 of the 6, retested 2 weeks to 7.67 months later, had returned to their pre-LSD rates. Group means in Table 4: 5.7% before vs 4.9% after (10 people); 0.0 vs 0.0 (6); 2.81 vs 3.57 (5) and 4.28 vs 5.91 (32) in the study of 37 patients by Tjio et al., not statistically significant; 1.0 vs 4.78 after intravenous LSD (3 people, the only significant difference).
key_findings.locator: Table 4 and caption (p. 434); Before and after LSD Use, 1st, 4th and 6th paragraphs (p. 435)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that moderate doses of pharmaceutical LSD taken by mouth do not break human chromosomes, qualified in the summary as their belief that such doses produce no chromosome damage "detectable by available methods", and relate positive reports to the more general effects of heavy illicit drug use rather than to LSD.
key_findings.locator: Illicit LSD and Chromosome Damage, last paragraph (p. 434); Before and after LSD Use, last paragraph (p. 436); Summary and Conclusion, 2nd paragraph (p. 439)

key_findings.finding: On cancer the authors found no significant research: the hypothesis came from chromosome patterns; the case reports were one person with acute leukaemia who had used illicit LSD and other drugs (a Ph1-like chromosome in all 35 blood cells examined) and two people with leukaemia after pharmaceutical LSD (one in a family with many childhood cancers, one without details). They conclude that, as of then, there appeared to be no definite evidence that LSD is a carcinogen.
key_findings.locator: Is LSD a Carcinogen?, 1st to 4th paragraphs (p. 436); Summary and Conclusion, 3rd paragraph (p. 439)

key_findings.finding: In fruit flies (Drosophila), LSD produced no increase in mutations at 0.28 to 500 μg/ml but significant increases in lethal mutations at 2,000 to 10,000 μg/ml; by injection, effects appeared only at 470 μg/g or more, which the authors equate to about 30 × 10^6 μg in a 70-kg man; fungus cells showed no effect at 20 to 50 μg/ml. The authors call LSD a weak mutagen effective only at extremely high doses.
key_findings.locator: Is LSD a Mutagen?, 1st to 5th paragraphs (p. 436, right column, to p. 437)

key_findings.finding: Animal teratology was inconsistent: malformations after doses early in gestation in several mouse strains (for example 57% of offspring vs 7.8% of controls in one study) but not in other strains; in hamsters, 5 to 8% malformations after doses on day 8 were not confirmed at higher doses; in Wistar rats malformation rates stayed near zero (0.0% to 1.0% in Table 5), but stunted and stillborn offspring followed an early dose, the same team's larger repeat found litter damage three to four times that in controls (Table 5 marks it positive), and very high doses disrupted pregnancy in another study. The authors summarize that a teratogenic effect had been reported in hamsters, rats and mice but that only the mouse data had been confirmed. In rhesus monkeys given repeated injections at doses at least 100 times the usual human experimental dose, one of four infants was normal, two were stillborn with facial deformities and one died at one month, while two controls were normal; the authors call these preliminary primate data suggestive of a teratogenic effect.
key_findings.locator: Table 5 (p. 436); Is LSD a Teratogen?, 2nd to 10th paragraphs (pp. 437–438) and 16th paragraph (p. 439)

key_findings.finding: Human pregnancy: of 14 children exposed to illicit LSD in utero, 10 had raised breakage rates, and all were healthy without birth defects; six malformed infants had been reported after maternal illicit LSD use (four with similar limb defects), none after pharmaceutical LSD. In one series of 148 pregnancies (McGlothlin et al.), spontaneous abortions were 37% when parents had used both pure and illicit LSD vs 15% with pure LSD only and 20% in the general population, but only 12 pregnancies involved LSD during gestation (3 with pure LSD), and one woman accounted for 5 of the 10 abortions in the combined group; without her, the rate was 24% in the group exposed to pure and illicit LSD before pregnancy and 14.4% for exposure during pregnancy.
key_findings.locator: Is LSD a Teratogen?, 11th to 14th paragraphs (p. 438, continuing on p. 439); Summary and Conclusion, 6th paragraph (p. 439)

key_findings.finding: The only study of human germ cells reviewed (a testicular biopsy, Hulten et al.) found no increase in meiotic chromosome aberrations 6 months after heavy use of illicit LSD and other drugs.
key_findings.locator: Is LSD a Teratogen?, 15th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: The closing paragraph, based on the authors' own work and their review of the literature, gives as their belief that pure LSD taken by mouth in moderate doses does not damage chromosomes in the body, causes no detectable genetic damage and is neither a teratogen nor a carcinogen in man; within these bounds they suggest that, other than during pregnancy, there was no present contraindication to continued controlled experimental use of pure LSD.
key_findings.locator: Summary and Conclusion, 7th paragraph (right column)

reporting_issues.issue: The control breakage rate in Irwin and Egozcue's first study is given as 11.0% in the text (p. 432) but as 11.9% in Table 2 and again in the text on p. 433.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the description nearly double fits 23.4% against 11.9% better than against 11.0%.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the positive pure-LSD row labelled ref. 48 (1 subject, 200 cells, 12.00% breaks; controls 6 subjects, 925 cells, 3.7%; sampled 8 months after LSD) matches the single patient of Cohen et al. (ref. 1), described on p. 435 as showing damage 8 months after the last LSD treatment, and the control cells of Cohen et al. in Table 1 (925 cells, 3.7%); ref. 48 is Tjio et al., described as a negative before-and-after study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reference label appears misprinted; readers tracing the single positive pure-LSD case would be sent to the wrong study.

reporting_issues.issue: For A/Cum mice the text gives malformed embryos of 19% vs 10% in controls (p. 437), while Table 5 gives 19% vs 3.3% for the same positive study (ref. 12, p. 436).
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the reported mouse effect differs between text and table.

reporting_issues.issue: The cross-study tallies count people whose breakage was above a control mean, or significantly above controls, as each study defined it, and some studies reported only rates within normal limits (Table 2). Editors' observation: even with no effect at all, a sizeable share of exposed people, up to about half, could exceed a control mean by chance, so less than half of people who used illicit LSD (90 of 184) is not in itself evidence against an effect, and the 14.29% vs 48.9% contrast compares different studies, laboratories and criteria rather than like-for-like rates.
reporting_issues.consequence: The more-than-threefold contrast between people given pure LSD and people using illicit LSD is a rough indication, not a rate ratio, though the authors' conclusion leans on it.

reporting_issues.issue: One person with a 9% breakage rate is excluded from a negative pure-LSD group (ref. 47) for being widely deviant (Table 3 footnote, p. 433), and the text counts that study as showing only one doubtful instance of damage (p. 435); no rule for such exclusions is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small in itself, but it shows the counts depend on the reviewers' judgment of single values.

reporting_issues.issue: Several tabulated data sets were unpublished: a personal communication of an unpublished pilot study (ref. 8, Table 1), the authors' own study in preparation (ref. 35, Tables 2–3: 14 people who used illicit LSD and 5 given pure LSD), work cited by Loughman et al. as in preparation that remained unpublished (ref. 36, Table 2: 5 people, within normal limits) and an unpublished study known only as cited by Tjio et al. (ref. 49, Table 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: These data cannot be checked against a published source, and they include the authors' own results.

design_detail: Cross-sectional cytogenetic comparison. Finger-prick blood from 8 people who said they had recently used illicit LSD heavily (clients of a welfare agency in San Francisco; 6 men, 2 women) and from one person with no history of drug use was cultured for 72 hours; squash preparations were scored, by a person who did not know the drug histories, for gross structural aberrations (697 cells in the LSD group, 112 in the control) and for chromosome counts (245 and 112 cells). Further comparisons: 18 earlier controls from the same laboratory (561 cells) and published control data (Schmickel; 1569 cells). The authors did not repeat the culture experiment of Cohen et al.
can_establish: That cultured lymphocytes from these 8 people who reported heavy recent LSD use showed no chromatid breaks in 697 cells scored without knowledge of drug history, a frequency no higher than in this laboratory's controls.
cannot_establish: That LSD does not damage chromosomes: the exposure is self-reported use of illicit drugs of unknown content, there were 8 people and one concurrent control, other drugs were common, only gross aberrations in blood lymphocytes were scored, and dividing tissues and germ cells were not examined.

sample.recruitment: Clients of a welfare agency in San Francisco who claimed recent use of LSD, alone or with other illegal drugs; histories and blood samples were taken at the agency (p. 508). How people were approached and how many declined are not reported. The concurrent control was one person with no history of drug use (p. 508); the 18 earlier controls came from the laboratory's previous work (Table 2, p. 509).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Claimed recent LSD use. The interview asked about the person's own and their parents' possible exposure to dangerous drugs, toxic chemicals, radiation and other agents thought to cause chromosome aberrations; it revealed no exposure to agents known to do so (p. 508). No formal criteria are stated.
sample.demographics: 6 men and 2 women (Table 1, p. 508); ages not reported. Age and sex of the concurrent control not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one sample per person). Chromosome counts are given for 245 of the 697 cells scored for aberrations, without explanation (Tables 2–3, p. 509).
sample.selection_effects: A small self-selected group from a welfare agency, chosen for claimed heavy use; one concurrent control; the earlier and published controls were processed at other times or in other laboratories.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in an extensive interview covering the claimed duration of illegal drug use, the size of each dose and the frequency of use (p. 508). The authors state they depended entirely on the subjects' statements and that the amounts are uncertain; cumulative (integral) doses are estimates from recalled typical dose and frequency (p. 508). No biological verification.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported exposure histories (Table 1, p. 508): typical doses from about 100 to 4000 µg; frequency from 12 to 100 times, or weekly for 9 months, or once or twice a month; estimated cumulative doses 5,000 to 150,000 µg (median 20,500 µg, editors' calculation); latest dose 300 to 4000 µg, taken 1 day (4 people), 5, 6, 7 or 22 days before sampling. One woman (M4) reported 4000 µg one day before sampling. Route not stated.
exposure.polysubstance: Other drugs reported (Table 1, p. 508): amphetamines (dexedrine, methedrine or benzedrine) by 7 of 8, heroin by 3 (code H, which the legend does not define) plus previous heroin addiction (the table's term) by 1, DMT by 2, marijuana by 2; one woman reported no other drugs. Other drugs were not analysed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 1 to 22 days since the latest reported LSD dose (Table 1, p. 508); self-reported.

comparison.controls: One concurrent control with no history of drug use (112 cells); 18 earlier controls from the same laboratory (561 cells); published control data from Schmickel (1569 cells) (Table 2, p. 509).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No sample before LSD use; age, smoking, alcohol, infections and occupational exposures not reported for anyone.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The concurrent control had no history of drug use; not reported for the earlier controls.

outcomes.instruments: 72-hour cultures of two drops of finger blood in NCTC 109 medium with 15 percent fetal bovine serum and 2 percent phytohemagglutinin-M; vinblastine (Velban) 0.5 µg added at 66 hours; hypotonic treatment, fixation in propionic acid, squash preparations in lacto-propionic orcein to reduce chromosome loss and breaks from air-drying (p. 508). Cells with apparently diploid complements were chosen at low power and examined at ×1500; all chosen cells were tabulated (p. 508).
outcomes.validity_norms: Only gross structural changes detectable without karyotyping were scored: dicentrics, rings, acentric fragments, marked changes in size or arm ratio, complex figures such as quadriradials, chromatid breaks and chromatid gaps; minor aberrations needing detailed karyotype analysis were not assessed (p. 508). The categories and the squash method differ from the break-equivalent count of Cohen et al., which the authors say cannot be compared directly with theirs (p. 509).
outcomes.operationalization: Percent of cells with chromatid gaps, chromatid breaks and all other aberrations, with 95% confidence limits; distribution of chromosome counts and polyploidy; mitotic index compared informally with 150 earlier routine cultures (pp. 508–509).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; t-tests at the 5 percent level for all classes of aberration (p. 508).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: An individual with no knowledge of the subjects' drug histories scored the aberrations and chromosome counts (p. 508); whether control and LSD-group slides were coded and mixed is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Chromatid breaks: 0 of 697 cells in the LSD group (95% limits printed 0.0–0.5%), 0 of 112 in the concurrent control, 1 of 561 (0.2%) in earlier controls, 11 of 1569 (0.7%) in published controls. Chromatid gaps: 3/697 (0.4%), 0/112, 4/561 (0.7%), 7/1569 (0.4%). All other aberrations: 0/697, 0/112, 1/561 (a quadriradial), 1/1569 (0.1%) (Table 2, p. 509). Chromosome counts: 46 chromosomes in 200 of 245 cells (81.6%) in the LSD group against 100 of 112 (89.3%) in the control; one tetraploid cell of 245 against none of 112 (Table 3, p. 509). Cells with 40 to 45 chromosomes: 44/245 (18.0%) against 12/112 (10.7%), Fisher exact P=0.09 (editors' calculation; the authors report no significant difference).
analysis.selective_reporting: Test statistics are not reported, only that there were no significant differences (p. 508). Large cells with multiple micronuclei were seen occasionally in LSD-group preparations and never in control cultures, but were not counted or tested (p. 510). Mitotic indices are called comparable without values (p. 509).
analysis.power: Not reported. With 0 breaks in 697 cells the exact upper 95% limit is about 0.5% of cells (editors' calculation, matching the printed limit), so break frequencies of several percent, as reported by laboratories that found damage, would probably have been visible; 8 people cannot exclude an effect in some people only.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people who reported heavy recent illicit LSD use, scored without knowledge of drug history; gap and other aberration frequencies no higher than in one concurrent control, the laboratory's earlier controls or published controls; somewhat more cells with fewer than 46 chromosomes in the LSD group, not significant.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says abnormalities were not significantly greater than in controls (p. 508). The conclusion says LSD in doses as high as 4000 µg "has not been shown to damage the chromosomes" of peripheral blood lymphocytes in vivo, cites unpublished observations (Petrakis) in support, and says other tissues must be examined before damage to dividing cells can be ruled out (p. 510). This stays close to the data, but the doses are self-reported amounts of illicit drugs of unknown content. The estimate that 100 µg in a person gives at most about the lowest concentration used by Cohen et al. (p. 509) rests on mouse distribution data, not on measurements in people. The micronucleated cells seen only in LSD-group preparations are argued away without counts (p. 510).

timeline.event: Cohen et al. reported increased breaks in cultured leukocytes exposed to LSD and 12 percent breakage in one patient treated with LSD; this paper set out to test the patient finding in people.

Irwin and Egozcue (Science 157:313), noted in proof as a comparable study supporting the opposite conclusion (p. 510); 23.6 percent aberrations in 8 people who had used LSD against 9.5 percent in 7 controls (as summarized by Tjio et al., 1969, p. 854; not read).
This paper: no chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use.
Sparkes et al. found break rates in 8 people exposed to LSD similar to those in 4 controls and describe their results as resembling this paper's (p. 1344).

Tjio et al. sampled 32 patients before and after one oral dose of pharmaceutical LSD and found no significant change; they summarize this paper as below 1 percent aberrations in 8 people and 19 controls (p. 854).
Review in Science of whether LSD damages chromosomes or is carcinogenic, mutagenic or teratogenic (not read for this card; to be appraised from its full text).

replication.where_it_stands: Among the studies of people's cells read in this round, this paper and Sparkes et al. (1968) found no excess in people exposed to LSD, and Tjio et al. (1969) found no significant change before and after pharmaceutical LSD. Positive reports from other laboratories (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn & Frosch, 1967) are known here only from these papers' summaries and have not been appraised. A later review (Dishotsky et al., 1971) is in the library but was not read for this card.

what_would_settle_it: Chromosome studies of the same people before and after LSD of known content and amount, with comparison people who take no LSD sampled at the same intervals, coded slides scored blind, enough cells per sample, and records of other drugs and infections (Tjio et al., 1969, did the before-and-after part without a concurrent untreated group).

domains.note: No adjustment; amphetamines used by 7 of 8 and heroin by 4 of 8; ages unknown; one concurrent control; earlier and published controls from other times and laboratories.
Self-reported illicit LSD of unknown content and amount; cumulative doses estimated from recall; no verification.
Convenience sample of welfare-agency clients claiming heavy use; how they were selected and how many declined not reported.

Chromosome counts on 245 of 697 cells without explanation; mitotic indices not given.

Scorer blind to drug histories, but cells were preselected as apparently diploid at low power, only gross aberrations were scored, and the squash method differs from that of the laboratories reporting damage.
No test statistics; micronucleated cells seen only in LSD-group preparations were not counted.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E for an observational comparison of exposed and unexposed people. The outcome was scored without knowledge of drug history and the counts are complete and internally consistent, so the null observation itself (no breaks in 697 cells) is credible for these 8 people. The overall judgment is high because the exposure is self-reported illicit drug use of unknown content, the 8 were a convenience sample from a welfare agency with frequent use of amphetamines and heroin, there was one concurrent control, ages are not reported, and only gross aberrations were scored in cells preselected as apparently diploid. Citable for: no chromatid breaks in cultured lymphocytes of 8 people reporting heavy recent illicit LSD use, with denominators and the comparison rates; the authors' argument that the control rate of Cohen et al. was high relative to published controls. Not citable for: absence of chromosome damage from LSD in general, effects on dividing tissues or germ cells, or the concentrations reached in people (the authors' estimate rests on mouse data).

key_findings.finding: From mouse data on carbon-14-labelled LSD, the authors estimate that 100 µg in a 70-kg person gives a uniform 0.0014 µg/g, about 0.0004 µg/g in blood after 30 minutes and on average about 0.0012 µg/g in the liver, about the lowest concentration used by Cohen et al., or a tenth of it if breakdown products are inactive; for the person who took 4000 µg the day before, about 40 times more, near Cohen's 0.01 and 0.1 µg/ml.
key_findings.locator: Text, 8th to 11th paragraphs (p. 509, left to right columns) and 12th paragraph (p. 509, right column, continuing on p. 510)

key_findings.finding: Large cells with multiple micronuclei were found occasionally in squash preparations from the LSD group and not in control cultures; no count or frequency is given. The authors say they might be the progeny of stem cells exposed to high LSD concentrations in the body, but set this aside because chromosome damage would then also be expected in cells reaching metaphase, and none was seen. Reason: the source never says they were not counted, and the card omitted the authors' stem-cell suggestion.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that LSD in doses as high as 4000 µg has not been shown to damage chromosomes of peripheral blood lymphocytes in vivo, and that other tissues must be examined before damage to actively dividing cells can be ruled out.

design_detail: Cross-sectional cytogenetic comparison of three groups of four: people who had taken LSD privately (psychiatric patients who had sought help, usually after LSD use; called the private-use group here), patients who had been treated with LSD for psychoneurotic reactions (the medically treated group), and hospital volunteers without known exposure to drugs, radiation or recent viral infection. Each person's blood was split and cultured separately in two laboratories (72-hour cultures, Giemsa stain); breaks, gaps and rearrangements were scored with the criteria of Cohen et al. in 198 to 245 cells per person, 2801 cells in all. Groups were compared with Mann-Whitney U tests.
can_establish: That in these eight people exposed to LSD, chromosome break frequencies in cultured lymphocytes were in the same range as in four unexposed volunteers, with the same result in two laboratories.
cannot_establish: Whether LSD damages chromosomes or not: four people per group give almost no power (with 4 against 4, a two-sided Mann-Whitney test reaches P<0.05 only if the groups do not overlap at all), the groups differ in age, psychiatric illness and other drugs, the amounts and content of privately taken LSD were unknown, and blinding of the scorers is not reported.

sample.recruitment: Controls: hospital volunteers not exposed to known causes of chromosome damage (p. 1343), chosen for no exposure to drugs or radiation and no recent viral infection (Table 1 legend). Private-use group: patients seeking psychiatric help, usually after LSD use. Medically treated group: patients treated with LSD for medical reasons (p. 1343). The acknowledgments thank J. T. Ungerleider for making patients available (ref. 8, p. 1345). How patients were chosen from those available is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Exposed groups: no unusual exposure to radiation and no recent viral infection (Table 1 legend, p. 1343). No other criteria reported.
sample.demographics: Controls: women aged 21 and 50, men aged 21 and 25 (p. 1343). Private-use group: aged 19 to 24, 2 women and 2 men; diagnoses psychotic reaction to LSD, schizoid personality, dysocial personality and schizophrenic reaction. Medically treated: aged 28 to 45, 1 woman and 3 men, all with psychoneurotic reactions (Table 1, p. 1343).
sample.attrition: None reported; all 12 people have results (Tables 2–3, p. 1344).
sample.selection_effects: Psychiatric patients, one of them with a psychotic reaction to LSD, compared with hospital volunteers; the groups differ in age; the private-use group was drawn from people who sought psychiatric help after LSD use, who are not representative of people who use LSD.

exposure.measurement: Private-use group: as reported by the patients; the authors note that people who take LSD privately may not know the amount or whether the drug was really LSD (p. 1343). Medically treated group: doses received in therapy; the source of these figures is not stated (Table 1). No biological verification.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure histories (Table 1, p. 1343). Private-use group: A, 50 doses of 250–1000 µg (total 25,000 µg) over 24 months, last dose 500 µg 1 month before bleeding; B, 75 doses of unknown size over 12 months, last dose 3 months before; C, unknown number and size over 18 months, last dose 300–1000 µg 0.25 month before; D, 10 doses of 350 µg (3,500 µg) over 5 months, last dose 6 months before. Medically treated group: E, 50 doses of 300 µg (15,000 µg) over 12 months, last dose 60 months before; F, 63 doses of 250 µg (15,750 µg) over 48 months, last dose 2 months before; G, 100 doses of 250 µg (25,000 µg) over 24 months, last dose 3 months before; H, 12 doses of 250–500 µg (3,500 µg) over 48 months, last dose 1 month before. Route not stated.
exposure.polysubstance: Private-use group: probable marijuana in all four; one person (A) also DMT and STP (4-methyl-2,5-dimethoxy-α-methylphenethylamine). Medically treated group: probable marijuana in one (F), methylphenidate (Ritalin) in one (G), none in two (Table 1, p. 1343). The authors note that most subjects had been exposed to other drugs, which makes any link with LSD less clear (p. 1344). Other drugs were not analysed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Last LSD dose 0.25 to 60 months before the blood sample (Table 1); private-use timing as reported by the patients.

comparison.controls: Four hospital volunteers (women aged 21 and 50, men aged 21 and 25) without known exposure to drugs, radiation or recent viral infection (p. 1343; Table 1 legend).
comparison.matching: None; the groups differ in age and psychiatric status.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No samples before LSD exposure; psychiatric illness and its treatments, smoking, alcohol and infections other than recent viral illness not addressed.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls were chosen for no exposure to drugs (Table 1 legend).

outcomes.instruments: Blood from each person divided between two laboratories. Laboratory 1: whole blood in TC-199 with L-glutamine and 20 percent fetal calf serum, phytohemagglutinin, 72 hours at 37°C in 5 percent CO2, colchicine for the last 3 hours, citrate hypotonic, ethanol–acetic acid fixation, flame-dried slides, Giemsa (p. 1343). Laboratory 2: F-10 medium with 20 percent fetal calf serum in closed tubes (p. 1343). Unbroken cells with minimal chromosome overlap were chosen at ×250 and photographed at ×1000; film negatives were viewed by two of the authors and damaged cells were printed and classified (p. 1343).
outcomes.validity_norms: Criteria of Cohen et al.: chromatid breaks, isochromatid breaks and fragments as single breaks; rings and dicentrics by the minimum number of breaks needed to form them; quadriradials as two-break aberrations; chromatid and isochromatid gaps recorded and added to breaks as an alternative measure (p. 1343). Results as percent of aberrant cells and aberrations per 100 cells, with and without gaps (Table 3, p. 1344). The authors note their control break rates were lower than those of laboratories reporting damage (p. 1343).
outcomes.operationalization: Chromosomal damage = breaks and their equivalents per cell, with a secondary measure that adds gaps.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported; several comparisons (each laboratory, laboratory against laboratory, group against group on combined data) are reported as non-significant without statistics (p. 1344).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported: the paper does not say whether slides or photographs were coded or whether the two authors who viewed them knew group membership (p. 1343).

analysis.effect_sizes: Aberrations from breaks only, per 100 cells: controls 1.6 (15/950), private-use group 2.2 (21/937), medically treated 1.5 (14/914); aberrant cells (breaks): 1.5% (14/950), 1.4% (13/937), 1.4% (13/914). Including gaps: aberrations 8.0% (76/950), 5.9% (55/937), 6.5% (59/914); aberrant cells 5.4% (51/950), 4.7% (44/937), 4.8% (44/914) (Table 3, p. 1344). Per person, break aberrations ranged 0.8 to 2.6 per 100 cells in controls, 0.9 to 3.4 in the private-use group and 0.4 to 2.5 in the medically treated group (Table 3). Mann-Whitney U tests: no significant differences, statistics not printed (p. 1344). Editors' recalculation on per-person break aberration rates: exact two-sided P=0.34 for controls against the private-use group and P=0.89 for controls against the medically treated group; with 4 against 4 the smallest possible two-sided P is 0.029.
analysis.selective_reporting: Results by laboratory are not shown, although the authors say they were analysed separately and did not differ (pp. 1343–1344); the correlation of damage with total exposure and with time since the last dose, and the comparison of chromosome counts, are reported without numbers (p. 1344).
analysis.power: Not reported. With four people per group only complete separation of two groups could reach P<0.05 (editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Break aberrations of 1.5 to 2.2 per 100 cells in the three groups of four, reported as similar in two laboratories; quadriradials only in people exposed to LSD (one each in 3 of 8); chromosome interchanges in one control (a ring) and one person in the private-use group (one tricentric and two dicentric chromosomes).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the studies "failed to demonstrate significant chromosomal damage" (p. 1343), and the text says no significant damage was found in vivo (p. 1343). The discussion is cautious: it notes the quadriradials in exposed people only, that samples from the same people before and after LSD would be more informative, that results in isolated cells may not represent cells in the body, that most subjects had other drugs, and that a possible increase in malignant potential by analogy should not be read as evidence of an oncogenic effect (p. 1344). It also says that, from the authors' experience and the literature, there appears to be no definite effect on the gametes of parents who took LSD, without presenting data (p. 1344). The main gap is power: a failure to demonstrate damage with four people per group says little about whether an effect exists.

timeline.event: Cohen et al. reported increased breaks in cultured leukocytes exposed to LSD and in one patient; this paper used their scoring criteria.

Irwin and Egozcue (Science 157:313) and Cohen, Hirschhorn and Frosch (N Engl J Med 277:1043) reported damage in people who had used LSD; this paper notes that both teams also had higher control break rates and less complete culture media (p. 1344; neither paper read).
Loughman et al. found no chromatid breaks in 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use; this paper describes its results as resembling theirs (p. 1344).
This paper: no significant difference between 4 controls, 4 people who had taken LSD privately and 4 patients treated with LSD; quadriradials only in exposed people.

Tjio et al. sampled 32 patients before and after one oral dose of pharmaceutical LSD and found no significant change; they summarize this paper as 1.8 percent aberrations in eight people against 1.6 percent in four controls (p. 854).
Review in Science of whether LSD damages chromosomes or is carcinogenic, mutagenic or teratogenic (not read for this card; to be appraised from its full text).

replication.where_it_stands: Among the studies of people's cells read in this round, this paper and Loughman et al. (1967) found no excess in people exposed to LSD, and Tjio et al. (1969) found no significant change before and after pharmaceutical LSD in the same patients; positive reports from other laboratories are known here only from these papers' summaries. A later review (Dishotsky et al., 1971) is in the library but was not read for this card.

what_would_settle_it: Chromosome studies of the same people before and after LSD of known content, with comparison people who take no LSD sampled at the same times, coded slides scored by readers who do not know group or timing, and enough people per group to detect a moderate rise in break frequency.

domains.note: No adjustment; groups differ in age (controls 21–50, private use 19–24, medically treated 28–45), psychiatric illness and other drugs (marijuana in 5 of 8 exposed, DMT and STP in one, methylphenidate in one).
Private use: self-reported, amounts unknown for two of four and content uncertain, as the authors note. Medically treated: doses given, source of the figures not stated.
Patients made available by a psychiatrist and hospital volunteers; how they were chosen and whether others declined is not reported.
Psychiatric treatment of the patients after LSD exposure, which could include other drugs, is not reported.
All 12 people reported with cell counts.
Duplicate culture in two laboratories with published criteria is a strength; blinding of the two scorers to group is not reported.
Per-laboratory results, the correlation with exposure and the chromosome counts are reported without numbers or test statistics.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E for an observational comparison of exposed and unexposed people. Duplicate culture in two laboratories and complete, internally consistent tables (Table 3 reproduces Table 2 under the stated scoring rules) are strengths. The overall judgment is high because groups of four differ in age, psychiatric illness and other drug use without adjustment, half of the exposed group's LSD amounts and content are unknown, the selection of patients is not described and blinding of the scorers is not reported; with four per group the non-significant tests carry almost no information about whether an effect exists. Citable for: break frequencies with denominators in these 12 people, similar in two laboratories; quadriradials in 3 of 8 exposed people and none of 4 controls, as an observation. Not citable for: absence of chromosome damage from LSD, effects on gametes or children (no data), or comparisons with other laboratories' rates (methods differ).

design_detail: Prospective before-and-after (pre–post) cytogenetic study nested in double-blind studies of LSD-assisted psychotherapy at Spring Grove State Hospital, Baltimore. 32 hospitalized patients with alcoholism or neurosis who had never taken LSD gave blood 0 to 66 days before and 1 to 10 days after one oral dose of pharmaceutical LSD: 50 µg (low-dose group, 11 patients) or 250 to 450 µg (high-dose group, 21). Coded specimens were cultured for 72 hours (macro cultures) at the National Institutes of Health, and at least 200 metaphases per sample were scored by one cytogeneticist who did not know treatment status or dose; the outcome was the percent of metaphases with any aberration (gaps not scored), compared before and after with Wilcoxon signed-ranks tests. Smaller series: 5 people with previous black-market LSD use sampled daily before and after oral LSD (1 and 2 µg/kg) in an NIH study; 8 people sampled only 2 months to 1¼ years after LSD given in research; 2 people who had never taken LSD sampled on 8 to 10 consecutive days; repeat samples in 8 patients, one of whom (BV) is not among the 32.
can_establish: Whether, in these patients, the share of cultured blood lymphocytes with chromosome aberrations changed between a sample taken before and a sample taken 1 to 10 days after one oral dose of pharmaceutical LSD, with scoring blind to treatment status.
cannot_establish: That LSD causes no chromosome damage in people: no concurrent group without LSD was sampled, so changes over time from other drugs, infections or chance are not separated from LSD; each patient was sampled once after the dose; only blood lymphocytes in 72-hour cultures were studied, not dividing tissues or germ cells; and the study says nothing direct about illicit LSD of unknown content or about repeated heavy use.

sample.recruitment: Hospitalized patients with alcoholism or neurosis who volunteered for double-blind controlled studies of LSD-assisted psychotherapy, part of NIMH-sponsored research at Spring Grove State Hospital, Baltimore, were designated for the chromosome study (p. 849). How the 32 were chosen among trial participants is not stated. The five people with previous black-market LSD use were volunteers in an NIH study of sensory, cognitive and perceptual function under LSD (p. 853). The eight research subjects had received LSD in earlier research experiments under medical control (p. 853). Two people who had never taken LSD served as serial controls (p. 853).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Patients: no previous exposure to LSD (p. 849). No other criteria stated.
sample.demographics: 32 patients: mean age 38.2 years in Table 2 (37.8 in the text), range 20 to 56; 5 women and 27 men (pp. 850–851). Five NIH volunteers aged 23 to 35; the two serial controls aged 30 and 38 (p. 853; Table 4).
sample.attrition: All 32 patients analysed. A 33rd patient, BV (350 µg), appears only in Table 3: his pre-LSD culture did not grow, his post-LSD rate was 11.11% and a repeat 3.38% (Table 3, p. 851); the text does not mention him. Patient AG could not be re-sampled (p. 853). In the NIH series two cultures showed no mitosis (Table 4, p. 852).
sample.selection_effects: Psychiatric inpatients, mostly in treatment for alcoholism and mostly receiving other drugs; results may not carry over to people taking LSD outside hospital. The NIH volunteers and research subjects had taken LSD before and agreed to further research.

exposure.measurement: Pharmaceutical LSD from 1-ml ampoules of 100 µg (p. 849), supplied by Sandoz (p. 856), given by mouth at doses set in the psychotherapy studies; at the time of bleeding the dose to be given, or already given, was not known to those handling the samples (p. 849).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: one oral dose of 50 µg (11 patients) or 250 to 450 µg (21 patients: 450 µg in 15, 350 µg in 4, 300 µg in 1, 250 µg in 1) (Tables 1–2, pp. 850–851); some patients had a second session before a repeat sample (Table 3). NIH series: LSD by mouth at 1 µg/kg and 2 µg/kg, twice in four people and three times in one, over consecutive days; earlier black-market use 4 to 36 times at an estimated 100 to 150 µg each (p. 853; Table 4). Research subjects sampled only afterwards: cumulative 300 to 4,800 µg over 1 to 26 sessions (Table 5, p. 852).
exposure.polysubstance: 31 of 32 patients received drugs in hospital before the pre-LSD sample (only BR did not): paraldehyde, phenobarbital, trihexyphenidyl, nortriptyline, amitriptyline, diphenylhydantoin, thioridazine, chlorpromazine, perphenazine, fluphenazine, imipramine and hydroxyzine; 6 (AC, AE, BB, BL, BS, BT) were taking one when the pre-LSD sample was drawn; BJ took phenformin 50 mg daily throughout, including the LSD day; 18 had a psychoactive drug within 14 days of the pre-LSD sample (p. 852). Most were in alcohol withdrawal and detoxification (p. 852). Drugs between the pre- and post-LSD samples are not reported. Other drug use by the NIH volunteers is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Patients had never taken LSD before the study. Post-LSD samples 1 to 10 days after the dose (Table 2); NIH series final samples within 48 hours of the last dose (p. 853).

comparison.controls: Each patient's own pre-LSD sample, drawn 0 to 66 days before the dose, more than half within 2 weeks (p. 850; Table 2). No concurrent group without LSD. Two people who had never taken LSD were sampled on 8 to 10 consecutive days (mean 2.65%) as a reference for day-to-day variation (p. 853; Table 4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Changes between the two samples other than LSD: other drugs, alcohol withdrawal, infections (four documented upper respiratory infections), laboratory variation and regression of unusually high baseline values; no untreated patients were sampled at the same intervals.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The two serial controls had never taken LSD; their other drug use is not reported.

outcomes.instruments: 72-hour macro cultures (8 ml minimum essential medium Eagle, 1 ml buffy-coat leukocyte suspension, 1 ml autologous serum, phytohemagglutinin M, plastic T-flasks), colcemide for the last two hours, citrate hypotonic, alcohol–acetic acid fixation, air-dried, Giemsa (pp. 849–850). At least 200 metaphases per sample analysed by J.H.T.; aberrations classified as chromatid breaks, isochromatid breaks, free fragments, chromatid exchanges, multiple aberrations (breaks, fragments or exchanges together, severe fragmentation) and chromosome-type aberrations (rings, dicentrics); gaps not scored because they can be confused with secondary constrictions (p. 850).
outcomes.validity_norms: The rate is the percent of metaphases with at least one aberration, not the number of breaks per cell used by Cohen et al.; the authors chose cells over individual aberrations because aberrations are hard to count objectively in cells with multiple damage, and report that total aberrations scored for the first 20 samples did not differ from the overall data, without showing them (p. 855).
outcomes.operationalization: Chromosome damage = percent of metaphases with aberrations of all types, before against after LSD (p. 850; Table 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the total and each of the six types were tested, all non-significant (p. 851).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Specimens were coded; at bleeding the dose was not known; the scorer had no knowledge of the subject's treatment status; samples were identified by treatment status and dose only after tabulation (pp. 849–850). Repeat cultures were coded and mixed with specimens from another drug study (p. 853). For the NIH series the same method and laboratory were used; blinding is not separately described (p. 853).

analysis.effect_sizes: Mean percent of metaphases with aberrations before and after LSD: low-dose group 4.05 and 9.26 (mean change +5.21; Wilcoxon P=0.15); high-dose group 4.39 and 4.16 (−0.23; P=0.8); all 32, 4.28 and 5.91 (+1.63; P=0.3) (Table 2, p. 851). Editors' calculations from Table 2: median change +0.46 points; 18 increased, 12 decreased, 2 unchanged; SD of the changes 8.19 points; 95% CI of the mean change about −1.3 to +4.6 points (t distribution; the changes are skewed by two large increases); exact two-sided Wilcoxon P=0.18 for the low-dose group. The low-dose mean change is driven by AD (+20.64) and AG (+34.42); without AD, AG and BJ the mean change of the remaining 29 is −0.53 (editors' calculation). NIH series: mean of last pre-LSD samples 2.81%, of final post-LSD samples 3.57% as printed (+0.76; not significant by Fisher's exact test) (p. 853; Table 6); two people who had never taken LSD averaged 2.65% (Table 4). Eight research subjects 67 to 443 days after their last session: mean 2.79%, range 1.96 to 3.85% (Table 5, p. 852).
analysis.covariates: None; exclusion analyses for infections and other drugs.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not shown, only reported as non-significant: the tests for each type of aberration (p. 851), the comparison across the ten post-LSD days for a peak (p. 855) and the total-aberration counts for the first 20 samples (p. 855). The standard deviations printed under Table 2 (2.12, 4.61 and 3.90) are those of the pre-LSD rates, not of the before–after changes (editors' recalculation). Patient BV is left out of the analysis without comment.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 32 pairs and an SD of change of about 8 points, the study could not exclude a mean increase of up to about 4.6 points (editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 32 patients given one oral dose of pharmaceutical LSD, the share of aberrant metaphases did not change significantly overall (4.28% before, 5.91% after), but 3 patients had large increases (to 23.08%, 43.92% and 14.16%); the two who could be re-sampled were back near their baseline 71 and 229 days later. Two patients with high pre-LSD rates, who had stopped their other medicines 6 days before that sample (p. 853), fell sharply. Five people with previous black-market use showed no significant change after laboratory LSD, and eight research subjects sampled months after LSD were within the range of the patients' baselines.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes there is "no definite evidence that pure LSD damages chromosomes" of human lymphocytes in vivo as studied in 72-hour cultures (p. 849), and the last paragraph says no definitive evidence (p. 856). This is close to the data, and the authors limit it to white blood cells in 72-hour cultures, not germ cells or cells dividing in the body (pp. 855–856). Overreach: the title calls the study A Controlled Experiment, but the control is each patient's earlier sample (the double-blind design belongs to the psychotherapy trials); non-significant tests on skewed changes are presented as consistent support; the conclusion of no dose relationship rests on comparing group means driven by two patients (p. 851); and the large transient increases are attributed to infection (AG) or set aside, although the authors acknowledge that large transient fluctuations occur with or without LSD (p. 855). The statement that LSD should not be given in pregnancy rests on mixed animal studies and case reports, not on this study (p. 856).

timeline.event: Cohen et al. reported increased breaks in cultured leukocytes exposed to LSD, which this paper names as the start of public concern (p. 849).

Studies of people who had used illicit LSD reporting more aberrations than controls, as summarized here (p. 854; not read): Irwin and Egozcue, 23.6% in 8 against 9.5% in 7 controls; Cohen, Hirschhorn and Frosch, 13.2% in 18 against 3.8% in 12; Zellweger et al., 8% in 3 against 3.5%; and in 1968 Egozcue, Irwin and Maruffo, 18.76% in 46 against 9.03% in 14, and Nielsen et al., more gaps and breaks in patients treated with LSD or with other psychotropic drugs than in controls.
Loughman et al.: no chromatid breaks in 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use.

Sparkes et al.: no significant difference between 8 people exposed to LSD and 4 controls; Bender and Sankar reported under 2% aberrations in 5 children given LSD (as summarized here, p. 854; not read).

Hungerford et al. (JAMA 206:2287), a before-and-after study of 3 patients: a transient increase during three LSD sessions, slight in two, with a return below pre-LSD levels 1 to 6 months later (as summarized here, p. 855; not read). Abuzzahab et al. (unpublished) found no difference before and after LSD in 6 patients with alcoholism (p. 855).
This paper: no significant change before and after one oral dose of pharmaceutical LSD in 32 patients.
Review in Science of whether LSD damages chromosomes or is carcinogenic, mutagenic or teratogenic (not read for this card; to be appraised from its full text).

replication.where_it_stands: This was the largest before-and-after study among those it reviews; the earlier ones had 3 patients (Hungerford et al., 1968: transient increase, then below baseline) and 6 patients (Abuzzahab et al., unpublished: no difference) (p. 855). Comparisons of people who had used illicit LSD with controls were split, four reporting more aberrations and three, plus unpublished observations, not (pp. 849, 854). A later review (Dishotsky et al., 1971) is in the library but was not read for this card.

what_would_settle_it: A before-and-after study with a concurrent randomized group given no LSD or an inactive placebo and sampled at the same intervals, several samples per person before and after, coded slides scored by more than one blinded reader, records of other drugs and infections in both groups, and a pre-specified analysis of the change with a stated threshold for a meaningful increase.

domains.note: Before-and-after comparison without a concurrent untreated group: other drugs (31 of 32 patients), alcohol withdrawal, infections and day-to-day variation, which the authors say can be large with or without LSD, change between samples; very high baselines fell (BG, BH), as regression to the mean would predict.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because LSD was given as a treatment in a clinical study and the question is a harm of that intervention; the tool is built for comparisons between groups, and here it is applied to each patient compared with an earlier self. Coded specimens scored blind to treatment status, with at least 200 metaphases per sample and a standard macro-culture method, make the outcome measurement the strongest of the LSD–chromosome studies read in this round. The overall judgment is serious because no concurrent group without LSD was sampled at the same intervals, so other drugs (given to 31 of 32), infections and day-to-day variation are not separated from LSD; the changes are skewed and the printed dispersion describes the baselines, not the changes; and several analyses are reported only as non-significant. Citable for: no significant change in the share of aberrant metaphases between samples taken before and 1 to 10 days after one oral dose of pharmaceutical LSD in 32 patients, with the means, the confidence interval of the change (editors' calculation) and the three large transient increases; the NIH and post-only series as small supporting observations. Not citable for: proof that LSD causes no chromosome damage, effects of repeated or illicit use, effects on dividing tissues or germ cells, or a conclusion about dose.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints P=0.15 for the low-dose group, while the text says P > 0.16 for all three comparisons; an exact recalculation from Table 2 gives P=0.18 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: None on the conclusion (non-significant either way); a sign of loose reporting.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives a mean age of 37.8 years for the 32 patients; Table 2 gives 38.2, which the listed ages reproduce (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The standard deviations printed under each part of Table 2 (2.12, 4.61, 3.90) equal the standard deviations of the pre-LSD rates, not of the before–after changes, although they are printed beside the test of the change; the SD of the changes is 11.59 (low dose), 5.11 (high dose) and 8.19 (all) (editors' recalculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot judge the precision of the mean change from the paper; the change is much more variable than the printed SDs suggest.

reporting_issues.issue: For the five NIH volunteers, the text and Table 6 give a post-LSD mean of 3.57% and a change of +0.76, but the final post-LSD values marked in Table 4 give 3.17% and +0.36; the pre-LSD mean (2.81%) is reproduced. The Fisher exact test is named without the table it was applied to or a P value.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the printed figures is wrong; either way the change is small and not significant, but the test cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the group means vary only from 2.65% to 5.31% (p. 854), but the 32 patients' post-LSD mean is 5.91% (Table 6, p. 853; Table 2, p. 851).
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated range understates the highest group mean; probably a misprint.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 includes a patient, BV, who is not among the 32 in Tables 1 and 2 and is not mentioned in the text: his pre-LSD culture did not grow, his post-LSD rate was 11.11% and a repeat 3.38%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A patient with one of the higher post-LSD rates is outside the analysis without explanation; he could not be paired, but his exclusion should have been stated.

reporting_issues.issue: Patient BL's dose is 350 µg in Tables 1 and 2 but 450 µg for both sessions in Table 3, and his repeat sample was scored on 104 cells, below the stated minimum of 200 per culture.
reporting_issues.consequence: One patient's dose is uncertain and one repeat value is less precise than the method states.

reporting_issues.issue: In summarizing earlier work, the paper reports Cohen et al.'s in vitro results as aberration rates of 6.7% to 36.8%, although those were breaks per cell and the lowest treated value was 0.050; it names Sparkes et al. as Sparks; and its reference to Cohen, Hirschhorn and Frosch gives volume 227 of the N Engl J Med where Sparkes et al. give 277.
reporting_issues.consequence: Comparisons across studies mix different measures; anyone building references from this list should check them.

design_detail: Report with three parts. (1) Cross-sectional comparison of cultured white blood cells from 18 patients with a history of taking LSD, all with a history of other drugs or medicines (Table 1), 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD (Table 3) and 14 drug-free controls, 2 of whom were left out after a viral illness that began within a day of sampling (Table 4); two replicate blood samples per person, coded, cultured in one laboratory and scored in another by one person; results as breaks per 100 cells. (2) Four children of three mothers who had taken LSD during pregnancy (Table 2), compared with the adult controls. (3) In vitro: white blood cells from 6 healthy people cultured for 72 hours with LSD-25 at 0.001 to 10 µg/ml for the last 4, 24 or 48 hours, against untreated cultures; coded slides; breaks per 100 cells, mitotic index and the distribution of breaks among chromosomes (Tables 5 and 6, Figure 2). One sampling time per person and none from before LSD; the only statistical test printed is a chi-square for the distribution of breaks in vitro.
can_establish: That in this laboratory, coded slides from 18 patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines showed more breaks (13.2 per 100 cells) than those of 12 controls without drugs (3.8); that 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD had rates similar to the LSD patients (12.6 on average); and that LSD added to cultured cells was followed by more breaks at every concentration and time tested, without a concentration-response.
cannot_establish: Whether LSD caused the excess in people: there was no sample from before LSD, recruitment and the source and content of the LSD are not described, every LSD patient had a history of other drugs or medicines and the paper's own group taking other drugs without LSD had similar rates, two controls with high rates were left out after the fact, and no statistical comparison is reported. The children were compared only with adults; the concentrations in the dish are not linked to levels in the body; and nothing was measured in germ cells, so nothing can be said about cancer, birth defects or inherited damage.

sample.recruitment: Not described for any group. The LSD group are called patients with a history of LSD ingestion (p. 1046); the third author was assistant director of the psychiatric division of Bellevue Hospital (p. 1043, footnote), and two of his papers are cited, one on untoward reactions to LSD that led to hospital admission (refs. 13 and 32, p. 1049), but where and how the patients, the 6 patients taking other drugs, the 14 controls and the 4 children were found, and how many declined, are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated for the people sampled. In vitro donors: healthy, with no history of prior drug ingestion, radiation exposure or recent viral infection (p. 1043). Two of the 14 controls were left out because a viral infection with high fever and diarrhoea began within 24 hours of their blood sampling; both had high break rates (p. 1046; Table 4).
sample.demographics: LSD group (Table 1, p. 1045): 12 men and 6 women aged 19 to 52 (mean 24.4, editors' calculation; all but one aged 19 to 29), all white (p. 1046). Controls kept (Table 4, p. 1046): 9 men and 3 women aged 22 to 55 (mean 29.2, editors' calculation), all white except one Black man; the two left out were women aged 37 and 23. Other-drug group (Table 3, p. 1045): 4 adults aged 20 to 34 (3 men, 1 woman) and 2 boys aged 9; 2 white and 4 Black. Children (Table 2, p. 1045): 2 girls and 2 boys aged 2 months to 5½ years.
sample.attrition: Two of the 14 controls left out (p. 1046). Cells scored per person ranged from 78 to 300 in the LSD group and from 100 to 314 among the controls (Tables 1 and 4), although the methods describe 4 to 6 cover slips of 50 metaphases each (p. 1044); the shortfall is not explained.
sample.selection_effects: Patients rather than a community sample, with recruitment undescribed; the LSD group was younger than the controls and all had used other drugs or medicines; the other-drug group mixes adults taking prescribed medicines (chlorpromazine in three up to the day of sampling), one man with a long history of several drugs and two 9-year-old boys; controls with high rates were removed after an illness that began after sampling, while infections in the other groups are not reported.

exposure.measurement: LSD use by history: the number of doses and the interval since the last dose for each patient (Table 1, p. 1045), the usual amount per occasion for the group (p. 1046) and other drugs according to the patients' histories (Table 1). Whether the LSD was given in treatment or obtained otherwise is not stated, and nothing was tested; no biological verification. Children: the number of maternal doses during pregnancy and other drugs used in pregnancy (Table 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As reported (Table 1, p. 1045): 2 to 300 doses; last dose 2 weeks to 8 months before sampling (1 month for 9 of the 18); usual amount 300 to 600 µg per occasion (p. 1046), with two patients marked as taking low doses (50 to 100 µg). Children (Table 2; p. 1046): 1 to 4 maternal doses; the two with high rates exposed in the third and fourth months of pregnancy, the two with low rates to low doses late in pregnancy. In vitro (p. 1043): 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10 µg/ml for the last 4, 24 or 48 hours of a 72-hour culture. In people the route is implied only by the word ingestion.
exposure.polysubstance: All 18 had a history of other drugs or medicines (Table 1; p. 1046): amphetamines 15, marijuana 14, other hallucinogens 12, phenothiazines 10 (chlorpromazine at the time of sampling in 2), opiates 5, barbiturates 4, cocaine 4 (editors' count); one patient (case 37) reported only phenothiazines and one (case 26) only marijuana. The authors report no apparent relation between the type or number of other drugs and the break rate (p. 1046), without a test. A separate group of 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD was sampled (Table 3).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 2 weeks to 8 months since the last LSD dose, by history (Table 1). Children: sampled 2 months to 5½ years after birth (Table 2).

comparison.controls: Twelve drug-free controls kept in the analysis (2.0 to 5.5 breaks per 100 cells; 102 breaks in 2674 cells, 3.8) after two with high rates (31.0 and 14.0) were left out for a viral illness beginning within 24 hours of sampling (Table 4, p. 1046); 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD (Table 3, p. 1045). The children were compared with the adult controls; no unexposed children were sampled. In vitro: untreated cultures from the same 6 donors (65 breaks in 1680 cells, 3.9; Table 5).
comparison.matching: The controls are said to have an age and sex distribution similar to that of the LSD patients (p. 1046); they were older on average (29.2 against 24.4 years) and included fewer women (3 of 12 against 6 of 18) (editors' calculation from Tables 1 and 4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No sample from before LSD use; psychiatric diagnoses, infections, x-ray exposure, smoking and alcohol are not reported for the LSD group or the other-drug group.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The controls are described as drug-free, without drug ingestion (p. 1046); alcohol, tobacco and medicines are not detailed.

outcomes.instruments: In people: two drops of capillary blood in microculture tubes, 72 hours at 37°C, vinblastine for the last 2 hours; cultures and slides made in another laboratory (K. H.), the samples coded by W. A. F. and the coded slides sent to Buffalo (M. M. C.); 4 to 6 cover slips per person, mounted at random two to a slide; 50 well-spread metaphases per cover slip chosen at ×250 by workers not involved in scoring; one person analysed the cells at ×2500, as in the in vitro study (pp. 1043–1044). In vitro: whole-blood microcultures, colcemide for the last 2 hours, aceto-orcein stain and phase-contrast microscopy; duplicate cultures of each treatment, two slides each, aiming at 100 cells per treatment per donor; mitotic index from 250 cells per slide (p. 1043).
outcomes.validity_norms: Chromatid and isochromatid breaks counted as single breaks, exchange figures and dicentrics as two; gaps noted but not counted (p. 1043); the two classes of break were combined deliberately (p. 1047). Results are breaks per 100 cells ('per cent breaks', with breaks over cells scored in brackets, Tables 1 to 4), not a share of cells, although Table 5's footnote and the text on case 15 call the figures percentages of cells. The authors call their control rate almost identical to that of the in vitro controls and to earlier published findings (p. 1046).
outcomes.operationalization: Per person, the number of breaks in the cells scored; 'increased' means above the control mean (p. 1046). In vitro, breaks per 100 cells for each concentration and time, the mitotic index and the distribution of breaks across chromosome groups (Tables 5 and 6, Figure 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The only test printed is a chi-square for the distribution of breaks among chromosome groups in vitro (Table 6); the significant mitotic inhibition and the highly significant excess in the LSD patients are reported without a named test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Coded slides, cells chosen by workers not involved in scoring, and one scorer (p. 1044); in vitro slides coded and evaluated blind (p. 1043). When the code was broken, and whether the two controls were left out before or after decoding, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: As printed: LSD patients 13.2 breaks per 100 cells (566 in 4282) against 3.8 (102 in 2674) in 12 controls, called more than three times the control mean and highly significant, without a test (p. 1046). Editors' calculations from Tables 1 and 4: per-person means 13.2 (SD 6.0) against 3.9 (SD 1.2), a difference of 9.3 (Welch 95% interval 6.2 to 12.3; Mann-Whitney P < 0.001); 16 of 18 above the highest control (5.5) and 2 within the control range (5.3 and 5.5). With the two controls left out after a viral illness included: 5.4 pooled (161 in 2974) and a per-person mean of 6.5, a difference in per-person means of 6.6 (1.5 to 11.7). Other-drug group (Table 3): mean of the six rates 12.6 (161 breaks in 1361 cells, 11.8), no different from the LSD group (Mann-Whitney P = 0.84; difference -0.6, 95% interval -7.3 to 6.1) and above the controls (P = 0.008); the paper itself makes neither comparison. Within the LSD group: no rank correlation of the break rate with the number of doses (-0.01) or with months since the last dose (0.10); the 10 with phenothiazines in their history 12.6 per 100 cells, the 8 without 14.0 (pooled counts). Children: 119 breaks in 1000 cells (11.9). In vitro (Table 5): 1009 breaks in 7735 treated cells (13.0) against 65 in 1680 (3.9), 7.7 to 17.5 across the 15 conditions with no consistent concentration-response; mitotic index 6.2% in controls and about 3.0% to 4.7% in treated cultures (Figure 2, editors' reading); breaks among chromosome groups chi-square 209.01, df 8, P < 0.001 (Table 6).
analysis.selective_reporting: No test statistic for the main comparison in people or for the in vitro break rates; per-person cell counts below the number the methods describe are not explained; infections were looked for in the controls but are not reported for the other groups; the six patients taking other drugs are described but compared neither with the LSD group nor with the controls.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines had about three times the break rate of 12 drug-free controls, and so did patients taking chlorpromazine or other drugs without LSD; LSD added to cultured cells was followed by more breaks at every concentration, without a concentration-response; two of four children exposed before birth had high rates, compared only with adults.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion states that "It is now apparent that LSD is capable of causing chromosomal damage" in cells in a dish and in the circulating white blood cells of people who take it (p. 1047, Discussion, 2nd paragraph). It takes the match between the patients' rates and those at 0.001 and 0.01 µg/ml as showing the concentrations cells meet in the body, although every concentration gave similar rates (p. 1047); it reads the children's results as evidence that LSD crosses the placenta and raises the possibility of birth defects, leukaemia and damage to germ cells passed on for generations (p. 1048, Discussion, 7th, 8th and 10th paragraphs), none of which was measured. It notes that 8 of the 18 had taken no phenothiazines yet had raised rates, and that the patients taking chlorpromazine without LSD also had raised rates (pp. 1047–1048), but it does not compare its other-drug group with the LSD group, whose rates were similar.

timeline.event: Cohen, Marinello and Back, the same laboratory: LSD added to cultured white blood cells of two donors at the same five concentrations and three exposure times raised breaks per cell; one man with schizophrenia had 12 percent breakage in 200 cells 8 months after 15 LSD treatments (ref. 2 of this paper).

Irwin and Egozcue: about twice the break rate in 8 volunteers who reported taking LSD as in 9 who had not (23.6 against 11.9 breaks per 100 cells, editors' calculation from their Table 2); cited here for its dicentric chromosomes (ref. 3).
Loughman et al.: no chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use, scored by someone who did not know their drug histories.
This report.

Sparkes et al.: no significant difference in breaks between 8 people exposed to LSD and 4 controls; they note that the laboratories reporting damage had higher control rates and less complete culture media.

The same group's later report (Cohen, Hirschhorn, Verbo and colleagues): 13 of 14 adults exposed to illicit LSD above the control mean (7.53% against 1.20%), and 9.2% in nine children exposed before birth against 4.0% in four whose mothers took LSD only before pregnancy; three adults of the present report not counted again (as described by Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 433 and Table 2; not read).
Tjio et al.: 32 hospital patients sampled before and after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, slides scored blind: no significant change in the share of cells with aberrations.

Dishotsky et al., review: lists this report as positive in vitro (Table 1, p. 432: 8725 treated cells, 7.7 to 17.5%; this report's Table 5 sums to 7735, editors' sum) and says it found a significant increase at the lowest concentration and shortest exposure, which Tjio did not confirm (p. 431), although no test is given here; lists it as positive in people (Table 2, p. 433: 18 people exposed to illicit LSD, 4282 cells, 13.2% against 3.8% in 12 controls), although this report does not say where its patients' LSD came from; and uses its 6 patients taking other drugs (12.6%, not significantly different from 13.2%, p. 434) to attribute raised breakage to drug use in general.

replication.where_it_stands: The excess in people was reported by two laboratories in 1967 and 1968 (this one and Irwin and Egozcue's) and not by others with lower control rates or before-and-after samples (Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969). This report's own group taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates, the basis of the 1971 review's conclusion that the raised rates reflected drug use in general rather than LSD. Its in vitro increase, without a concentration-response, may include the cultures of the same laboratory's earlier report, which the review counts as a separate study. No study read here sampled people before and after LSD with an unexposed group sampled at the same times.
