what_would_settle_it: Blood samples from the same people before and after LSD of known content, with comparison groups matched for age, sex and other drugs and medicines (chlorpromazine in particular) and sampled at the same times, infections recorded in every group in advance, rules for excluding samples fixed before decoding, slides scored blind by more than one reader and a pre-specified statistical comparison; for children, unexposed children of the same ages; for inherited risk, studies of germ cells rather than blood cells.

domains.note: No adjustment. Every LSD patient had a history of other drugs or medicines (amphetamines 15 of 18, phenothiazines 10), and the paper's own group taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates, so confounding could account for the whole excess; the controls were older and included fewer women; infections, x-rays and psychiatric illness are not reported for the patients.
LSD use by history; source, content and amounts unknown; no verification.
Recruitment of patients, controls and children not described; patients rather than a community sample.

Phenothiazines, which the authors say are often given to end a difficult LSD experience, in 10 of 18 (2 at sampling); patients taking chlorpromazine without LSD had raised rates, although the 8 without phenothiazines also had raised rates.

Two of 14 controls left out after an illness that began after sampling (including them reduces the difference from 9.3 to 6.6 breaks per 100 cells, editors' calculation); fewer cells than the methods describe for several people.

Coded slides, cells chosen by others and one scorer are strengths; but the measure is labelled inconsistently, chromatid lesions that can arise in culture dominate, and when the code was broken relative to the exclusions is not stated.
No test for the main comparisons; the comparison of the LSD group with the other-drug group, which the data allow, is not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E for an observational comparison of exposed and unexposed people. Coded slides scored by one person, cells chosen by others, and complete, internally consistent tables (every rate matches its counts, and Tables 5 and 6 agree on 1009 breaks) are strengths, so the rates are credible as measurements. The overall judgment is very high because the comparison of LSD patients with drug-free controls cannot separate LSD from the other drugs and medicines every patient had taken: the paper's own patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates. Recruitment, the source of the LSD and infections in the patients are not described, two controls with high rates were left out after the fact, and no statistical comparison is reported. A second reader may judge confounding high rather than very high; the overall judgment is at least high either way. Citable for: the break rates with denominators in each group, including the similar rates in the other-drug group; the in vitro rates and the absence of a concentration-response; the children's rates as observations. Not citable for: LSD causing chromosome damage in people, the concentrations reached in the body, or any risk of cancer, birth defects or inherited damage.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Human peripheral blood white cells in 72-hour whole-blood microcultures from 6 healthy people (3 men, 3 women) with no history of prior drug ingestion, radiation exposure or recent viral infection (p. 1043). Whether they include the two donors of the same laboratory's earlier report is not stated.
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: LSD-25 in sterile distilled water added at final concentrations of 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 µg/ml 48, 24 or 4 hours before harvest of 72-hour cultures; colcemide for the last 2 hours; duplicate cultures of each treatment; untreated cultures as controls (p. 1043).
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None measured. The authors infer from the similar break rates that 0.001 to 0.01 µg/ml corresponds to what cells meet in the body (p. 1047), an inference Table 5 cannot support, because all five concentrations gave similar rates.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: No: dividing cells kept at a fixed concentration for hours in a dish; the authors themselves note the difficulty of extrapolating from cells in a dish to people (p. 1047).

key_findings.finding: Sampling and blinding: cultures from 22 people who had taken LSD (Table 1) or been exposed to it before birth (Table 2), 6 patients taking other drugs but no LSD (Table 3) and 14 drug-free controls (Table 4); two replicate blood samples per person, collected and coded by one author (W. A. F.); cultures and slides made in another laboratory (K. H.); the coded slides sent to Buffalo (M. M. C.), where workers not involved in scoring chose 50 well-spread metaphases per cover slip on 4 to 6 cover slips per person, and one person analysed them. Specimens from several people were cultured twice.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › In Vivo Studies, 1st paragraph (p. 1043, right column, continuing on p. 1044, left column)

key_findings.finding: Table 1, 18 patients with a history of LSD (12 men, 6 women, aged 19 to 52; 2 to 300 doses; last dose 2 weeks to 8 months before sampling): breaks per 100 cells from 5.3 (16 in 300) to 25.1 (44 in 175); in all, 566 breaks in 4282 cells (13.2). All were white and all had a history of other drugs; 2 (cases 6 and 28) were taking chlorpromazine when sampled. The usual amount per occasion was 300 to 600 µg.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 1045); Results › In Vivo Studies, 2nd paragraph (p. 1046, left column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Controls, Table 4: of 14 people without drug ingestion, said to be of similar age and sex distribution, two women (cases 4 and 13) developed a viral infection with high fever and diarrhoea within 24 hours of sampling and had 31.0 (31 in 100) and 14.0 (28 in 200) breaks per 100 cells; they were left out. The other 12 had 2.0 to 5.5 (102 breaks in 2674 cells, 3.8), which the authors call almost identical to their in vitro controls and earlier published findings.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 and footnotes; Results › In Vivo Studies, 1st paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: controls kept 9 men and 3 women, mean age 29.2, against 12 men and 6 women, mean age 24.4, in the LSD group. With the two controls left out included, the controls' rate is 5.4 (161 in 2974).

key_findings.finding: The authors report that every LSD patient was above the control mean, that the increase was more than three times the control mean and highly significant (no test or statistic given), that there was no apparent correlation of the break rate with the number of doses, the amount per dose or the interval since the last dose, and no apparent relation with the type or number of other drugs; 12 dicentrics and 5 exchange figures were seen in the LSD group and no structural rearrangements in the controls.
key_findings.locator: Results › In Vivo Studies, 2nd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations from Tables 1 and 4: per-person means 13.2 (SD 6.0) against 3.9 (SD 1.2), difference 9.3 (Welch 95% interval 6.2 to 12.3; Mann-Whitney P < 0.001); 16 of 18 above the highest control (5.5), 2 within the control range (cases 28 and 29, 5.3 and 5.5). With the two controls left out included: difference 6.6 (1.5 to 11.7). Spearman rank correlation of the break rate with the number of doses -0.01 and with months since the last dose 0.10.

key_findings.finding: Other drugs in the LSD group by history (Table 1 key): amphetamines in 15 of 18, marijuana 14, other hallucinogens 12, phenothiazines 10 (2 at the time of sampling), opiates 5, barbiturates 4, cocaine 4; case 37 reported only phenothiazines and case 26 only marijuana.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and footnotes
key_findings.note: Editors' count. Pooled break rates: 10 with phenothiazines in their history 12.6 per 100 cells (editors' calculation), 8 without 14.0.

key_findings.finding: Table 3, six patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD: three taking chlorpromazine up to the day of sampling, 17.4 (34 in 195), 21.5 (43 in 200; this woman had also used marijuana for 10 years) and 13.7 (28 in 205) breaks per 100 cells; a man with a history of amphetamines, opiates, marijuana and barbiturates, 9.0 (18 in 200); a 9-year-old boy taking diphenhydramine, 10.0 (26 in 261); and a 9-year-old boy given chlorpromazine and thioridazine until a month before sampling and diphenhydramine in the last week, born with opioid dependence after exposure throughout pregnancy, 4.0 (12 in 300). The authors say the patients receiving chlorpromazine showed a marked increase and were taking it at the time of testing, that 8 of the 18 LSD patients had no phenothiazines and still showed raised rates, that a combined effect of the two drugs cannot be judged, and that controlled studies of chlorpromazine are in progress. Note: editors' calculation as printed (12.6; 161 in 1361, 11.8; P = 0.84; -0.6, -7.3 to 6.1; P = 0.008). The paper reports neither comparison; the 1971 review presents the comparison as Cohen et al.'s and calls 12.6 and 13.2 not significantly different without naming a test (Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 434).
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (p. 1045); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 1047, right column, continuing on p. 1048, left column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: mean of the six rates 12.6 (161 breaks in 1361 cells, 11.8), no different from the 18 LSD patients (Mann-Whitney P = 0.84; difference -0.6, 95% interval -7.3 to 6.1) and higher than the 12 controls (P = 0.008). The paper reports neither comparison; the 1971 review's 'not significantly different' (Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 434) is the review's own.

key_findings.finding: Children exposed before birth (Table 2), four children of three mothers listed by number (2, 14 and 9), numbers that match three of the women in Table 1 (mother 9 is marked as taking low doses in both tables): a girl of 11 months, 4 maternal doses, also amphetamines, cocaine and marijuana in pregnancy, 19.0 (57 in 300); a boy of 2½ years, 1 dose, no other drugs, 13.0 (39 in 300); a girl of 5½ years, 2 doses, marijuana, 7.5 (15 in 200); a boy of 2 months, 4 doses, cocaine and marijuana, 4.0 (8 in 200); in all 119 breaks in 1000 cells (11.9). The two with high rates were exposed in the third and fourth months of pregnancy to the usual amounts, the two with low rates (the same mother) to low doses late in pregnancy. No obvious physical or behavioural abnormalities had been noted in the four children.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 1045); Results › In Vivo Studies, 3rd paragraph (p. 1046, right column); Discussion, 9th paragraph (p. 1048, right column)
key_findings.note: No unexposed children were sampled; the children are compared with adult controls.

key_findings.finding: In vitro, Table 5 (separate cultures from 6 donors, the results pooled for each condition because, the authors say without data, the donors did not differ significantly from each other or by sex): breaks per 100 cells after 48 hours 12.6, 7.7, 17.5, 10.7 and 12.5 at 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 µg/ml; after 24 hours 11.5, 15.8, 13.0, 15.4 and 10.8; after 4 hours 17.1, 10.6, 13.1, 15.2 and 11.2 (65 breaks in 578 cells at 0.001 µg/ml); untreated cultures 3.9 (65 in 1680). The text calls the lowest treated rate almost twice the control and the highest over four times; no test is reported. Most aberrations were chromatid and isochromatid breaks, with a few chromatid exchanges and dicentrics and no rings. (Note unchanged.)
key_findings.locator: Results › In Vitro Studies, 2nd paragraph (p. 1044, left column, continuing in the right column); Table 5 (p. 1046)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 1009 breaks in 7735 treated cells (13.0); the highest rate falls at a different concentration for each exposure time, so there is no concentration-response over a 10,000-fold range. Every condition has more cells and more breaks than the same condition in the laboratory's earlier report (Cohen, Marinello and Back, 1967, Table 1, p. 1417), and the highest rate at each exposure time falls at the same concentration in both (0.1 µg/ml at 48 hours, 1 µg/ml at 24 hours, 10 µg/ml at 4 hours), consistent with the earlier cultures being pooled here, which the paper does not say.

key_findings.finding: Mitotic index: 16,000 cells scored on control slides and about 6000 per treatment; mitosis 6.2% in controls; the authors report significant inhibition at every concentration (no test given), greater with longer exposure (Figure 2: treated cultures about 3.0% to 4.7%, editors' reading). They note that the inhibition was not as obvious in people.
key_findings.locator: Results › In Vitro Studies, 1st paragraph (p. 1044, left column); Figure 2 (p. 1044); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 1047, left column)

key_findings.finding: Distribution of breaks in vitro (Table 6): 930 breaks assigned to chromosomes and 79 unidentifiable; more than expected from chromosome length on chromosome 1 (154 against 80.82), chromosome 2 (119 against 75.70) and group C (420 against 346.52), fewer in groups D, E, F and G; chi-square 209.01, df 8, P < 0.001. Breaks clustered near centromeres and in regions the authors describe as secondary constrictions.
key_findings.locator: Results › In Vitro Studies, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 1045, left column, continuing in the right column and on p. 1046); Table 6 (p. 1047); Figure 3 (p. 1046)
key_findings.note: Editors' check: 930 + 79 = 1009, the sum of the treated breaks in Table 5, so Table 6 covers the in vitro cultures only. The test treats each break as independent, although breaks cluster within cells, cultures and donors.

key_findings.finding: Agreement between replicates, as reported: one control (case 30) 1, 2, 2, 1 and 1 breaks per 50 metaphases on five cover slips from two tubes; another control (case 19) 5 in 100 and 6 in 100 in successive cultures; an LSD patient (case 36) 9/50, 11/45, 9/36, 12/50, 8/50 and 9/33 on six cover slips; a child exposed before birth (case 1) 24 in 100 and 33 in 200 in successive cultures. The authors call the agreement close.

reporting_issues.issue: The measure is labelled inconsistently: Tables 1 to 4 give 'per cent breaks' as breaks over cells scored (Table 4 footnote), but Table 5's footnote calls its percentages '% of cells with breaks', the text calls the in vitro control rate a percentage of cells with abnormalities, and the discussion calls case 15's 13.0 the percentage of cells with damage. Table 5's numerators sum to 1009, the number of breaks distributed in Table 6, so they are breaks.
reporting_issues.consequence: All figures are breaks per 100 cells; comparisons with studies that count the share of cells with an aberration (Tjio et al., 1969) are not like with like.

reporting_issues.issue: No statistical test is given for the main comparison in people ('highly significant'), for the in vitro break rates, for the mitotic inhibition ('significant') or for the absence of differences between the six donors; the only test printed, the chi-square of Table 6, treats 930 breaks as independent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size and precision of the differences had to be recomputed (editors' calculations); Table 6's P < 0.001 overstates the certainty.

reporting_issues.issue: Two controls with high rates (31.0 and 14.0) were left out because a viral illness began within 24 hours of their sampling; the paper does not say when this decision was made or whether infections were looked for in the LSD and other-drug groups (the 1971 review calls the two retrospectively eliminated, p. 433).
reporting_issues.consequence: Including them lowers the difference from 9.3 to 6.6 breaks per 100 cells (editors' calculation) but does not remove it; the exclusion rule was applied to one group only.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods describe 4 to 6 cover slips of 50 metaphases per person (p. 1044), but five LSD patients had fewer than 200 cells scored (78 to 184) and so did two controls (100 and 182) and one excluded control (100) (Tables 1 and 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; some rates rest on few cells (case 2: 5 breaks in 78 cells).

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion takes the match between the patients' mean rate and the rates at 0.001 and 0.01 µg/ml as support that these are the concentrations cells meet in the body (p. 1047), but in Table 5 all five concentrations from 0.001 to 10 µg/ml gave similar rates (10.6 to 17.5, apart from 7.7).
reporting_issues.consequence: With no concentration-response, matching rates cannot identify the concentration reached in the body.

reporting_issues.issue: The group taking other drugs but no LSD is presented as exposed to the kinds of drugs LSD patients take (p. 1047), but five of the six had been taking medicines up to or shortly before sampling (chlorpromazine in four, thioridazine in one, diphenhydramine in two), two of them boys of 9; the one woman, taking chlorpromazine, had also used marijuana for 10 years, and only one man had a history of several non-medical drugs (Table 3); the group is not compared with the LSD group, whose rates were similar.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's own data do not separate LSD from other drugs and medicines; the comparison is left to the reader and was later presented by the 1971 review, as Cohen et al.'s, without a stated test.

reporting_issues.issue: Replicates are said to agree closely (p. 1047), but the child's two successive cultures gave 24 and 16.5 breaks per 100 cells.
reporting_issues.consequence: Within-person variation between cultures can be of the same size as the group difference; one culture per person can misplace a person by several points.

reporting_issues.issue: The children (aged 2 months to 5½ years) are compared only with adult controls (Table 4), and their raised rates are read as evidence that LSD crosses the placenta (p. 1048).
reporting_issues.consequence: Without unexposed children of the same ages, and with other drugs in pregnancy for three of the four, the children's rates cannot be attributed to LSD.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper does not say whether case 37 of Table 1 is the single patient of its own earlier report (ref. 2), whom he matches in sex, number of LSD treatments, interval since the last and phenothiazine treatment, nor whether the in vitro data of Table 5 include the earlier report's cultures, which every condition's larger counts and identical peak concentrations would allow.
reporting_issues.consequence: If either overlap holds, the two reports are not independent; the 1971 review counts both reports' in vitro data as separate studies (Table 1, p. 432) and would count the patient twice, once among 126 people given pharmaceutical LSD (Table 3, p. 433) and once among 184 exposed to illicit LSD (Table 2, p. 433).

design_detail: Cross-sectional cytogenetic comparison in a two-page Science report. Blood from 8 volunteers who said they had taken LSD-25 (an estimated 4 to 200 times) and from 9 volunteers who had not taken it was cultured for 72 hours; the samples were given random numbers and scored blind, 200 metaphases per person, for chromatid and isochromatid breaks, exchange figures, dicentric chromosomes and rings (Table 1), summarized per person as the percentage of abnormal cells and as breaks per 100 cells (Table 2). One sample per person and none from before LSD use; no statistical test is named.
can_establish: That in this laboratory, cultured white blood cells from these 8 men who reported taking LSD, scored without knowledge of group, had about twice the break rate of these 9 volunteers who had not taken it (23.6 against 11.9 breaks per 100 cells, editors' calculation), with overlapping ranges.
cannot_establish: Whether LSD caused the difference, or how large any effect of LSD is: there was no sample from before LSD use, the source and content of the LSD and the amounts are the participants' own estimates, some had also taken other hallucinogens that were not counted, the groups differ in sex and in reported x-ray exposure, age, infections and medicines are not reported, and how the volunteers were found is not described; cultured blood cells say nothing directly about dividing tissues, sperm or eggs, cancer or birth defects.

sample.recruitment: The paper says only that the subjects were selected at random from a volunteer group of people who used LSD-25 and from a cross section of volunteers who did not (p. 313, Text, 2nd paragraph); where the volunteers came from, how they were approached, how the random selection was made and how many declined are not reported. The authors worked at the Oregon Regional Primate Research Center and the University of Oregon Medical School (p. 314).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated beyond LSD use or its absence. X-ray exposure is reported afterwards, not as a criterion: none of the LSD group had x-ray treatment or diagnostic x-rays within several months of sampling, while two controls had (p. 313, Text, 4th paragraph).
sample.demographics: Sex only, from the case labels of Tables 1 and 2 (p. 314): LSD group 8 men; controls 6 men and 3 women. Age, race, occupation and health are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one sample per person). 200 cells were classified for every person (p. 313, Text, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 legend, p. 314).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers in both groups from an undescribed pool; the controls are a cross section of volunteers, not matched on anything reported; the groups differ in sex (no women in the LSD group); the two controls with the highest rates were the two with x-ray exposure (diagnostic x-rays of the head and neck 1 to 2 months before sampling, and x-ray treatment of the skin for acne 22 years earlier).

exposure.measurement: Self-report: for each person, the number of times LSD had been taken, the average and largest amounts and the days since the last dose, all given as estimates (Table 2, p. 314; the text calls the amounts estimated, p. 313). The source of the LSD is not stated and nothing was tested; no biological verification.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As estimated by the participants (Table 2, p. 314): 4 to 200 occasions; average amount 200 to 500 µg (the text says 200 to 600 µg, p. 313); largest single amount 400 to 2800 µg; last dose 1 to 180 days before sampling. Route not stated.
exposure.polysubstance: Some of the LSD group had also taken several doses of cannabis, mescaline or peyote, psilocybin or DMT, or combinations of these; how many people, which drugs and how much are not reported, and the list is garbled as printed (p. 313, Text, 4th paragraph). Alcohol, tobacco, other drugs and medicines are not mentioned for either group. Other drugs were not analysed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 1 to 180 days since the last self-reported LSD dose: 1 to 30 days for 6 of the 8, about 3 and 6 months for the other two (Table 2; p. 314, Text, 5th paragraph).

comparison.controls: Nine volunteers who had not taken LSD (6 men, 3 women), sampled and scored in the same way (Tables 1 and 2, p. 314).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No sample from before LSD use. Age, smoking, alcohol, other drugs, recent infections, medicines and occupational exposures are not reported for anyone; x-ray exposure is reported only for the two controls who had it.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported: the controls are described only as not having taken LSD (p. 313, Text, 2nd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: A 5-ml blood sample in heparinized tubes; 72-hour cultures at 37°C by a standard procedure (ref. 2, a method paper by the second author); Colcemid for the last 2 hours; bleu de Unna stain; well-spread metaphases chosen at ×125 and classified under oil immersion at ×1250; every cell chosen at low power was included; 200 cells per person (p. 313, Text, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: A break was a clear discontinuity of the chromatids: chromatid breaks (one chromatid) and isochromatid breaks (both, at the same point); single fragments counted as chromatid breaks, double fragments and a small Philadelphia-like (Ph1-like) chromosome as isochromatid breaks; dicentrics and exchange figures as two breaks; an exchange figure counted as one abnormality for the share of abnormal cells (p. 313, Text, 3rd paragraph). Gaps are not mentioned. Chromatid breaks, the kind most often produced by culture itself, make up 307 of the LSD group's 378 breaks and 174 of the controls' 215 (editors' sums from Table 1). The controls' average of 11.9 breaks per 100 cells (editors' calculation) was later criticized as unusually high (Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 433).
outcomes.operationalization: Two per-person measures out of 200 cells (Table 2, p. 314): the percentage of abnormal cells and the number of breaks per 100 cells (printed as 'Breaks (%)'). 'Damage' is a 'significant increase' at P < .05 for an individual person, with no test and no reference value named (p. 313, Text, 4th paragraph; Table 2 legend).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported; no test is named.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Samples were given random numbers and processed for chromosome assessment on a blind basis (p. 313, Text, 2nd paragraph); who scored, and how many scorers there were, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: No group means, test statistics or intervals are printed; the text gives P < .05 for six of the eight in the LSD group and one of the nine controls, each judged individually (p. 313, Text, 4th paragraph; Table 2 legend, p. 314). Editors' calculations from Table 2: breaks per 100 cells, LSD group mean 23.6 (SD 8.8; 378 breaks in 1600 cells) against 11.9 (SD 5.8; 215 in 1800 cells) in the 9 controls, a difference of 11.7 (Welch 95% interval 3.7 to 19.7; two-sided Mann-Whitney P about 0.009, ties corrected); abnormal cells 22.3% (357 of 1600) against 11.1% (200 of 1800), a difference of 11.2 points (3.9 to 18.5). Without the two controls with x-ray exposure, the controls average 9.4 breaks per 100 cells (difference 14.2, 6.8 to 21.6). Ranges overlap: LSD group 12.0 to 38.0, controls 7.0 to 25.0; 5 of the 8 LSD-group values lie within the controls' range, and all 8 lie above the control mean. Within the LSD group (n = 8), Spearman rank correlations with the break rate: self-estimated average amount 0.86 (P = 0.006), number of occasions 0.48, largest amount 0.42, days since the last dose -0.28 (four correlations tried).
analysis.selective_reporting: The statistical method, group means and any comparison of the groups are not reported; significance is asserted person by person without the test or the reference distribution. The authors call breakage unrelated to the number or size of doses, then single out the two people with the lowest average amount as the two without raised rates, and conclude that as few as four doses appear to induce abnormalities, a threshold read from one person (p. 313, Text, 5th paragraph; p. 314, Text, 8th paragraph).
analysis.power: Not reported. Eight against nine people; the editors' 95% interval for the difference in break rates is 3.7 to 19.7 per 100 cells.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Blind-scored cultured white blood cells from 8 men who reported taking LSD had about twice the break rate of 9 volunteers who had not taken it (editors' calculation), with overlapping ranges; two men in the LSD group showed Ph1-like chromosomes and three showed quadriradials; the control with x-ray treatment 22 years earlier had a rate as high as most of the LSD group. Nothing was measured before LSD use, and other drug use was not counted.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports a significant increase of abnormalities in six of eight people who used LSD against one of nine controls, and notes that the two without damage reported the lowest average dose (p. 313). The conclusion says it is too early to assess the significance of the findings, yet that the abnormalities "appear to be induced by as little as four doses of LSD-25" (p. 314, Text, 8th paragraph): a causal reading of a cross-sectional comparison without samples from before LSD use, with self-estimated amounts of LSD of unstated source, other hallucinogens in some, and controls of different sex make-up. The discussion links quadriradials to Fanconi's anaemia and Bloom's syndrome, inherited conditions with more cancer, and the Ph1-like chromosome to chronic myeloid leukaemia (p. 314, Text, 6th and 7th paragraphs), without any data on cancer in these people.

timeline.event: Cohen, Marinello and Back: LSD added to cultured white blood cells from two donors raised breaks per cell, and one patient with schizophrenia had 12 percent breakage 8 months after 15 LSD treatments; this report set out to test those observations in people who use LSD (p. 313, ref. 1).
This report: about twice the break rate in 8 volunteers who reported taking LSD as in 9 who had not, scored blind.

Loughman et al.: no chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use, scored by someone who did not know their drug histories; a note added in proof cites this report as a comparable study supporting the opposite conclusion.

Cohen, Hirschhorn and Frosch: 13.2 breaks per 100 cells in 18 patients with a history of LSD and other drugs against 3.8 in 12 controls, but similar rates in 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD; they cite this report for its dicentric chromosomes.

Sparkes et al.: no significant difference in breaks between 8 people exposed to LSD and 4 controls; they note that the laboratories reporting damage had higher control rates and less complete culture media.

Egozcue and Irwin (J Am Med Assoc 204, as the review cites it), the same laboratory's larger study: 18.76% in 46 people exposed to illicit LSD against 9.03% in controls, and raised rates in 3 of 4 children exposed before birth (as described by Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 432; not read).
Tjio et al.: 32 hospital patients sampled before and after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, slides scored blind: no significant change in the share of cells with aberrations.

Dishotsky et al., review: lists this report as positive (Table 2, p. 433: 8 people, 1600 cells, 23.4% against 11.9% in 9 controls; 11.0% for the controls in the text, p. 432), describes the participants as people using illicit LSD and the controls as people who did not use drugs, which the report does not state, and says these laboratories did not report chromatid- and chromosome-type changes separately, although this report's Table 1 does. The report prints no group means; its Table 2 gives 23.6 and 11.9 breaks per 100 cells (editors' calculation).

replication.where_it_stands: This was the first report of raised breakage in people who had taken LSD. The excess was matched in the same year by Cohen, Hirschhorn and Frosch and, as the 1971 review describes it, in 1968 by a larger study from this laboratory, but not by other laboratories with lower control rates or before-and-after samples (Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969). The 1971 review attributed the positive findings to illicit drug use in general rather than to LSD. No study read here sampled the same people before and after LSD use with an unexposed group sampled at the same times.

what_would_settle_it: Blood samples from the same people before and after LSD of known content, with an unexposed group of similar age and sex sampled at the same times, other drugs, medicines, infections and x-rays recorded for everyone in advance, coded slides scored by more than one reader, and a pre-specified comparison of group means; and, for any lasting or inherited harm, studies of dividing tissues and germ cells rather than cultured blood cells.

domains.note: No adjustment; the LSD group were all men against 6 men and 3 women; ages not reported; other hallucinogens in some of the LSD group, uncounted; alcohol, tobacco, medicines and infections not reported for anyone; x-ray exposure in two controls.
Self-estimated number of occasions and amounts of LSD of unstated source and unknown content; no verification.
Volunteers from an undescribed pool, said to be chosen at random by an unreported method; controls a cross section of volunteers with no matching.
None reported between the last dose and sampling (1 to 180 days).
200 cells for every person; all 17 people reported.

Samples numbered at random and scored blind, a strength; but the number of scorers is not stated, chromatid lesions that can arise in culture dominate, rings are scored by an unstated rule, and the control rate was high compared with other laboratories.
No test named and no group statistics; significance asserted person by person; a dose threshold drawn from one person.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E for an observational comparison of exposed and unexposed people. Blind scoring of randomly numbered samples and complete, internally consistent tables (Table 1's counts give Table 2's break rates for all 17 people) are strengths, so the difference in these 17 volunteers is credible as a measurement. The overall judgment is high because the exposure is self-estimated LSD use of unstated source, recruitment is not described, the groups differ in sex and in reported x-ray exposure, other drugs were not counted, and no statistical method is given. Citable for: the per-person rates of breaks and abnormal cells and the counts by type, scored blind; Ph1-like chromosomes in two and quadriradials in three of the LSD group, as observations. Not citable for: LSD causing chromosome damage, a dose threshold, or any risk of cancer or birth defects.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the mean estimated dose as between 200 and 600 µg (p. 313, Text, 5th paragraph), but the average amounts in Table 2 range from 200 to 500 µg (p. 314).

reporting_issues.issue: No statistical method is named: P < .05 is attached to individual people (six of eight, one of nine) in the text and, in Table 2's legend, to abnormal cells and breaks, without saying against what reference or with which test; no group means, test statistics or intervals are printed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The per-person classification cannot be checked, and the size and precision of the group difference had to be recomputed (editors' calculation: 11.7 breaks per 100 cells, 95% interval 3.7 to 19.7).

reporting_issues.issue: The authors say the percentage of abnormalities seemed unrelated to the number or size of doses, then single out the two people with the lowest average amount as the two without raised rates and conclude that as few as four doses appear to induce abnormalities, a threshold read from one person (pp. 313–314, Text, 5th and 8th paragraphs). In Table 2 the self-estimated average amount ranks closely with the break rate (Spearman 0.86, n = 8, editors' calculation), while the number of occasions, the largest amount and the days since the last dose do not.
reporting_issues.consequence: With eight self-estimates of drugs of unknown content and four measures to choose from, neither the absence of a relation nor a threshold can be read from these data; the 1971 review's statement that no positive study showed a dose relation (Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 433) does not fit this table's average amounts.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods count dicentrics and exchange figures as two breaks but say nothing of rings; Table 2's break rate for the one control with a ring (7.0) matches Table 1 only if the ring counts as two breaks.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the scoring rule is incompletely stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The list of other drugs is garbled as printed (cannabis followed by mescaline or peyote in brackets, then psilocybin or DMT, and combinations 'of the three'), and the number of people who took each is not given (p. 313, Text, 4th paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Other drug use in the LSD group cannot be described or taken into account.

design_detail: Double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled crossover trial with random, counterbalanced order (registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03604744), University Hospital Basel: 28 healthy participants (14 women, 14 men) each had five 25-h sessions at least 10 days apart, receiving placebo, LSD 100 µg and 200 µg (oral solution) and psilocybin 15 mg and 30 mg (capsules). Primary outcome: the 5 Dimensions of Altered States of Consciousness scale (5D-ASC), rated 24 h after dosing for peak effects. Also: visual analogue scales over 24 h, the Adjective Mood Rating Scale, Mystical Effects Questionnaires (MEQ43, MEQ30), onset, offset and duration of effects from a pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic link model, blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature, pupil size, the List of Complaints (adverse effects), cortisol, prolactin, oxytocin and BDNF, plasma LSD and psilocin over 24 h, and participants' guesses of the condition. Peak values analysed by repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests. Most statistics are in an online supplement that was not among the files read.
can_establish: That in 28 healthy, mostly drug-inexperienced volunteers in a hospital room, LSD 100 and 200 µg and psilocybin 30 mg produced peak self-rated effects that did not differ significantly on most scales, that LSD's effects started earlier and lasted longer (mean 9.3 and 11 h against 5.6 and 6.5 h for psilocybin 15 and 30 mg), that psilocybin 30 mg raised blood pressure and body temperature more and LSD raised heart rate more, and that acute adverse-effect scores rose with every active dose, under the doses this study chose.
cannot_establish: That the two drugs' effects are the same in kind (non-significant post hoc tests in 28 people are not evidence of equivalence, and most statistics are in an unread supplement); that LSD's faster onset belongs to the drug rather than to its liquid form (the authors attribute it to the formulation); how mushrooms, other doses, other settings or people with psychiatric conditions would respond; or any dose equivalence between the drugs, which the paper extrapolates from doses it did not test.

sample.recruitment: Word of mouth or a pool of volunteers who had contacted the research group because they were interested in a psychedelic trial; paid for participation (p. 1181, Methods and materials › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 25–65; exclusions: pregnancy; personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder (semi-structured clinical interview by a trained psychiatrist); medications that may interfere (e.g. antidepressants, antipsychotics, sedatives); chronic or acute physical illness; smoking more than 10 cigarettes a day; lifetime illicit drug use more than 10 times (cannabis excepted); illicit drug use in the last 2 months or during the study (urine tests). Alcohol limited to 10 standard drinks a week and one drink on the day before sessions (p. 1181).
sample.demographics: 14 men and 14 women; mean age 35 (SD 9.4) years, range 25–52. Prior use: 14 had used a psychedelic (LSD 11 people, 1–5 times; psilocybin 6, 1–3 times; 5-MeO-DMT 1, twice), 12 MDMA (1–5 times), 13 a stimulant (methylphenidate 2, amphetamine 9, cocaine 6), 1 2C-B, 1 ketamine; 10 had never used an illicit drug other than cannabis (p. 1181).
sample.attrition: Not reported as such; results are presented for 28 participants in every figure legend, and the F(3,81) of Table 1 matches 28 people with complete data (editors' check: 3 × 27 = 81).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers interested in psychedelic research, screened healthy, with at most 10 lifetime uses of illicit drugs other than cannabis and no personal or family history of major psychiatric disorder. People who use psychedelics outside studies, usually with more experience, other forms (such as mushrooms) and other settings, and people with psychiatric conditions, are not represented.

exposure.measurement: Given in the laboratory, double-dummy: LSD base (>99% purity) as an oral solution in units labelled 100 µg in 1 ml of 96% ethanol, analytically confirmed content 84.5 ± 0.98 µg (n = 10 samples); psilocybin (99.7% purity) in opaque capsules of 5 mg psilocybin dihydrate, confirmed content 4.61 ± 0.09 mg (n = 10); placebo solutions of ethanol only and capsules of mannitol (p. 1181, Study drugs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions, single oral doses in random order at 9:00 after baseline measures: placebo; LSD 100 µg; LSD 200 µg; psilocybin 15 mg; psilocybin 30 mg; at least 10 days between sessions (p. 1181). Doses are named by their nominal amounts; the measured LSD content was about 15% below the label, which the authors note was 11–14% lower than in their own earlier studies with the same formulation (p. 1185).
exposure.polysubstance: Illicit drug use in the past 2 months and during the study excluded by urine tests; alcohol limited; heavy smoking excluded (p. 1181).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Urine drug test at the start of each session; at least 10 days between sessions (p. 1181).

comparison.controls: Within-person: a placebo session and the other active conditions in the same 28 people; LSD and psilocybin compared directly under double-dummy blinding.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (crossover; equal numbers of women and men).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Expectations and prior psychedelic experience (half had used a psychedelic before) were not analysed as moderators.

outcomes.instruments: 5D-ASC (primary outcome; rated 24 h after dosing for peak effects); visual analogue scales 1 h before and at 22 time points to 24 h after dosing (e.g. any drug effect, good drug effect, bad drug effect, drug liking, feeling high, stimulated, fear, ego dissolution); Adjective Mood Rating Scale at 3, 6, 9, 12 and 24 h; States of Consciousness Questionnaire with MEQ43 and MEQ30 at 24 h; onset, time to maximum, offset and duration of the any-drug-effect response from a PK-PD link model (threshold 10% of each person's maximum); blood pressure, heart rate and tympanic temperature at baseline and 22 time points; pupil size and light reflex at baseline and six time points to 24 h; List of Complaints before and 12 and 24 h after dosing; cortisol, prolactin and oxytocin before and 2.5 h after; BDNF at baseline, 4, 6 and 12 h; plasma LSD and psilocin by UHPLC-MS/MS (p. 1181).
outcomes.validity_norms: Validated psychometric instruments (5D-ASC, MEQ43, MEQ30, Adjective Mood Rating Scale, List of Complaints) and visual analogue scales; detailed methods for the subjective measures are in the unread supplement.
outcomes.operationalization: Peak (Emax or Emin) or peak change from baseline; adverse effects as List of Complaints totals for 0–12 h (acute) and 12–24 h (subacute) and as spontaneously reported events within 48 h; duration from the model-predicted any-drug-effect curve.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Tukey post hoc tests within each outcome; no correction across the outcomes (at least 42 countable from the main text: 10 visual analogue items, 15 5D-ASC scores, 5 effect-time parameters, 6 autonomic measures, 2 adverse-effect scores and 4 hormones or markers, plus the MEQ and mood scales in the supplement).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind, double-dummy. Participants' guesses after each session: placebo identified in 96% of sessions; each active condition named correctly in 57–64% of sessions (p. 1184).

analysis.effect_sizes: No standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals; peak values and statistics for subjective, autonomic, adverse, endocrine and blinding outcomes are in Supplementary Tables S1–S8 (not read). Main text: Table 1 (mean ± SD, range; psilocybin 15 mg, psilocybin 30 mg, LSD 100 µg, LSD 200 µg): time to onset 0.8 ± 0.3, 0.8 ± 0.4, 0.6 ± 0.2, 0.4 ± 0.2 h (F(3,81) = 12.5); time to offset 6.4 ± 2.1, 7.3 ± 2.3, 10 ± 3.1, 11 ± 3.6 h (F = 31.2); effect duration 5.6 ± 2.2, 6.5 ± 2.4, 9.3 ± 3.2, 11 ± 3.7 h (F = 34.4); maximal effect 58 ± 25, 80 ± 18, 77 ± 18, 87 ± 13% (F = 20.0). Pharmacokinetics (geometric mean, range): LSD peak 1.9 (1.1–3.3) and 3.4 (1.6–5.8) ng/ml, half-life 4.3 (2.5–6.0) and 4.0 (2.3–7.1) h; psilocin peak 13 (7–21) and 25 (14–41) ng/ml, half-life 2.4 (1.7–3.1) and 2.7 (1.9–3.4) h. Ego dissolution 200 vs 100 µg LSD p < 0.05; anxiety trend p = 0.054; 15 mg psilocybin vs 200 µg LSD on any drug effect, good drug effect, stimulated, perception of time and ego dissolution p < 0.001.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03604744 (p. 1181). The registry record was not read, so agreement between registered and reported outcomes was not checked. The paper names the 5D-ASC as the primary outcome.
analysis.selective_reporting: Nearly all numbers for subjective, autonomic, adverse, endocrine, pharmacokinetic and blinding results are in the supplement (Supplementary Tables S1–S8); the main text reports mostly direction and significance. The rate-pressure product, on which the abstract bases its statement of comparable cardiostimulation, has no statistics in the main text.

interpretation_gap.results_show: LSD 100 and 200 µg and psilocybin 30 mg produced peak self-ratings that did not differ significantly on the visual analogue scales and 5D-ASC (psilocybin 15 mg gave clearly lower ratings); 200 µg LSD differed from 30 mg psilocybin only on MEQ ineffability; LSD's effects started earlier and lasted longer; psilocybin 30 mg raised blood pressure and body temperature more and LSD raised heart rate more; LSD raised emotional excitation on the mood scale more than psilocybin; acute adverse-effect scores rose with every active dose and subacute scores with the two higher doses.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that the alterations of mind induced by LSD and psilocybin do not differ beyond the duration of effects and that any differences depend on dose rather than substance (p. 1180). This rests on non-significant post hoc tests in 28 people without equivalence testing, while the paper itself reports substance differences in heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, pupil reflex, emotional excitation and onset. The discussion says the study was “well blinded” (p. 1185), yet placebo was recognised in 96% of sessions and each active condition was named correctly in 57–64% of sessions where guessing among five conditions would give 20% (p. 1184). The duration difference is said to be fully explained by pharmacokinetics (p. 1185) without a formal test. The abstract and conclusion derive a dose equivalence between the two drugs from doses that were not tested in this study, one of them taken from a separate study by the same group (pp. 1180, 1185–1186); the card does not record those figures, under the editors' rule against strength comparisons. The autonomic effects are called moderate, transient and not a safety concern (p. 1185) on the basis of screened healthy volunteers.

replication.where_it_stands: The authors present this as the first study comparing both drugs within the same people; it comes from one laboratory, whose other studies supply the dose-equivalence reasoning. No independent replication is cited.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized double-blind crossover comparison of the two drugs given in the same formulation, at several doses including those the authors propose as equivalent, in a larger and more drug-experienced sample, with pre-specified equivalence margins for the subjective scales and full reporting of adverse effects and blinding in the main paper.

domains.note: Random, counterbalanced order is stated; how the sequence was generated and concealed is not described.
At least 10 days between sessions, urine drug tests at each session, and half-lives of a few hours.

Double-dummy, but placebo was recognised in 96% of sessions and each active condition was named correctly in 57–64%; expectancy can shape self-ratings, though less so for comparisons between the two active drugs.
All 28 participants are presented; degrees of freedom fit complete data.
Self-ratings by participants who often knew their condition, the primary outcome rated retrospectively at 24 h; blood pressure, heart rate, temperature and drug levels are objective.
Registered (registry not checked); most statistics only in the supplement; many outcomes without correction across them; impossible values printed in Table 1 and the pharmacokinetics paragraph.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A registered, randomized, double-dummy crossover with all 28 participants analysed. Concerns: unblinding typical of psychedelic studies, self-rated outcomes, a supplement that holds most statistics, and several impossible printed values. The paper may be cited for the measured differences under the doses this study chose: earlier onset and longer duration of LSD's effects, similar peak self-ratings for LSD 100 and 200 µg and psilocybin 30 mg, greater blood-pressure and temperature rises with psilocybin 30 mg and greater heart-rate rises with LSD, and the adverse effects listed. It may not be cited as showing that the two drugs' effects are identical in kind, for any dose equivalence or comparison of strength, or for people other than screened healthy volunteers in a hospital.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 28 healthy volunteers (14 women, 14 men; mean age 35, range 25–52), half of whom had used a psychedelic before and 10 of whom had never used an illicit drug other than cannabis, each received placebo, LSD 100 µg, LSD 200 µg, psilocybin 15 mg and psilocybin 30 mg in random, counterbalanced order, double-blind and double-dummy, in five sessions at least 10 days apart in a hospital room with one investigator.

key_findings.finding: Doses as given: the LSD solution labelled 100 µg per unit contained 84.5 ± 0.98 µg on analysis (n = 10 samples), and the 5 mg psilocybin capsules contained 4.61 ± 0.09 mg (n = 10).

key_findings.finding: Peak subjective effects: LSD 100 and 200 µg and psilocybin 30 mg produced comparable effects, with no significant difference between psilocybin 30 mg and either LSD dose on any visual analogue scale or 5D-ASC subscale; 200 µg LSD differed from 30 mg psilocybin only on MEQ ineffability. LSD 200 µg produced more ego dissolution than 100 µg (p < 0.05) and a trend to more anxiety (p = 0.054). Psilocybin 15 mg gave significantly lower ratings than 200 µg LSD on any drug effect, good drug effect, stimulated, perception of time and ego dissolution (each p < 0.001), talkative (p < 0.01), and the 5D-ASC total and all main dimensions (p < 0.001).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints, for 100 µg LSD, a time to offset of 10 ± 3.1 h with range 6.3–8.8 h and a time to maximal effect of 2.5 ± 0.5 h with range 1.8–2.4 h: both means lie outside their own ranges, which is impossible.

reporting_issues.issue: The time to peak concentration for 100 µg LSD is printed as 1.6 h with range 1.75–3.0 h, a geometric mean below the range minimum.

reporting_issues.issue: The results say both LSD doses had an earlier onset than both psilocybin doses, but Table 1 marks the 100 µg LSD onset (0.6 h) as different only from psilocybin 30 mg (p < 0.05), not from 15 mg (0.8 h).
reporting_issues.consequence: The earlier onset holds for 200 µg LSD against both psilocybin doses and for 100 µg only against 30 mg; the authors in any case attribute it to the formulation.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says no clear distinction between LSD and psilocybin could be made, but its own percentages show the correct substance (either dose) was named in at least 86% of psilocybin 30 mg sessions, 78% of LSD 100 µg sessions and 79% of LSD 200 µg sessions (editors' calculation from the printed percentages; the full table is in Supplementary Table S8).
reporting_issues.consequence: Blinding between the two drugs was weaker than described, so expectancy could have contributed to self-rated similarities and differences.

reporting_issues.issue: Flashbacks are reported as nine episodes in five people with a parenthesis of one to 20 times within 72 h; what was counted is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The frequency of flashback-like experiences cannot be stated precisely.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 200 µg LSD induced more anxiety than 100 µg; the results text gives a trend (p = 0.054) without naming the instrument, while the Fig. 1 legend says the 5D-ASC anxiety subscale differed significantly.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the anxiety difference between the two LSD doses was significant depends on an instrument the results do not name; the card should not assign the trend to the visual analogue scales.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract bases its statement of comparable cardiostimulant properties on the rate-pressure product, for which the main text gives no statistics; in Fig. 3 the mean curve for 200 µg LSD peaks visibly above that for psilocybin 30 mg (approximate reading).
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim of comparable overall cardiovascular stimulation cannot be checked without Supplementary Table S5.

reporting_issues.issue: Doses are labelled 100 and 200 µg throughout, but the analysed LSD content was 84.5 µg per 100 µg unit, so the amounts given were about 85 and 169 µg (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed content is given in the methods and discussed on p. 1185, but the abstract, results and figures use the labels; comparisons with other studies by labelled amount are approximate.
